sources.title: Sam Parr on copywriting: long-form, AIDA, plain writing and copy work
sources.originalTitle: Level up your copywriting w/ Sam Parr | E2226
sources.summary: Sam explains why he obsessed over copywriting (sales on paper scales one-to-one selling) and which timeless principles still work: long copy, AIDA, fourth-grade writing, and hand-copying great sales pages. He also argues for leading with a feeling and the founder's story.

principles.text: Copywriting is sales on paper: it scales one-to-one selling to an unlimited audience.
principles.quote: if I could take my ability to sell one-to-one, which I eventually learned how to do, and put it on paper, you could sell one to an infinite number.

principles.text: Long copy usually beats short copy; the real enemy is boring, not length.
principles.quote: There's no such thing as too long. There's only such a thing as too uninteresting.

principles.text: Structure copy as AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action) so readers slide to one specific next step.
principles.quote: I want you to fall down this slippery slope where you start where you're interested, you get a little bit more desire, and finally I get you to take action.

principles.text: Write simply at a 4th-5th grade level (use Hemingway App), in active voice, without adverbs.
principles.quote: The goal is to write at a fourth or fifth grade reading level.

principles.text: Train by copy work: hand-write great sales pages or books word for word to absorb their texture.
principles.quote: You write it word for word. And you feel the texture of the words and that changes your brain and it changes what you do.

principles.text: Lead a page with a feeling and the founder's personal story, not a feature list.
principles.quote: Above the fold should be a feeling, I think.

sources.title: Sam Parr on copywriting: hooks, slippery slope, long copy and copy work
sources.originalTitle: Become a Dangerously Good Writer in 55 Minutes w/ Sam Parr
sources.summary: Sam Parr breaks down the copywriting frameworks he used at The Hustle and Hampton: punchy first lines, the curiosity gap, stories with the customer as hero, and short sentences. He also explains why long copy beats short if it's interesting, and how copy work builds taste.

principles.text: Each sentence only exists to get the next one read; the first line must punch.
principles.quote: the purpose of the first sentence is to get you read the second sentence and the purpose of the second sentence is to get you to read the third sentence and so on.

principles.text: Long copy converts better than short as long as it's interesting; boring is the real problem.
principles.quote: long will almost always convert better. Ugly will almost always convert better, but it just has to be interesting.

principles.text: Use stories to sell; there is no too long, only too boring.
principles.quote: There's no such thing as too long, just too boring.

principles.text: Make the customer the hero and your brand the guide.
principles.quote: a good brand positions themselves as the guide and the hero of the story is your customer.

principles.text: Write simply: one point per sentence, swap commas for periods, seventh-grade reading level.
principles.quote: usually when you need to have a comma, use a period. Short sentences uh are the best.

principles.text: Build taste by copying great work by hand for months until you learn its rules.
principles.quote: that's the number one thing to do is just to blindly copy until you find the rules of the language that you're trying to speak.

sources.title: How Sam Parr built The Hustle newsletter and how to reach $3M/year solo: math, writing, growth
sources.originalTitle: How YOU Can Build A $3,000,000 Newsletter Business Without ANY Employees! | Sam Parr
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how he went from HustleCon conferences to a daily newsletter that reached ~2M readers and sold to HubSpot. He covers the audience-value math (CPM, niche, B2B), copywriting practice with AIDA, early Reddit/blog growth, selling ads, and why risk-derisking and confidence matter.

principles.text: Learn writing through daily copy work: hand-copy great writing, keep a swipe file, then apply it to real sends.
principles.quote: I would spend an hour every day word for word writing it by hand and that's how I learned how to do it.

principles.text: Use the AIDA framework (attention, interest, desire, action) for everything you write or sell.
principles.quote: I like ADA, attention, interest, desire, action. Uh and that's like a way better format.

principles.text: Before choosing a newsletter niche, do the math: subscribers x sends per month x CPM. Niche and buyer spending power matter more than passion.
principles.quote: one makes two grand a month, one makes $1.2 million a month.

principles.text: Newsletter value is audience size times engagement/influence times the price of what they buy; B2B beats consumer.
principles.quote: number of people multiplied by how engaged they are... Multiplied by uh uh the price of the product.

principles.text: Write like a friend to one reader; personal tone builds the loyalty that makes ads sell.
principles.quote: The cool thing about a newsletter is you write it as if it's just me writing to you, not me to millions of people.

principles.text: Grow by going where your exact target reader already hangs out, with headline-first long-form content, and keep advertisers whole to drive repeat buyers.
principles.quote: with the advertising business as well as any other business, repeat customers is key.

sources.title: Sam Parr on newsletters, differentiation, and building Hampton to last
sources.originalTitle: The Secret to Building Companies That Last for Generations! w/ Sam Parr
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how he grew The Hustle to 100,000 subscribers with zero ad spend, then scaled it with paid acquisition and ad sales. He also covers why he built Hampton as a forever business, how niche B2B newsletters monetize, and why depth beats breadth in learning.

principles.text: Aim to be different, not better; perceived differentiation wins.
principles.quote: it's a lot better and easier to be different than it is better.

principles.text: Grow a newsletter by finding where your audience already lives and siphoning them over.
principles.quote: make a decision on where your market already exists and what content can you get can you create that gets popular on that channel and then you siphon them off into your newsletter.

principles.text: Once organic works, compute subscriber value and buy ads up to your payback window.
principles.quote: we calculated how much money each subscriber is worth to us and then we went and spent money on Facebook ads to acquire a customer to bring them onto our platform.

principles.text: Niche B2B newsletters monetize far better because advertisers can't reach those buyers elsewhere.
principles.quote: which industries can I enter where there's enough people buying ads but it's really hard you they can't spend it on Facebook

principles.text: Build a business you love enough to keep; compounding needs decades, not an exit.
principles.quote: huge growth and huge money, if you do it right, it should compound.

principles.text: Master a few books deeply instead of reading widely.
principles.quote: there's an overemphasis on breath of knowledge and not depth. And I think depth is where real value is created.

sources.title: Sam Parr on writing, copy and growth: how The Hustle got to 150K subscribers in year one
sources.originalTitle: Inside the Mind of a Newsletter Mogul (Sam Parr Interview)
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how he built The Hustle's newsletter audience: do the email math, siphon traffic from subreddits with viral stunts, and obsess over headlines and welcome copy. He also covers hiring writers, copy work, memorable phrasing, and defining what a brand stands against.

principles.text: Go where your target audience already gathers and siphon them off; use viral stunts in niche communities.
principles.quote: my whole strategy was go to where the people who you want already are and siphon them off

principles.text: Do the math on owned channels: email reaches a subscriber daily, unlike a website people must keep returning to.
principles.quote: if I get a million people to subscribe to my newsletter and I email them every day I bet you I could make like $2 million a month doing that

principles.text: Don't ignore the 'forgotten text' like thank-you pages and welcome emails; make them good.
principles.quote: that was like the whole trick was like the Forgotten text it always has to be good

principles.text: Study a company's early copy via the web archive, not its polished current version.
principles.quote: you got to go to web archive

principles.text: Headlines matter: you can lift click-through from 1% to 10%, and long pieces just need a slippery slope.
principles.quote: you got to spend time on the headline because you can change 1% to 10% pretty easily

principles.text: Hire writers by buying stock early: find people writing for fun and probe the bottom fourth of their resume.
principles.quote: I'm going to buy her stock early before the market finds out

sources.title: Sam Parr on plotting, bootstrapping Hampton, and building cash-flow businesses fast
sources.originalTitle: The Founder Creating Insane Internet Companies | Sam Parr
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how he validates and launches businesses: research obsessively, then act within 24 hours and sell by hand before building anything. He covers why he bootstraps Hampton, how to grow an email list, and copywriting via copy work.

principles.text: Plot hard before committing: research the market, then go all in and focus on one thing.
principles.quote: I plot hardcore. And so, like, before I started the Hustle, I was plotting. I spent like 12 months. I'm like, "All right. What are the economics of this?

principles.text: Do research by cold-calling bankers, founders, and ex-employees, and reading reviews.
principles.quote: I'll go and find out who the bankers were that sold the companies in the space and I'll just cold call them.

principles.text: Launch with a doc and a form, then sell hand-to-hand before building a website.
principles.quote: I created a Google Doc that outlined what it was. And at the bottom of the Google Doc, it was a Typeform that says if you're interested, fill this out.

principles.text: Do things manually first; Hampton hit millions in run rate before it had a website.
principles.quote: We got to many millions in sales before we even um or run rate before we even like had a website.

principles.text: Bootstrap when you can self-fund; owning most of a company beats raising for most wealth outcomes.
principles.quote: I think if you have a little bit of cash and you could self-fund it, I think you can get wealthier owning something.

principles.text: Don't do paid marketing until content is proven; paid growth hides a leaky bucket.
principles.quote: I think you shouldn't do any paid marketing until you have like 20, 30, 40,000 people.

sources.title: Sam Parr: Reddit growth hacks, collecting people, and building a decades-long business like Hampton
sources.originalTitle: Sam Parr's secret millionaire club is on track for $1B
sources.summary: Sam Parr tells how The Hustle got its first 100-150k subscribers through Reddit and Hacker News stunts, why he surrounds himself with more successful people, and why he now builds for decades with Hampton. He also covers cold outreach, media versus product businesses, and how to pick a next company.

principles.text: Be around people far more successful than you; the gap in ability is much smaller than the gap in results, which builds confidence.
principles.quote: they are not 10 times smarter than me some of them were but most are not but they're like 10 or 20 times more successful than I am

principles.text: Early audience growth: write stunt-style posts built to rank in specific subreddits, then convert the traffic with a strong pop-up.
principles.quote: I would write these blog posts that I thought would like go quote viral or rank high in a particular subreddit

principles.text: It's easier to build media around a product people love than to start with media and bolt a product on.
principles.quote: I think it's easier to have a product that people love and then to build media around it than it is to have media and then build a product around it

principles.text: Cold outreach works when it shows finished results, not ideas or offers to work for free.
principles.quote: it's far more interesting where it's like I've already done X Y and Z here's the website and here's the results

principles.text: Before a second company, research many industries methodically and interview founders, employees and customers before committing.
principles.quote: create like a notion dock of different categories of styles of companies and go and research them like crazy and go and interview the founders

principles.text: To build something that lasts, anchor on what customers will always want, as Amazon did, then innovate within that.
principles.quote: they're like what will customers always want they're always going to want cheap prices fast shipping and a large select selection of stuff so like let's just build our business on top of that

sources.title: The 5 levels of making money: Sam Parr on $10K to $100M and what changes at each stage
sources.originalTitle: The 5 Levels of Making Money ft. Sam Parr
sources.outlet: Grant Owen and My First Million
sources.summary: Sam Parr walks through the stages from $10K to $100M. Early on it's selling a service, asking for money and cold emailing. At the middle stages you need distribution, hiring and systems. Past $10M it's time and patience. He also covers copywriting, peers, intentional goals and integrity.

principles.text: The easiest first $10K is a service: do it free for 2-3 companies, get a testimonial, then charge. Ask for the money and price higher than you think.
principles.quote: it would probably be finding two or three companies that need a service, doing it to them for free, asking for a testimonial, and getting proof, and then going and charging for that service.

principles.text: Copywriting is the most valuable skill at any stage because it's just sales: getting what's in your head into someone else's and moving them to act.
principles.quote: copywriting is the act of figuring out how to get what's in my brain into your brain and figuring out how to get you to do what I want you to do.

principles.text: Cold outreach is a numbers game. Follow up relentlessly (he emailed one speaker 52 times) and use attention, interest, desire, action.
principles.quote: I emailed him 52 times. And on the 52nd one, he was like, "Yeah, sure."

principles.text: Past roughly $100K a month you need real distribution (audience, ads, cold email or calls, conferences). Reaching 3-5M is straightforward, past that you need teams, systems and leadership.
principles.quote: getting to like 3, four, 5 million is a pretty straightforward path. Getting past five, six, seven million, that requires uh teams and systems and leadership and that is challenging.

principles.text: Hiring is the highest leverage for a founder. Hire people strong where you're weak, and keep doing sales and marketing yourself until about $5M.
principles.quote: the highest form of leverage for an entrepreneur is hiring.

principles.text: Most businesses can reach $10M+ if you stay patient and build systems. The common failure is impatience, quitting something that's working.
principles.quote: I will say every single business or service or product can get to 10 million in revenue.

sources.title: Sam Parr: Why he bootstrapped Hampton instead of raising VC, and how he designs a business around a rich life
sources.originalTitle: Sam Parr:"I Failed to Raise Money, So I Built a $20M+ Company Instead" | The Further, Faster Podcast
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains why he chose not to raise venture capital for Hampton, how he reverse-engineers a business from constraints (Ikigai plus email CPM math), and why aligning co-founders on lifestyle non-negotiables up front matters. He also covers prioritizing audience over advertisers, protecting community quality, and timing exits for liquidity.

principles.text: Bootstrapping fits founders who want freedom and money for themselves; VC fits those who want to go huge. Pick deliberately.
principles.quote: My thought is if your main goal is freedom and like making money for yourself, bootstrapping is 100% the way to go.

principles.text: Your cap table is one of the few business mistakes you can't undo; raising money commits you to optimizing for investor returns.
principles.quote: there's basically like only maybe one or two mistakes in business that you can't undo, and your cap table's one of them.

principles.text: Choose a business model that doesn't need outside capital: charge up front and use that cash to improve the product.
principles.quote: we purposely picked like a business model where we didn't need to raise money. And so, the constraint was, we don't want to raise money, so what can we do without raising money?

principles.text: Design a business from hard constraints: market CPM, your skills, what you love, and what the world will pay for.
principles.quote: it's what's the world want, what's the world willing to pay for, what am I good at, what do I love doing? And you get something right in the middle.

principles.text: Get specific about your ideal life with co-founders up front, including what you won't sacrifice, before building together.
principles.quote: Okay, we are unwilling to sacrifice family time. Okay, cool. So, if we I'm I'm on board with that, he's on board with that.

principles.text: Prioritize your core audience over advertisers; it costs revenue short term but earns more long term.
principles.quote: I think you ultimately do make more in the end if you are like appeal to a very particular type of person.

sources.title: Sam Parr on insecurity as fuel, delegating to a CEO, and a boring daily routine
sources.originalTitle: From Hot Dog Stand to Millions: The Untold Story of Sam Parr
sources.summary: Sam Parr tells Andrew Wilkinson how he went from a hot dog stand to The Hustle exit, MFM and Hampton. He covers why feeling inadequate drives ambition, why meeting successful founders removed his fear, hiring a CEO to run Hampton, and the narrow circle of trust and fixed routines he keeps.

principles.text: Admire peers instead of tearing them down; aim to build your own skyscraper next to theirs.
principles.quote: I don't want to crush your Tower it's like I want to have a skyscraper just as big because I want to feel adequate

principles.text: Successful people are as flawed and fearful as you, so don't let them intimidate you out of competing.
principles.quote: the people I admire are screw-ups and fearful just like I am and it felt like I used to have bad eyesight and once I met these people and got to intimately know them I put good eyeglasses on

principles.text: Hire a CEO to run daily operations while you focus on the few things where you add the most value, like marketing and spotting opportunities.
principles.quote: I'm like the marketing department because I've got the podcast and I've got my personality whatever you want to call my brand and that drives growth

principles.text: Delegating people problems is a big upside; you still work as much but only on high-value work.
principles.quote: I only focus on things that I actually add a significant amount of value towards

principles.text: Build a small, fully trusted inner circle and be guarded with everyone else.
principles.quote: it's important you just have this tight tribe

principles.text: Seek time freedom: work hard for a short period so you can spend your time how you want.
principles.quote: the best way to win is to have enough money that you could tell anyone to go [ __ ] themselves and I could spend my time how I want

sources.title: Sam Parr: audience vs community, pricing high, and building brand before spreadsheets
sources.originalTitle: How Sam Parr Retired With Over $20 Million by Age 31 | 019
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains why he sold The Hustle to HubSpot and what he changed building Hampton. He covers prioritizing brand over finance early, charging more, launching businesses to an audience, and the real difference between an audience and a community.

principles.text: Ignore admin early; brand and product are the parts you can't fix later.
principles.quote: the brand stuff and like the making the product that stuff you can't figure out later you got to nail that

principles.text: Get a first sale before spending on domains or legal setup.
principles.quote: go and get a sale or collect some type of money for your for your product before you even have a domain name

principles.text: An audience is one-to-many; a community is many-to-many and grows without you.
principles.quote: an audience is one to many it's Nick posting videos it's Sam posting a podcast a community is many to many

principles.text: First-time founders underinvest in marketing and distribution, and underprice.
principles.quote: a lot of first-time entrepreneurs they care about like product and stuff like that which is important but not enough about marketing and distribution so like getting eyeballs and customers

principles.text: Price high enough to fund a good service and acquire customers; go upmarket.
principles.quote: in order to make the service good I had to charge a lot of money

principles.text: Build an audience, then launch real businesses to it instead of just selling ads.
principles.quote: instead I think you should launch businesses to your audience and I think that that's a really interesting move

sources.title: How Sam Parr vets business ideas: back-of-envelope math and a free research toolkit
sources.originalTitle: How Sam Parr Comes Up With $10,000,000 Dollar Business Ideas (#62)
sources.summary: Sam argues ideas matter for people who actually ship, and that you vet them with quick back-of-envelope math plus lots of cheap research, not spreadsheets. He shares his research stack (Companies House, SimilarWeb, annual reports, Web Archive), how he cold-emails mentors, and why fear makes companies boring.

principles.text: Ideas matter for people who actually ship; if you only talk, send the link when it's live.
principles.quote: if you do have the skill of doing, which I would say all three of us have that I, I think ideas do matter because if you are trying to build something that grows quickly, you don't wanna put yourself down the wrong path.

principles.text: Vet ideas with back-of-envelope math. Detailed spreadsheet modeling early is fear-driven procrastination.
principles.quote: you just need back of the envelope math.

principles.text: Check a big player already exists in the market to confirm the idea is physically big enough, then add your own flavor.
principles.quote: I look at like, well who else out there is in the market? Well, how big are they? Oh, they're a billion dollars in revenue? Okay, I know that it's physically possible that this is a big enough idea.

principles.text: Research constantly with free tools like Companies House, SimilarWeb, annual reports and Web Archive to see how businesses really work.
principles.quote: I use annualreports.com, I use Similar Web, and I use Company's House.

principles.text: Test demand cheaply before building: a tiny version plus a few hundred dollars of ads can validate a business.
principles.quote: I spent $500 promoting the story and at the bottom of the website it said pay $5 a month to get part two

principles.text: Don't operationalize a new initiative too early; pilot small so people feel free to take risks and be weird.
principles.quote: I think a lot of times people, companies do boring stuff is because they're trying to operationalize things too much too early.

sources.title: Sam Parr on building media and communities: study winners, narrow niche, avoid ads-only revenue
sources.originalTitle: Sam Parr on The Hustle, Hampton & Why the OpenAI-TBPN Deal Was a Mistake
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how he reverse-engineers successful businesses, builds from a narrow niche, and uses staged goals and stakes to scale. He covers newsletter and podcast content tradeoffs, the founder growth stage shift around $10M revenue, and how Hampton plans to scale through trained local moderators.

principles.text: Become a historian of your category: study winners and losers, copy what works, avoid what drags them down, then apply it in your own niche.
principles.quote: you kind of have to become a historian for like 6 months and you're like, tell me everything about every company. Then you find the first employees and then you find current employees and you go and interview them

principles.text: Set a far goal (Z), then focus only on the next step, and only after reaching it define the next one.
principles.quote: I create a Z goal. So for you that let's just say hypothetically it's 50 million in revenue by year. In five years, I want to be at 50 million in revenue.

principles.text: Use stakes and systems, not discipline, to force yourself toward a goal.
principles.quote: I think that you need stakes. I think without stakes, it's almost impossible to get like discipline is not nearly enough.

principles.text: Founder problems change near $10M revenue: below it money problems dominate, above it hiring and scaling problems do.
principles.quote: between 3 million and 10 million in revenue, those people talked about money problems a lot. After 10 million, it's about hiring problems and scaling problems.

principles.text: To get attention as a startup, pick a super narrow, jargon-filled niche, post daily, and be clear about who you do not appeal to.
principles.quote: Pick a super niche, narrow field, probably one that you think is too small, and share about it every single day.

principles.text: Don't depend on advertising as the main revenue source; it creates conflicts with telling the truth.
principles.quote: I'm not against advertising. I just don't want it to be the main way that I make money.

sources.title: Sam Parr: Selling The Hustle to HubSpot and growing a newsletter to 2M subscribers
sources.originalTitle: Sam Parr - Growing to 2M Subscribers and Selling Your Newsletter - The Nathan Barry Show 030
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle grew to nearly 2M subscribers, what due diligence on the HubSpot sale was like, and how he hires and hands off. He gives concrete advice on paid newsletters: charge more, bill annually, and use a long-form sales page as your homepage.

principles.text: Charge far more for paid newsletters; higher prices raise revenue and make customers value the product more.
principles.quote: If you actually want to make a living at this and provide value, you got to charge more money. How are you going to make a living if you're charging $4 a month?

principles.text: Push annual billing only; if you offer monthly, price it high as an anchor so annual is a no-brainer.
principles.quote: if you're going to awfully offer a monthly price, make it like crazy expensive so it puts an anchor so it makes the annual a no-brainer.

principles.text: Make a long-form sales page your homepage and gate checkout behind an email capture to build a lead list.
principles.quote: I would make it so you have to enter your email to see the next the checkout page because what's the average conversion rate? Like 3%, but you can collect probably 10 or 12% of those people's email

principles.text: Finding acquisition sources matters as much as content; co-registration partnerships can be paid per lead or only for engaged users.
principles.quote: people think if you have good content, you're going to make it. It's acquiring users is it's like is as important as the content.

principles.text: Start new things yourself, then hand them to skilled operators, set targets, and only step in when asked for help.
principles.quote: I'm the type of guy who I like to start stuff and then hand it off.

principles.text: Study profitable direct-response operators like Agora and Motley Fool and apply their tactics ethically, rather than copying Substack peers.
principles.quote: let's figure out what they're doing that's really good and make apply that to a good product with a high integrity team.

sources.title: Sam Parr on money, sobriety, and what "enough" means after selling The Hustle
sources.originalTitle: Finding Enough, Getting Sober, and Improving Your Life | Sam Parr (My First Million)
sources.summary: Sam Parr talks with Ryan Holiday about setting a $20M goal at 24 and hitting it by 31, why he still wants more, and why success never feels like arriving. He also covers investing in the business machine, email newsletters as a business model, buy-it-for-life, and getting sober. Mostly mindset, with a few sharp business lessons.

principles.text: Set a concrete number goal, work backwards from it, and hit it.
principles.quote: what sum do I need to have that I could spend that if I wanted to and never run out of money for the rest of my life and I came up with that number roughly $20 million and so I said by 30 I want to post post tax have that invested

principles.text: Spend on a business machine that turns $1 into more than $1. Treat spend as investment.
principles.quote: if I have a machine that turns $1 into $150 I want to spend all of my money into that machine

principles.text: Build a machine whose output exceeds its input. Costs rising alongside revenue is fine.
principles.quote: there's an input and then you have to build a machine that has the output that's higher than the input and that's actually kind of easy to do or rather it's simple to do

principles.text: Monetize early, because you need money to keep making the thing and attention fades.
principles.quote: is your product good and they're like yeah I'm like do you want to keep doing it yeah yeah then [ __ ] Char money and make money so you can continue doing it

principles.text: Email newsletters are a great business: few people, huge reach, high revenue per send.
principles.quote: is the email newsletter potentially one of the greatest business models of all time

principles.text: Success never feels like arriving. Even top founders feel insecure, so you can be insecure and still succeed.
principles.quote: it's awesome that I can be insecure and good at my job and succeed

sources.title: How Sam Parr launched Hampton, a founder peer network, to ~$1M ARR with no website
sources.originalTitle: Why Sam Parr is Building a $100M Community for Founders
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how he and co-founder Joe Spiser tested demand with a public tweet, personally called every respondent, and sold group spots through a Stripe link before building anything. He covers co-founder alignment, designing groups around fast vulnerability, selective admissions, and why hiring a CEO too early backfired.

principles.text: Validate demand by publicly posting a generic offer and counting replies. If one audience doesn't respond, switch audiences.
principles.quote: And I got like another 300 replies. And I started calling them and they were like, "Take my money. I'm in."

principles.text: Skip the website and polish at the start. Personally interview every lead and take payment through a simple link.
principles.quote: I had the 300 people on that list. I called all of them and I interviewed 100% of them and at the end of the interview it was like Joe I think this person wants in.

principles.text: Before partnering, each person writes answers to the same questions separately (goals, limits, values), then compare them.
principles.quote: I put it in a document and I go, "Copy this document and you go write your answers. I'll go write my answers."

principles.text: Design community experiences for speed to vulnerability. Candid, confrontational-with-love conversations create the value.
principles.quote: it's speed to vulnerability. I think that's like the key is how do I make someone break really fast?

principles.text: Don't grow for growth's sake. Curate who gets in and be willing to turn away money to protect the product.
principles.quote: you can't grow for growth's sake. I can't just throw people into this. That will ruin it.

principles.text: Don't hire a CEO to hand off a problem you're intimidated by. Handing off out of fear is abdication, not delegation.
principles.quote: I also think I was intimidated a little bit by the opportunity and how to pull it off. And so I wanted to hand that off to someone which is uh not a good reason probably to hire someone.

sources.title: Community building: why Sam Parr says start low-friction, run it as a dictatorship, and charge more
sources.originalTitle: The “Build A $100 Million Community” Playbook - Sam Parr, My First Million | INBOUND 2023
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how he thinks about building paid communities (Hustle Trends, Hampton). He separates an audience from a community, says to launch where people already are, seed it with a leader posting daily, scale slowly and meticulously, and charge more than you think. He backs it all with simple back-of-the-envelope math.

principles.text: If content stops and conversation doesn't continue without you, you have an audience, not a community.
principles.quote: if you quit creating content for like two or three weeks does more conversations happen when you're gone than when you were there if not you have an audience not a community

principles.text: Start a community in the lowest-friction place, where your people already are (Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, Facebook), not a new site or app.
principles.quote: you should start a community in the lowest friction place

principles.text: Seed it by posting daily yourself and getting smart friends to post; real traction took about six months before members commented on their own.
principles.quote: I would post in there every single day for like a year

principles.text: You need a cult-leader-style founder who embodies the culture and is constantly active, setting norms like a CEO would.
principles.quote: you need a leader who embodies it's basically like a cult you need like your cult leader who like embodies like the rituals and the culture

principles.text: Grow slowly and meticulously: let people in deliberately and indoctrinate them with norms, because a community that scales too fast loses its culture.
principles.quote: if it gets too big and and too fast it sucks and there's no culture and there's no soul to it

principles.text: If the community is the business, charge real money, more than you think. Underpricing ($300/yr) forced huge member counts and weaker service.
principles.quote: if you want Community to be the business my opinion you have to charge money and you should probably charge more money than you think

sources.title: Sam Parr on cold email, copy work and long-form copy: AIDA, 50 follow-ups, picking businesses
sources.originalTitle: The Cold Email Formula That Made Over $1,000,000 with Sam Parr | Horizons Pod
sources.outlet: Horizons Marketing Podcast with Nate Desmond
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how copy work trained his writing, why long-form copy and simple stories convert, and how he writes cold emails with attention, interest, desire, action plus heavy follow-up. He also covers going viral by angering a segment, and hiring by reading people's writing.

principles.text: Write cold emails with AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action, ending on one very specific ask.
principles.quote: the best way to write a cold email is to use this thing called ADA. It's it means attention, interest, desire, action.

principles.text: Follow-ups are the key to cold email; persistence reaches almost anyone.
principles.quote: you're like 50 cold emails away from like everyone on Earth. Like one initial email and 49 follow-ups. Like the follow-up is key.

principles.text: Make follow-ups useful: send event updates and social proof, not nagging.
principles.quote: I would just update them on like the current event of how things were going.

principles.text: Long-form copy converts best because it answers every objection and stories make people feel.
principles.quote: you want to overcome every objection a buyer has. So you need to give them lots of information

principles.text: To go viral, deliberately anger a certain group; make some people love you and others mad.
principles.quote: If you want to go viral with content, the goal should be to piss off a certain type of person.

principles.text: Learn writing by copying great work word for word to absorb rhythm and patterns.
principles.quote: So you just copy word for word writing that you love

sources.title: How Sam Parr Builds Businesses: deal climbing, pricing, focus and zero friction
sources.originalTitle: How Sam Parr Builds Businesses (like The Hustle)
sources.summary: Sam Parr traces his climb from $10 hot dogs to the Hustle's sale to HubSpot, showing how each larger deal came from delivering more value. He covers copywriting, pricing mistakes, selling to early advertisers, negotiating an acquisition, staying focused, and cutting friction when starting.

principles.text: Price by value delivered: you take a small fraction of the value, so higher-value offers justify higher prices.
principles.quote: it's all about value given so the value you get from one meal isn't significant the value that you get from finding a place to live is quite high

principles.text: Copywriting is the most important skill: understand what motivates people and use it to persuade them.
principles.quote: copywriting is the most important skill not only in business but life

principles.text: Avoid the $299 no-man's-land price. Go clearly cheap (impulse buy) or much higher, since buyers at $299 would pay far more.
principles.quote: i should have charged either 99 or 2 000 3.99 or 299 is no man's land

principles.text: Pre-sell with a simple document and strong copy before building. Trends took $50K in pre-sales from a Word doc.
principles.quote: we actually had fifty thousand dollars in pre-sales just from like a word document that explained what it was

principles.text: In an acquisition conversation, surface all your flaws up front to flush out dealbreakers fast and remove their later leverage.
principles.quote: i'm going to email you a list of all the reasons why you shouldn't buy us and if any of those are red flags we can continue talking

principles.text: Small companies beat big ones on speed and focus. Pick one metric, review it weekly, and say no to everything else.
principles.quote: small companies we really only have two advantages over big companies which is speed and focus

sources.title: How Sam Parr ran a sold-out 120-person event for $1,090 profit
sources.originalTitle: How to Make Money Hosting a Conference
sources.summary: Sam Parr's 2014 breakdown of hosting Bootstrap LIVE, a 3-hour meetup. He explains landing a "whale" speaker first, standing out with a handwritten letter, getting a free venue by appealing to the host's interests, selling tickets through free channels, and the actual P&L.

principles.text: Land one credible anchor first; make it effortless for them to say yes by pre-building the event page.
principles.quote: Before we even asked him we created the event page on Eventbrite with all the details like speakers, schedule, location, and stuff like that.

principles.text: Stand out to busy, in-demand people with a personal gesture and make the benefit to them crystal clear.
principles.quote: In Andrew’s case, it was a handwritten letter and bottle of scotch. In the letter, we made it very, very, very clear about how this event would benefit him.

principles.text: Pick speakers who are real practitioners with great stories, not self-proclaimed experts.
principles.quote: We wanted accomplished people who were actually experts in their field, had a great story, and were genuinely nice and fun people

principles.text: Get free venues by pitching what's in it for them; people only care about their own interests.
principles.quote: NO ONE CARES ABOUT YOU…THEY ONLY CARE ABOUT THEMSELVES.

principles.text: Map every free channel up front and trade free tickets for promotion; word of mouth sells most tickets.
principles.quote: Besides $50 in Facebook ads, all of the advertising was free.

principles.text: Set a clear purpose, write a plan, then over-prepare and sweat the details; ignorance of how events usually go helps.
principles.quote: Once we had a plan we executed like crazy.

sources.title: Write for a 5th grader: Sam Parr's copywriting rule for making people keep reading
sources.originalTitle: How To Use Words To Get People To Do What You Want Them To Do
sources.summary: A 2015 essay on writing that gets people to act. Sam's core rule: write like you're talking to a 5th grader, using short words, short sentences, and short paragraphs so each sentence earns the next. He also lists the books, courses, and tools he used to study persuasion.

principles.text: Write as if to a 5th grader: one or two syllable words, short sentences, short paragraphs.
principles.quote: whenever you write, act like you’re writing to a 5th grader.

principles.text: Each sentence has one job: get the reader to read the next sentence.
principles.quote: the point of the first sentence is to get you to read the second sentence. And the point of the second sentence is to get you to read the third sentence.

principles.text: Good copy creates a slippery slope where the reader melts into the text.
principles.quote: A well written email, blog post, or book creates a slippery slope. The reader melts away into the copy.

principles.text: You don't need to be a great writer; studying human psychology is what beats most people.
principles.quote: I don’t consider myself a great writer. My grammar sucks. I am notorious for typos. But I am better than most.

principles.text: Learn persuasion by studying what makes humans tick, not just grammar.
principles.quote: Because I study humans and what makes them tick.

principles.text: Use a readability tool like Hemingway App and aim for a 5th grade level while writing.
principles.quote: Use Hemingway App while writing. Aim for a 5th grade level.

sources.title: How to make ideas stick: Sam Parr's six-principle Made to Stick cheat sheet
sources.originalTitle: How to make ideas stick forever
sources.summary: A 2014 essay where Sam Parr summarizes Made to Stick into six principles (simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, story) with examples from his own campaigns. Useful as a basic messaging and content framework, especially for finding the core, naming people to drive shares, and appealing to self-interest and identity.

principles.text: Find the single core of your message and put it first; cut everything not 100% needed.
principles.quote: Use the technique of the inverted pyramid from journalism: Tell most important aspect first, then tailor, then add details. This forces prioritization.

principles.text: Name the people or companies in your content; the ones you mention are the ones who share it.
principles.quote: We implemented this principle in The Typical Roommates Infographic and The Holiday Gift Guide. The people who shared this most were the folks mentioned in the infographic.

principles.text: Make ideas concrete: something people can see or sense beats an abstract number.
principles.quote: Something becomes concrete when it can be described or detected by the human senses.

principles.text: Always pitch the reader's benefit. Say "you", not "people", and sell the outcome, not yourself.
principles.quote: ALWAYS appeal to your reader, user, or customer’s interest. Use the word “you” not “people.” Remember: no one cares about YOU…they only care about themselves.

principles.text: People decide based on identity, not logic, so frame messages around who they are or want to be.
principles.quote: People does not make decisions rationally, they make them based on identity.

principles.text: Collect stories as you come across them and save them for later rather than trying to invent them.
principles.quote: The best way to use a story is to always be on the look out for them. Think of a good idea for a story? Write it down and save it for later.

sources.title: The reciprocity rule: how a $1.99 Coke saved $400 on a Craigslist motorcycle
sources.originalTitle: I saved $400 using human engineering…here’s how.
sources.summary: A 2014 Sam Parr essay on using the reciprocity rule in negotiation. Give a small, unrequested gift before you ask for something, and the other person feels indebted. He shows it with a Coke on a motorcycle deal, a free speaking slot, and tipping and donation data.

principles.text: If you want something from someone, do them a favor or give a gift first, even an unrequested one.
principles.quote: If you want something from someone, do them a favor or give them a gift first…even if they don’t ask for it.

principles.text: Gifts work especially well on counterparties braced for a fight, because kindness catches them off guard.
principles.quote: Sellers are ready to go to war. They anticipate lowballers, tire-kickers, and flakes…so when a prospective buyer does something nice for you, even if it’s as small as smile and give you a Coke, you’re completely caught off guard with the kindness.

principles.text: Judge cheap tactics by expected value; a small cost is worth it if it even modestly raises your odds.
principles.quote: I’m willing to give a $1.99 gift even if it only increases the chances by 30%.

principles.text: Use gifts to land high-value asks: a thoughtful gift plus a handwritten note got a popular speaker to waive his fee.
principles.quote: I landed Andrew Warner, a popular internet personality, to speak at my conference for free by first giving him a bottle of scotch and a handwritten letter as a gift and then asking if he’d speak.

principles.text: Reciprocity is measurable: candy with the bill raised tips, and a delayed second piece raised them most.
principles.quote: Waiters who give a piece of candy with the bill get 3.3% larger tips. Waiters who give two pieces of candy get 14.1% larger tips. Waiters who delayed the action of giving the second piece of candy, for emphasis, raised tips by 23%.

principles.text: Give for real reasons, not just as manipulation; gift giving is good regardless of what you get back.
principles.quote: Gift giving is GOOD…regardless if you get something from it or not. Don’t use this powerful tool to become an evil genius.

sources.title: Sam Parr's best business books: Titan, 48 Laws, Carnegie, Sugarman, Cialdini
sources.originalTitle: The Best Business Books Ever (Updated 2019)
sources.summary: A 2017 reading list from Sam's old blog naming the business books that shaped him. His emphasis falls on perseverance, networking by being interested in others, and copywriting and persuasion as the core skills of business. Light on tactics, but it shows what he values.

principles.text: Copywriting is the single most important skill a businessperson can have.
principles.quote: Learning how to use the written word to communicate effectively is, hands down, without a doubt, no questions asked THE most important skill any business person can have.

principles.text: Learning to influence others is essential because copywriting is the top business skill; study persuasion research.
principles.quote: Copywriting is the most important business skill you can develop. Because of that, learning how to influence others is essential.

principles.text: Perseverance is the quality most essential to success; it overcomes almost everything.
principles.quote: I do not think that there is any other quality so essential to success of any kind as the quality of perseverance. It overcomes almost everything, even nature

principles.text: Make friends by getting interested in other people rather than trying to get them interested in you.
principles.quote: You can make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you.

principles.text: Good copy should pull readers through it so they can't stop until they finish.
principles.quote: Your readers should be so compelled to read your copy that they cannot stop reading until they read all of it as if sliding down a slippery slope.

principles.text: Understand how power and ruthless players operate, since they can damage your career even if they self-destruct.
principles.quote: many people live by a very different set of rules, and while most of these folks eventually self-destruct, they can inflict severe damage on our personal and professional lives in the process.

sources.title: How to measure risk: write out worst cases and plan around each before taking a leap
sources.originalTitle: How to measure risk
sources.summary: A 2017 essay where Sam Parr lays out his process for deciding on a risky move like quitting a job for a startup. List the worst-case scenarios, build a contingency plan for each, and only then weigh the upside. Writing it down shows that downsides are usually smaller than they feel.

principles.text: Most people are bad at analyzing risk; use a deliberate process instead of gut emotion.
principles.quote: I think most people are HORRIBLE at measuring risk…

principles.text: Start by writing out the exact risk you're deciding on, then list the possible worst-case scenarios.
principles.quote: Write out the risk you’re deciding on.

principles.text: For each worst case, decide if you could be happy if it happened. If not, build solutions that make it nearly impossible.
principles.quote: Address each possible worst case scenario and decide if you’re willing and able to be happy if that scenario happens.

principles.text: Make downside plans concrete with numbers: savings, monthly burn cap, runway, and a fallback job you'd accept.
principles.quote: I have $30k in savings. So as long as I spend less than $3k a month, I’ll have 10 months of runway.

principles.text: Only after you're comfortable with the downsides and confident in your contingency plans should you consider the upside; if you like it, do it.
principles.quote: If I’m comfortable with all the downsides I’ve listed out and am confident that I can execute on the contingency plans all while living a life that I’m willing to live, then I consider the upsides.

principles.text: The value is in the process: writing outcomes down shows downsides are usually not that bad, so emotions stop holding you back.
principles.quote: Most people let their emotions hold them back from doing what they really want.

sources.title: Sam Parr's summary of the 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing: own a word, be first, be the opposite
sources.originalTitle: 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing
sources.summary: Sam Parr summarizes the book The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing (which he rates 9/10) law by law. The core theme is positioning: win by being first in the customer's mind, owning one simple idea, sacrificing breadth, and defining yourself against the leader rather than copying them.

principles.text: Being first beats being better; if you can't be first, invent a new category you can lead.
principles.quote: It’s better to be first than it is to be better. The first brand in a customer’s mind almost always wins, regardless of product quality.

principles.text: Marketing is perception, not product: the best perceived product wins, not the best product.
principles.quote: Marketing is not about products…it’s about perceptions. The best product doesn’t win, the best perceived product does.

principles.text: Own one simple word or idea in the customer's mind; trying to mean many things means nothing.
principles.quote: Owning one simple word or idea in the customer’s mind is power. Brands that try to mean too many things mean nothing.

principles.text: If you're not the leader, don't copy them. Be the opposite to stand out.
principles.quote: If you’re not the leader, don’t copy them…be the opposite. That’s how you stand out.

principles.text: Winning requires saying no to customers, features and markets; stretching the brand across many products weakens it.
principles.quote: Winning requires saying no to customers, features, and markets. You have to give something up to stand for something.

principles.text: Discounting wins short-term but trains customers to never pay full price and damages the brand long-term.
principles.quote: Discounting boosts sales briefly, but eventually trains customers to never pay full price.

sources.title: What kind of successful people Sam Parr likes: kind, curious, humble, and often once poor
sources.originalTitle: The type of successful people I like all have these things in common
sources.summary: Sam describes the traits shared by the successful people he enjoys being around. He prefers kind over cut-throat, people who talk about life and ideas over business, people who grew up poor or middle class, and those who are humble and self-deprecating. It's a personal-taste essay on who to surround yourself with, not a tactical playbook.

principles.text: Prefer kind successful people over cut-throat ones; plenty of rich people are not ruthless.
principles.quote: I don’t like cut throat people. I prefer kind people.

principles.text: Success comes in all flavors; not all wealthy people put metrics above everything.
principles.quote: Some, but not all (not even the majority, perhaps) are cut throat.

principles.text: Seek successful people who talk about life and ideas more than business; deep conversation beats shop talk.
principles.quote: I like successful people who talk more about life than business

principles.text: Sam gets along best with people who came from poor or middle-class backgrounds.
principles.quote: The successful people I tend to get along with grew up in a poor or middle class family.

principles.text: The best successful people are humble and can make fun of themselves.
principles.quote: The best ones are humble and self-deprecating.

principles.text: Define success for yourself beyond money or job title; a poor teacher can be successful.
principles.quote: My personal definition of “successful” doesn’t involve money or your job. A poor teacher can be successful to me.

sources.title: Notes from hanging out with a powerful person: what Sam Parr learned meeting Lloyd Blankfein
sources.originalTitle: Notes from hanging out with a powerful person
sources.summary: Sam Parr's field notes after recording My First Million with ex-Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein. The takeaways are about mindset: thick skin, relatability as a leadership trait, studying history, and the difference between climbing an institution and owning a business.

principles.text: Greatness draws critics, so build thick skin and accept criticism as part of the price.
principles.quote: I think he did a great job of internalizing that in order to achieve greatness, you’ll have a lot of critics and that’s just part of it.

principles.text: Study history to get better at investing, because history moves in cycles.
principles.quote: He said the number one thing to study, if you want to be a great investor, is history. History goes in cycles, so it helps to know what happened in the past.

principles.text: Top leaders are warm and fully present with everyone, which is a big reason they rise.
principles.quote: when he talked to a peon like me…he was locked in, kind, charming, and very, very relatable. I can see why he became CEO.

principles.text: Even big companies tend to be run like small businesses; Sam prefers the entrepreneur path to climbing an institution.
principles.quote: even if a business is $10b+, most still act like small business owners in some ways.

principles.text: Early money scarcity shapes your habits for life, even after you become wealthy.
principles.quote: growing up poor impacts you for life.

sources.title: Set goals with A, B, Z: a 3-5 year ambitious Z, a 3-6 month near-term B, and ignore the rest
sources.originalTitle: Set a goal
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains his A, B, Z goal framework: start at A, pick a near-term B 3-6 months out, and set an ambitious 3-5 year Z, working backwards from Z. Goals must be specific, include both process and outcome, and be shared for accountability. He gives finance and fitness examples and a fill-in template.

principles.text: Most successful people set goals, and getting specific about them creates breakthroughs.
principles.quote: Most successful people I’ve met set goals. And the process of getting specific about goals creates breakthroughs.

principles.text: Use A, B, Z: current start, a B about 3-6 months out, and a 3-5 year Z. Ignore the steps in between until you reach them.
principles.quote: Often, B is about 3-6 months away from your starting point (A). Z is my big, 3-5 year plan.

principles.text: A, B, Z limits distractions, since doing A and B gives you the insight to figure out later steps.
principles.quote: too often people don’t do step A or B because they’re worried about the other stops. You’ll likely figure it out when you get there because in doing A and B, you’ll gain new insight.

principles.text: Direction matters more than horsepower for ambitious people; Z is the steering wheel, and you work backwards from it.
principles.quote: For many potential winners, the issue isn’t the ability (or not) to push down on the gas pedal. Its which direction the steering wheel is pointing.

principles.text: Make goals specific and pair outcome with process, not vague aims like 'lose weight'.
principles.quote: Goals must be both process and outcome. “weigh 198 pounds by May 1st, 2026 by eating 2,000 calories a day and lifting weights 3 days a week.”

principles.text: Calibrate ambition: Z should have about a 50% chance, B about 75%, and tell a few people for accountability.
principles.quote: Goal Z should be ambitious. 50% chance of happening. Goal B should have a 75% chance of happening.

sources.title: Why 35% growth is boring: the tedious price of Buffett-style steady growth and profitability
sources.originalTitle: 35% growth is boring
sources.summary: Sam reflects on Warren Buffett's time on the Washington Post board, where revenue grew a steady 12% a year and profitability surged but the company became stodgy. He argues that building a Buffett-like company takes tedious, boring work, and entrepreneurs should check whether that fits their own tastes.

principles.text: Steady growth and high profitability can cost you excitement; boredom is a real price of the Buffett model.
principles.quote: What’s the price of creating a company with good, steady revenue growth and profitability? Boredom (potenially).

principles.text: There are many valid ways to build a successful company; pick the one that fits your tastes.
principles.quote: There are a million ways to build a successful company (however success is defined as). Get big fast, like OpenAI. Grow a family dynasty over 100 years. Stay a small mom and pop business.

principles.text: Before copying Buffett's results, consider the day-to-day work required and whether you'd enjoy it.
principles.quote: But…I don’t think we think enough about the day to day work to achieve what he did and how it fits into our own tastes.

principles.text: Mastery in any field requires decades of tedious, boring work, and that boredom is acceptable.
principles.quote: I think you can argue that to be the best at anything (sports, art, etc), it requires decades of tedious, boring work.

principles.text: Even a founder who loves starting things and exciting parts of business must sometimes accept tedium to achieve greatness.
principles.quote: greatness might occasionally require accepting tedious and boring.

principles.text: A company can be exciting by nature (a newspaper) yet become boring once it prioritizes financial success under disciplined control.
principles.quote: But once it got under Buffett’s control and became more financially successful…it was much more boring.

sources.title: Sam Parr: Inside the life of a $100m person (paywalled newsletter teaser)
sources.originalTitle: Inside the life of a $100m person
sources.summary: A truncated, subscriber-gated newsletter essay. The visible part covers Sam's Boston Inbound talk "Be Chalant: The Art of Giving a Damn" and one lesson: acting uncool and openly enthusiastic attracted investors, employees and customers. The rest of the essay is locked.

principles.text: Showing real enthusiasm, rather than acting like you don't care, makes people drawn to you, including investors, employees and customers.
principles.quote: So in my 20’s when I started my first company, I began openly showing more enthusiasm. People were more attracted to me. Investors. Employees. Customers. Everyone.

principles.text: Acting indifferent to seem cool is a mistake; it doesn't work.
principles.quote: My takeaway from those book was to be “cool” and act like I don’t care. That was dumb (and I got no girls).

sources.title: Why a 2.9-decisions-a-year investor beat the market: make few decisions, study deeply, wait
sources.originalTitle: 2.9 decisions a year (and $50 million)
sources.summary: Sam profiles an investor who turned ~$10m into ~$50m making about 2.9 buy/sell decisions a year. He distills four habits of successful stock pickers (few decisions, don't agonize over reversible ones, stay in your circle of competence, write decisions down) and applies them to CEOs. The essay is paywalled, so only the opening is available.

principles.text: Motion is not progress: for CEOs and people with leverage, fewer decisions often beat constant activity.
principles.quote: we often correlate motion with good results. But for the average CEO or person with leverage, that isn’t the case.

principles.text: Make few decisions; patient inaction can be the core of a winning strategy.
principles.quote: They make few decisions. “Lethargy bordering on sloth remains the cornerstone of our investment style,” Warren Buffett once said.

principles.text: Sort decisions into irreversible and reversible; don't agonize over two-way doors.
principles.quote: Decisions are split into ones they can’t undo and ones they can easily reverse. Most decisions are two-way doors and don’t deserve agonizing.

principles.text: Know your circle of competence and say no often to things outside it, regardless of whether they look good.
principles.quote: They say “no” often. Not because something is good or bad, but because it’s not within their area of expertise.

principles.text: Write big decisions down with a pre-mortem and your reasoning, then review afterward to judge the reasoning.
principles.quote: Writing pre-mortems (imagine it’s a year later and why the decision blew up) and writing their thought process before the decision. Then they review it after to see if their reasoning was good or bad.

principles.text: Go deep on a few things you can understand, keep detailed notes, and wait for the right opportunity.
principles.quote: I study a few things I feel I can understand, and I study them very deeply. I keep very detailed notes and then just wait for an opportunity.

sources.title: Natural moneymakers: the unemotional deal-makers who look like they're cheating
sources.originalTitle: Natural moneymakers
sources.summary: Sam Parr introduces his newsletter and the idea of "natural moneymakers", entrepreneurs who make $100m to $1b through deal making and brokering. He says they are unemotional and logical about money. The essay is paywalled, so only the opening is available.

principles.text: Some founders are so good at making money it looks like cheating; Sam calls them natural moneymakers.
principles.quote: Some entrepreneurs are so violently good at making money it looks like cheating.

principles.text: Natural moneymakers tend to work in deal making, brokering and inserting themselves into situations, and they rarely build in public.
principles.quote: These people tend to be in roles that involve deal making, brokering, and inserting themselves into a situation. They rarely build in public.

principles.text: You can be a rich, successful founder without being a natural moneymaker; vision, risk and charisma are a different skill.
principles.quote: You can be successful and rich and still not be a natural money maker.

principles.text: Natural moneymakers treat business unemotionally and logically, even though they feel anxiety like everyone else.
principles.quote: Natural money makers have anxiety like everyone else. But they use emotions to make money.

principles.text: Passion and emotion help most founders succeed, but natural moneymakers are colder and more logical about money.
principles.quote: Being emotional and passionate helps founders succeed. Natural moneymakers are more cold about money. More logical.

sources.title: Sam Parr: creators are making $1m-$10m+ a year with tiny teams
sources.originalTitle: $10m a year 1 person biz
sources.summary: A short, paywalled teaser from Sam Parr's newsletter test. He reports that content creators he spoke with are earning $1m to $10m+ a year with small teams, cites The Hustle's growth to ~$13m revenue and 1.7m daily readers, and says he believes he can reach $10m+ with 2-4 people in 2-3 years. Most of the essay is behind a subscriber wall.

principles.text: Creators with tech audiences can build $1m-$10m+ a year businesses with very small teams.
principles.quote: 3 were small with less than 100k followers on their platform of choice. Each made over $1m/year.

principles.text: Bigger creators on the scale of My First Million can exceed $10m a year while staying lean.
principles.quote: They were doing over $10m/year with tiny teams.

principles.text: Sam believes a newsletter-led business can reach $10m+ in revenue with only 2-4 people in 2-3 years.
principles.quote: Knowing what I know now, I think I can grow to +$10m in revenue with 2-4 people. And do it in 2-3 years.

principles.text: Sam's newsletter can compound into a media business: The Hustle grew to ~$13m revenue and 1.7m daily readers, plus podcasts and events, by year five.
principles.quote: We grew it to around $13m in revenue and 1.7m daily readers plus podcasts and events by year ~5 into the business.

sources.title: Why Sam Parr started Hampton: a CEO peer group born from his own
sources.originalTitle: My new company…
sources.summary: Short announcement of Hampton, an executive peer group for CEOs. Sam says the peer group he built while running The Hustle helped him grow and sell the company, which is why he started Hampton. Includes the membership bar of $1m revenue minimum.

principles.text: Build the product you personally benefited from: Hampton came from a peer group that helped him grow and sell The Hustle.
principles.quote: I started it because I used a peer group that I created when running The Hustle. And it changed my life. Helped me sell the company, helped me grow it…everything.

principles.text: A peer group of fellow CEOs is a growth lever for running and exiting a company.
principles.quote: Helped me sell the company, helped me grow it…everything.

principles.text: Set a clear membership bar so the community stays relevant to its members.
principles.quote: Members need at least $1m in revenue. But our average member has like $20m in revenue.

sources.title: Sam Parr's 2023 year in review: the four F's framework and 13 income streams
sources.originalTitle: 2023 End of Year Review: Finance, Fitness, Family, Fun
sources.summary: Sam's annual personal review organized as Family, Fitness, Finance, Fun. Mostly personal, but it shows how he sets goals, how his income accumulated from side projects, and what he learned from real estate and courses.

principles.text: Set annual and quarterly goals in a few simple categories (Family, Fitness, Finance, Fun) and write a yearly review.
principles.quote: I always set my goals in the following categories: Family, Fitness, Finance, Fun.

principles.text: Income streams can accumulate from side projects over years, even if you never set out to build them.
principles.quote: My goal has never been to make a ton of annual cash flow or have multiple streams of income. I thought I’d make more money starting and selling startups. I just did a few projects on the side and, over the years, its accumulated.

principles.text: Partner with people whose values and communication match yours; a good co-founder relationship compounds.
principles.quote: Its a wonderful partnership. Our values are aligned, communication is great, and we have a ton of respect for one another.

principles.text: Hire lean and set rules up front, but expect reality to override them as the company grows.
principles.quote: We had strict rules when starting: don’t hire lots of people and try to avoid big city folks as they complain too much. Welp, 18 months in and we have ~16 employees, most of them in NYC.

principles.text: Make products (like courses) in response to repeated audience demand, even if you dislike making them.
principles.quote: I don’t love making courses, but people always ask me about copywriting and researching businesses. So I thought what the hell, I’ll make it.

principles.text: Don't invest in a category you find boring; real estate sucked for Sam, so he is selling it all despite a poor market.
principles.quote: The outcome: real estate sucks. I hate it! Even though our stuff makes decent revenue, I just find it boring.

sources.title: Sam Parr: Every piece of success advice has a successful opposite, so don't treat any as law
sources.originalTitle: We're all idiots
sources.summary: After 800+ founder conversations and hundreds of books, Sam concludes that for any advice from a successful person, you can still win by doing the opposite. He backs this with paired founder quotes on focus, raising VC, grinding, goals, risk, remote work and ads, then closes on building a life that earns admiration.

principles.text: For any advice from a successful person, assume you can still win by doing the opposite.
principles.quote: for any one piece of advice from a successful person, assume you can still win by doing the opposite.

principles.text: Startup maxims raise your odds, but they aren't required to win. You can ignore them and still succeed.
principles.quote: That advice can be great and oftentimes will increase the odds of success. But know this: you can do the opposite and still be successful.

principles.text: Contradictory winners exist on focus, funding, hours, goals, risk, remote work and ad spend, so pick what fits you.
principles.quote: Over the last 10 years I’ve done 800+ conversations with successful founders and read hundreds of books on the topic of “how to be successful.”

principles.text: Sam set a concrete big financial goal early, even though other successful founders deliberately avoid goals.
principles.quote: I had a goal to make $20 million liquid by the age of 30.

principles.text: In your 20s, work today to make your future self proud. With a family, do things that make your future family proud.
principles.quote: In my 20’s I became obsessed with the idea that I should put the work in today that will make my future self proud.

principles.text: Admiration is a quality worth looking for in the people you do life and business with, and worth earning yourself.
principles.quote: all of this has made me think a lot about admiration and how that’s a wonderful quality to look for in people you do life with.

sources.title: Overnight success takes years: Sam Parr's 2013 CEO Doc on apprenticeship and mastery
sources.originalTitle: How Many Years Does it Take to Become a Millionaire?
sources.summary: A 2013 essay from Sam Parr's old blog arguing that "overnight success" is mostly a myth. Drawing on Robert Greene's Mastery, he says most monetary success takes decades of apprenticeship, and he built a spreadsheet (the CEO Doc) tracking how long famous founders worked before breaking out.

principles.text: "Overnight success" is mostly nonsense; most monetary success takes decades.
principles.quote: for the majority of people who’ve achieve monetary success, it took decades

principles.text: Behind nearly every success are years and years of hard work, not months from idea to IPO.
principles.quote: Behind (nearly) every success is years, and years of hard work.

principles.text: Mastery requires roughly 5 to 10 years of intense study, basically an apprenticeship.
principles.quote: To master your craft, you must study intensely for 5 to 10 years…so basically, an apprenticeship.

principles.text: Successful people are those who have mastered their craft.
principles.quote: Successful people, (and “geniuses”) are folks who have mastered their craft.

sources.title: Sam Parr on quitting alcohol: 6 lessons from one year sober (2014)
sources.originalTitle: 6 Things I Learned From Not Drinking For 1 Year
sources.summary: A 2014 personal essay where Sam Parr shares what changed after a year of sobriety: fitness, confidence, clarity, and emotional control. Mostly personal reflection, with durable mindset lessons about facing stress head-on, exercise as a mood and work-ethic driver, and conviction building confidence.

principles.text: Exercise boosts mood, alertness, confidence and work ethic; skipping it makes you feel bad.
principles.quote: After working out, I felt happy, more alert, and best of all, confident. I noticed an increase in my work ethic too.

principles.text: Sticking to your convictions builds real confidence, which makes you more attractive than relying on false confidence.
principles.quote: Women like confident men and in the past I relied on booze for false confidence.

principles.text: Facing stressful, high-stakes moments clear-headed is a rush; embrace obstacles instead of numbing yourself.
principles.quote: In fact, I now embrace obstacles because I love the exhilarating emotion of feeling the stress, pain, and achievement when overcoming it.

principles.text: Starting a business is scary and stressful; feeling every emotion fully is what makes it energizing.
principles.quote: Yes, starting a new business is scary and stressful, but I felt every emotion and loved it.

principles.text: Controlling your emotions lets you step back, analyze, and decide well instead of acting impulsively.
principles.quote: When something bad happens I’m able to calmly take a step back, analyze what’s going on, how I feel, then make a proper decision

principles.text: Removing a habit that wrecks your energy frees you to commit to mornings, health and action.
principles.quote: For years I’d never commit to Saturday or Sunday morning activities because I knew I’d still be drunk or hungover in the AM.

sources.title: How Sam Parr gets useful negative feedback: an anonymous two-question Google Form
sources.originalTitle: The Power of Negative Feedback
sources.summary: Sam argues negative feedback is more valuable and actionable than positive feedback, provided you separate your performance from your self-worth. He shares a simple three-step method: send an anonymous strengths/weaknesses form to 10 close contacts, then act on the most common weaknesses.

principles.text: Negative feedback is more valuable and actionable than positive feedback, so actively seek it out.
principles.quote: Negative feedback is far more valuable and actionable than positive feedback

principles.text: Decouple performance from self-esteem so critique is about what you did, not who you are.
principles.quote: De-couple the performance from the self-esteem.

principles.text: Ask 10 close friends and co-workers for 3 strengths and 3 weaknesses via an anonymous form.
principles.quote: Create a Google Form with two questions: What are my 3 biggest strengths and 3 biggest weaknesses.

principles.text: Ask for strengths too as a red herring; it gets people talking and speaking their mind.
principles.quote: I added the 3 strengths part as a red herring…it’s a great way to get people to start speaking their mind.

principles.text: Make the form anonymous and frame it as self-improvement to get honest, useful answers.
principles.quote: Tell them you’re working on yourself and want feedback because you appreciate their opinion. Make sure to tell them the form is anonymous.

principles.text: Focus on the most common weaknesses mentioned, and keep them visible so you act on them.
principles.quote: Take the three most common weaknesses mentioned, print them out, and tape them to your bedroom door.

sources.title: How to complain to companies and actually get refunds and credits
sources.originalTitle: Customer service: how to complain and still get what you want!
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how to give customer service feedback so it gets results. Stay polite, say you want to keep using the product, and mention a competitor. His rewritten Uber email got a friend $50 back plus a $20 credit, and a tweet tagging Spotify earned him 3 free months of Premium.

principles.text: Angry, insulting complaints accomplish nothing; a polite one that explains the issue gets results.
principles.quote: This email wouldn’t accomplish a THING

principles.text: Say you want to remain a customer if they fix the problem, which gives them a reason to help.
principles.quote: Explain how you want to continue to be a customer if they can address the issue.

principles.text: Mention that you'll switch to a competitor; companies fear competitors more than unhappy customers.
principles.quote: Let them know that you will use their competitor’s service.

principles.text: Companies care more about beating rivals than pleasing you, so tag the competitor in a public tweet.
principles.quote: most companies care WAYYYYY more about beating their competitors then they care about making you happy. Use this.

principles.text: Complaining politely works: the rewritten Uber email got his friend $50 back and a $20 credit.
principles.quote: My buddy ended up getting $50 back and a $20 credit for his next ride.

sources.title: How Sam Parr saves over 50% of his income: a 7-step savings system
sources.originalTitle: How I Save Over 50% of My Income
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains his personal finance process from his early 20s: track spending obsessively, calculate burn and runway, set tiered savings goals up to 36 months, and deliberately feel the pain of underspending. The point is financial independence, not being cheap. Written in 2019 on his old blog.

principles.text: Saving is not being cheap; it frees money for things that truly make you happy instead of empty overconsumption.
principles.quote: Saving is **not** being cheap. It’s about having money to spend on things that truly make you happy instead of over consuming on stuff that leaves you empty.

principles.text: Entrepreneurs should hold far more runway than the standard 6 months because income is the first thing to stop.
principles.quote: I’m also very conservative with money as I’m an entrepreneur. When business is booming, I’m rolling in it. But when business sucks or I’m starting something new, my income is the first thing that stops.

principles.text: Know your numbers: average trailing 3 months of spending as burn, divide liquid assets by burn to get runway.
