principles.quote: Look at your trailing 3 months of spending on Personal Capital. Average it. That’s your burn. In your spreadsheet, divide that by your liquid assets. That’s your runway.

principles.text: Track every expense manually; measuring something forces you to notice it and usually improves it.
principles.quote: tracking something forces you to notice it and typically leads to improvement.

principles.text: Set stepped runway benchmarks (3, 6, 12, 24, 36 months) and reach each before aiming for the next.
principles.quote: 3 months, 6 months, 12 months, 24 months, 36 months. Make those your benchmarks. If you have less than 3 months in cash, your goal is to get there first.

principles.text: Cut what doesn't make you happy and aim for a 50% savings rate; if you're not hurting, you're not saving enough.
principles.quote: If you’re not hurting then you’re not saving enough. Just do it.

sources.title: Sam Parr on moving from creative founder to capital allocator, inspired by Syed Balkhi
sources.originalTitle: I just spoke with one of the most impressive businessmen I’ve ever chatted with
sources.summary: Sam Parr recaps Syed Balkhi's path from a WordPress blog to a bootstrapped company with over $100m in revenue, built by buying plugins. He reflects that creativity and gut get you initial traction, but later stages call for a more disciplined capital allocator mindset.

principles.text: You can't spreadsheet your way to initial traction; early on you need creativity to invent a better mousetrap.
principles.quote: I don’t think you can Excel sheet your way to initial traction. At least I can’t. You need to invent a better mousetrap and that takes creativity.

principles.text: Once you have money, success and an audience, level up from creative founder to disciplined capital allocator.
principles.quote: I have some money, success, and an audience. But I’ve not always been great at leveling up. Talking to him really encouraged me to level up. Focus more on a capital allocator mindset.

principles.text: Sam's default style is idea-driven and gut-led: think of ideas, do them, and see which work.
principles.quote: I think of ideas and do them and sometimes they work. I follow my gut.

principles.text: Discipline is what impressed Sam most about a bootstrapped founder who grew a blog into a $1B+ plugin company by acquiring products over a decade.
principles.quote: The reason why he interested me: he was incredibly disciplined. He talked about how he went from becoming an internet founder to a capital allocator.

sources.title: Owning stuff: measure cost in maintenance hours, not purchase price
sources.originalTitle: Owning stuff
sources.summary: Sam argues the real cost of an asset is the maintenance time it demands, not what you paid for it. He went from owning cars and houses to renting and owning little, and says his mind is lighter and life more convenient, even if it earns him criticism.

principles.text: Judge the cost of owning something by the maintenance hours it consumes, not its purchase price.
principles.quote: Maintenance hours, not purchase price. That’s how much something cost.

principles.text: Owning fewer things removes a long tail of recurring chores: fixing, registering, renewing, insuring, updating, subscribing.
principles.quote: Fewer things to maintain. To fix. To register. To renew. Insure. Update. Subscribe.

principles.text: Optimize for a lighter mind and a more convenient life, even when conventional wisdom says you're losing money.
principles.quote: But what I do know definitely is that my mind is lighter and my life more convenient.

principles.text: Ignore criticism of unconventional choices like renting instead of buying a home when you're happier and possibly earning more.
principles.quote: I think I like make more money now not owning stuff.

sources.title: How The Hustle writes: Sam Parr's 14-step process for high-volume content
sources.originalTitle: Write Like The Hustle: The Boring Stuff About Writing That No One Talks About
sources.summary: Sam Parr shares the repeatable writing process he and John used to launch The Hustle, publishing 3-6 posts a day without formal writing backgrounds. It covers headline-first writing, ugly drafts, ruthless cutting, hooks, and simple language.

principles.text: Treat the headline as most of the work: write about 25 and test them on friends.
principles.quote: 90% of people will read your headline without consuming your article. Yet, people rarely spend time perfecting their headline. Write 25 of them.

principles.text: Write a terrible first draft; getting words on the page matters more than quality.
principles.quote: Accept that this is a dump and that it'll suck. Get all your thoughts on paper.

principles.text: Step away from the draft before editing; distance produces new ideas.
principles.quote: Ironically, not focusing on a problem actually helps you come up with new ideas

principles.text: Cut hard: every word must earn its place, and word count targets are a trap.
principles.quote: Every single word must be necessary. Nothing more, nothing less. Don't use 1,500 words to explain something if you need 500.

principles.text: Each sentence exists only to get the reader to the next one, starting with a punchy first line.
principles.quote: The sole purpose of the first sentence is to get you to read the second sentence. The sole purpose of the second sentence is to get you to read the third sentence

principles.text: Aim for simple, plain writing; the value is in the story and insight, not fancy prose.
principles.quote: A great post has C+ writing and A+ storytelling, insight, or analysis.

sources.title: Sam Parr on selling The Hustle to HubSpot and optimizing for time, not titles
sources.originalTitle: Sam Parr on Bootstrapping a Multimillion Dollar Company - EP 76
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle's revenue streams (ads, conferences, subscriptions) were valued by a strategic buyer, why he took cash and stock with no earn-out, and why he optimizes for time. He also covers a "big hit, then reflect" career model, de-risking via real estate, and cold-emailing 50 people out of his league.

principles.text: Strategic buyers value media by customer count and lifetime value, so sell to someone who already earns from your audience.
principles.quote: They valued it by like basically how many customers do they have and what's the lifetime value of those customers, and how many customers do they think they can get from The Hustle over the next five years.

principles.text: Take a certain deal when the future is uncertain rather than holding out for upside you can't control.
principles.quote: I've only been at this for four years like I'm set after this. Maybe I should just take it and not worry about what it could be worth in the future.

principles.text: Set a concrete financial target and work backwards from it so key life decisions stop being constrained by money.
principles.quote: I said, "I want $20 million by the time I'm 30." Because if you have 20 million by the time you're 30, you're set

principles.text: Optimize for owning your time; the bigger the company, the more it owns you.
principles.quote: I want to be a time billionaire. That's really all I care about is my time.

principles.text: Build in bursts: get a big win, reflect and rest, pick the next thing methodically, then go all in.
principles.quote: get a little hit, a big hit or a hit in your 20s or 30s, chill for a minute, reflect, find the next thing very methodically and then go all in, and maybe that can be even huger.

principles.text: Take outsized action on access: cold email 50 people far out of your league and keep following up.
principles.quote: make a list of 50 people who you admire who are way out of your league and cold email all of them and keep following up until they tell you to F off.

sources.title: How Sam Parr built The Hustle to millions of readers and an 8-figure exit with content and no ad spend
sources.originalTitle: Sam Parr: How He Disrupted Media and Got an 8-Figure Exit (Cap Con 5 transcript)
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle grew to roughly 2M daily email readers and sold to HubSpot by starting every piece of content with distribution, riding conversations already happening on Reddit and Hacker News, and writing authentically for one niche. He also admits the biggest mistake was under-spending on growth once the machine worked.

principles.text: Start content with distribution: decide who you want to reach and where they are before choosing the idea.
principles.quote: So I always start with distribution. So, before I even have an article idea, I say, who do I want to reach? And where are they?

principles.text: Mine communities like Reddit and Hacker News for what's already trending, then add your own different take.
principles.quote: I want to know what the people are already talking about, what type of content is trending with my desired audience. And I'm going to figure out a way how to make my version touch on that but be different.

principles.text: Once a growth machine works, pour money into it; don't stay frugal out of scarcity mindset.
principles.quote: If you have a machine that turns $1 into $2, what do you do? You load up a dump truck with as much money as you possibly can and you just back it into that machine.

principles.text: Care deeply about your niche and don't fake it; online audiences punish inauthentic content.
principles.quote: internet people have the greatest bullshit detector there is. And what's the best way to circumvent someone's bullshit detector? You don't bullshit.

principles.text: Media value is audience quality times audience size times your influence over them.
principles.quote: the enterprise value of media is basically equal to the quality of people who you have consuming your stuff, multiplied by the number of people, multiplied by your influence over them.

principles.text: Sending email more often can raise open rates when the product is a habit-forming daily utility.
principles.quote: The more we sent, the higher the open rate went up.

sources.title: Sam Parr: how The Hustle and My First Million grew via content, copywriting and paid ads
sources.originalTitle: Sam Parr on The Creator Science Podcast (transcript)
sources.summary: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle grew from a conference blog to a 1.5M-subscriber newsletter without ad spend, and when he started paying for growth. He also covers learning copywriting by copying, spotting attention arbitrage, and growing My First Million with ads and fan-made clips.

principles.text: Early distribution can come from useful content plus email capture, not ads.
principles.quote: And I would just write a blog post, I would get traffic from Hacker News or Reddit. 3% of people would enter in their email.

principles.text: Learn copywriting by hand-copying great copy, the way musicians learn by copying songs.
principles.quote: You spend years copying other people's music, and you learn the texture of what makes a good song you learn the recipe of what makes a good meal.

principles.text: Look for the gap between attention supply and creator supply on a platform, and exploit it before it closes.
principles.quote: But what you look for is the arbitrage between supply and demand of attention versus creators.

principles.text: Once your unit economics are proven, spend hard on paid acquisition before the window closes.
principles.quote: one of my mistakes in building the company was I didn't spend enough, I was too frugal, I should have went harder because Facebook ads are way more expensive now

principles.text: Don't build a creator business that traps you in daily output; decide early whether to hire and delegate.
principles.quote: So you have to make sure you don't build a prison.

principles.text: Pay fans to make short clips of your long content; it spreads reach cheaply.
principles.quote: we told our fans that we'll give five grand to the people who make videos from our YouTube clips and put it on Tik Tok, and make it cool.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam explains why he obsessed over copywriting (sales on paper scales one-to-one selling) and which timeless principles still work: long copy, AIDA, fourth-grade writing, and hand-copying great sales pages. He also argues for leading with a feeling and the founder's story.

chunks.heading: Sam's origin in copywriting and why it is "sales on paper"
chunks.text:
- Sam started with a hot dog stand in college ("Southern Sam's Wieners as big as a baby's arm"). The product was nothing special, so he began Googling how to be a salesperson around 2010 and found copywriting.
- His core insight: if you can sell one-to-one and put it on paper, you can sell to an infinite number of people. He defines copywriting as "just sales on paper".
- He got hooked by early internet marketers. One example: David DeAngelo wrote 5,000-word plain-text emails and made about $30 million a year selling ebooks on picking up women. Sam admits it was shady, but he wanted to master the technique and use it to sell things he loved.
- Founders who think "ads don't work on me" are wrong. Human nature has not changed, and the same words still convince people to buy.
- Founders must first be convinced it is worth studying. His starting recommendation is David Ogilvy's *Ogilvy on Advertising*, then *Confessions of an Advertising Man*, and Joe Sugarman's *Adweek Copywriting Handbook* (the title he gives is "Adweek Guide to Copywriting"), which he calls his favorite.

chunks.heading: Why learn from pre-internet direct-mail copywriters
chunks.text:
- Before the internet, from the 1930s through the 1990s, people like Ogilvy sold products (e.g. a vacuum to a housewife) by mailing typed letters to a million households.
- That was expensive, so the letters had to earn their cost back. This forced copywriters to learn exactly which words get people to take action.
- Sam says these are the best teachers: "Those are the best places to learn from."
- Ogilvy started as a copywriter writing sales letters, then built Ogilvy & Mather into a multi-tens-of-billions-of-dollars ad firm.
- Sam says "Everyone says the same thing": the principles from these writers still hold today.
- His example of the same principles at work: Amazon and Apple product pages are long, with many photos, reviews and words. An Amazon book page has tens of thousands of words once reviews are counted.

chunks.heading: Why long-form beats short-form: the AIDA slippery slope
chunks.text:
- Sam's claim: "Long-form copy typically is almost always better than short-form copy." Anyone who sells a lot of anything knows this.
- Reason 1: people skim, so a long page gives many places to grab attention and pull them back down.
- Reason 2: copy works as a "slippery slope" that takes the reader from interested to ready to buy. The framework is AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action.
  - Attention: grab it.
  - Interest: keep it.
  - Desire: make them want what you want them to want.
  - Action: tell them very specifically what to do next.
- The goal is the fewest words that are most effective. Often that takes a lot of words.
- Sam's water example: "Have you ever seen those big muscular guys at the gym carrying around gallons of jugs of water?" (attention), then a claim that water carries amino acids needed to build protein (interest and desire), then "fill up this gallon of water and drink all of it before noon" (action). He notes he made up the facts for the demo.
- Instagram influencers teach the same thing as "hook, meat, CTA".
- "There's no such thing as too long. There's only such a thing as too uninteresting." Long tweets and threads get shared most because they make people emotionally invested.
- The aim is not for 100% of people to read it. It is for the right 5% to read it and share at a high rate.
- Good copy makes the reader feel the writer knows their thoughts better than they do. His weight-loss ad example: "I know why you stand on the edge of your friends when you take a photograph with your buddies at the beach. I know why you wear that cover-up." He says to use this power for good.

chunks.heading: Sam's rules for writing clearly
chunks.text:
1. Start with the big idea, also called the hook or angle. It is the one-liner you'd use to describe a movie to a friend (e.g. "a talking bear who's really vulgar").
2. Write like you talk. Write simply, at a fourth or fifth grade reading level. If you have to look a word up in a thesaurus, don't use it. The free tool hemingwayapp.com checks this.
3. Use the active voice. "The boy kicked the ball" is good; "the ball was kicked by the boy" is bad. Someone should be doing something.
4. Remove adverbs. He cites Stephen King: "the road to hell is paved with adverbs."
5. For a big sales page or cold email, pretend you are writing to one person and literally write them a letter.

- Warren Buffett example: his annual letters run about 18 words per sentence at roughly a sixth-grade reading level, and he uses simple analogies (the tide going out and who isn't wearing a swimsuit). Sam calls Buffett "a brilliant marketer".
- Grammarly and Hemingway help bad writers become good and good writers become great, and Grammarly flags passive voice accurately. He says ideas matter most.

chunks.heading: Using AI for copy, and training your writing
chunks.text:
- Sam uses AI to find the big idea, not to write. His view: "it can never do a good job of writing."
- Example: for Hampton and conference marketing, he asked AI for phrases describing what it means to be around other high performers and got "the Michelangelo effect" (greatness is already in you; every great person you meet chisels away the unnecessary stone).
- Another example: for the "you're the average of your five best friends" idea, he asked ChatGPT for evidence and got a 1976 study of 20,000 people on obesity, poverty and happiness. He did not know the study himself. He says this evidence-finding is where large language models "have changed everything".
- Copy work is his main training method. He credits the old way of teaching writing. Like learning piano by playing existing songs first, you take the best sales letter or even a novel (he did it with *Catcher in the Rye*) and copy it word for word by hand on a yellow notepad.
  - Do it 15 minutes to an hour at a time. 20 minutes a day for 20 days will make you better.
  - Before an important sales page, hand-copy a great one. He names hey.com as a very good sales page.
  - You "feel the texture of the words", and that changes how you write.
- Social media gives instant feedback on whether your writing resonates, so use it as a testing ground.
- Writing is clarity of thought, and a clear writer is always a clear thinker. He worries AI note-takers let people skip processing what they hear.

chunks.heading: What goes above the fold on a product page
chunks.text:
- Sam's rule: above the fold should be a feeling, not a feature list. Using TaxGPT as the example, he would sell the emotion (calmer life during tax season, "taking the terror out of tax season") rather than "AI tax assistant for tax professionals".
- Sell the feeling by intimately describing one the customer has. For accountants, the scramble around tax day, or a client getting a surprise tax bill they wish they'd seen coming.
- Find the lines by testing them. Pitch 10 to 20 customers and watch which ones make them lean in, like a comedian testing jokes in small rooms before the big stage.
- Founders fall into a "feature death march" (his co-host Jason's term, which Sam builds on): leading with the last three features shipped instead of the big vision.
- Words usually beat images, and video beats everything. He says copywriting also covers video and audio.
- For a small, early company, a founder letter near the top works well: "Hey there, fellow accountant. You're probably wondering what this is. Well, let me explain."
- Put a picture of the founder and team up front. The About Us page is typically the second most visited page on a site.
- His bet: with just a Google Sheet or Form and plain text, he could sell more of most things than a site full of fancy photos. His advice is to "lean into the personal side."

chunks.heading: Founder story as the strongest copy (Hampton's About page)
chunks.text:
- Sam's Hampton About Us page tells a story about his co-founder Joe: Joe sold a company for $114 million at age 24, then built the viral blog Little Things to about $70 million in revenue. A Facebook algorithm change cut revenue from $60 million to $10 million just before a planned $100 million sale, and the company closed three months later. A photo from an Inc. magazine story about it sits at the top.
- Sam ends it with how that led to the idea for Hampton.
- His view: anyone can build a product now, so the founder's intent and the "why" matter most. A strong mission is a story (Palantir and Anduril cited as examples).
- Technical founders do not need to be on camera: "you could do all of this via a keyboard."
- Takeaway in his words: it's "rooted in compelling storytelling."

chunks.heading: Hampton: how Sam markets and structures it
chunks.text:
- Hampton is a members-only community for founders. It runs on three things: an eight-founder in-person core group meeting monthly with a trained moderator, local chapters (e.g. about 190 members in New York) with events, and a Slack group of 1,000+ members where questions get answers within about 20 minutes.
- Membership is selective: only about 4% are accepted. Last month it got about 2,300 applications. Every applicant gets a roughly 45-minute interview, then Sam or co-founder Joe watches it, then the community votes thumbs up or down.
- Entry requires at least $3 million in revenue, $3 million in funding, or a $10 million company sale, plus a digital or internet business. Price for new members from January is $15,000 a year; he said earlier pricing was lower.
- Sam pivoted from digital to in-person after launch. Hampton hosted 150 events in the year, uses 100+ paid and trained moderators, and has a four-person team to find and train them.
- Business model: no outside funding. He wants it to last 50 to 100 years, modeled on YPO (1950s) and Vistage (1962, about 40,000 members at roughly $20,000 a year on average). He says it could bootstrap to a multi-billion-dollar company over about 20 years.
- Brand name: he is from Hampton Avenue in St. Louis, and it also evokes the Hamptons. His principle: "Brand is when you associate two things."
- MoneyWise (his podcast) works as marketing for Hampton. He noticed the most popular Hampton threads were about money (estates, spending, portfolios), so he got ultra-high-net-worth people to reveal income, expenses and portfolio allocation, and asked how they were "messed up" too. First guest example: Anne, who sold Solidcore for $250 million and has about $94 million.

chunks.heading: How Sam picks role models and plans exits
chunks.text:
- He studied about five media people before building The Hustle and says he "just copied" Jason: build a media company around tech people rather than pretend to be a tech builder, then add conferences.
- He admires Felix Dennis (*How to Get Rich*, which he calls possibly the best book he has read), who advised making as much money as possible by about 35 and then relaxing. Sam's own goal was serious money by 31, and he says Jason's quick $30 million exit at 18 months fit the plan.
- He also studied Ted Turner. Sam loves that Turner was scrappy, made unilateral decisions on instinct, didn't take himself too seriously, and saved the buffalo population. Sam calls this type a "manifest cowboy": someone who turns dreams into reality in a shoot-from-the-hip way.
- On selling early: Sam says he sold The Hustle too early, since competitor Morning Brew is now at about $90 million in revenue. He had predicted $100 million within 10 years. Having "FU money" lets you play long rather than scared.
- Podcasts he recommends: Founders, and *How to Take Over the World* by Ben Wilson, which he calls "Acquired, but for people".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr breaks down the copywriting frameworks he used at The Hustle and Hampton: punchy first lines, the curiosity gap, stories with the customer as hero, and short sentences. He also explains why long copy beats short if it's interesting, and how copy work builds taste.

chunks.heading: Sam's core principle: copywriting is understanding people and getting them to act
chunks.text:
- Sam's definition: "copywriting isn't just writing words. It's understanding what people want and how to get them to do what you want them to do." Good copy gets what's in his head into yours and influences behavior.
- He uses the same tools in dating and sales. For a first date with his wife, he opened with a joke to grab attention (ADA: attention, interest, desire, action).
- He tells salespeople that in sales and flirting you can say almost anything as long as you make the person laugh.
- He recommends "restaurant owner energy": talk to a stranger as if you already know them.
- He cites David Ogilvy: on average five times as many people read the headline as read the body, so the headline is 80 cents of your dollar.
- Sam says most of what he writes about copywriting is "really just stealing" from Ogilvy and Joe Sugarman. He recommends the Ogilvy book because the less popular a book is, the less likely anyone notices you borrowed from it.

chunks.heading: Headlines: mind the gap and create open loops
chunks.text:
- The curiosity gap ("minding the gap") works like music needing resolution. People can't leave a cliffhanger alone, so a headline should grab attention and make them read on to resolve it.
- Examples he cites:
  - The Rolls-Royce ad by Ogilvy: "At 60 mph, the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock."
  - The classic piano ad: "They laughed when I sat down at the piano, but then I started to play." (a course on writing music)
  - Upworthy-style clickbait ("You're not going to believe number seven"). A competitor run by his partner Joe went from zero to 200 million monthly visitors in about 6 months using this style.
- Open loops apply to short-form video too: stack one on another. A creator on the show adds a curiosity gap roughly every 8 seconds.
- The "you're reading this not because you want to, but because I want you to" hook is one Sam used often. It breaks the fourth wall and pulls the reader down the page.
- Tease what's coming ("what I'm about to tell you next will blow your mind, but really quick, let me tell you this"). Tony Robbins does this throughout his books. Sam says the same trick comes from pickup artist books: put a time constraint on the conversation so people relax and let you finish.

chunks.heading: Long copy, ugly pages, and the slippery slope
chunks.text:
- Sam disagrees that attention spans have changed: "long means bad" is wrong. Long still almost always converts better; the real problem is boring, not long. "Ugly will almost always convert better, but it just has to be interesting."
- Affiliate marketers selling GLP-1 products run 27-minute video sales letters, and he says they work.
- His site copythat.com is about 2,000 words of black text on a white background and converts at roughly 5% of visitors. He says it earns a full-time salary and pays for much of his living expenses.
- The slippery slope, from Joe Sugarman: the first sentence exists only to get the second read, the second to get the third, and so on.
- It leans on the rule of consistency. Example he gives: ask someone to put a small sticker in their window, then two weeks later ask for a big yard sign. Compliance is far higher, he says roughly 40% higher.
- The goal is not for 100% to buy: "It's to get the right person to read all of the ad and a large percentage of them are eventually going to buy."
- The first word or sentence should "punch you in the face".

chunks.heading: Targeting a niche in the headline
chunks.text:
- Name the specific person and they self-select in. "Niches make riches."
- Examples he gives:
  - BuzzFeed-style "50 reasons you know you're from Denver" gets about 30% of Denver readers to click.
  - Homesick Candles sold state-scented candles (e.g. Washington smells of evergreen) to natives and to people buying gifts for family back home.
  - Rolex's "The men who shape destinies wear Rolex" is his favorite.
- Hampton ads he runs say "if you make over $3 million a year, I know exactly how you feel" and then speak to that person intimately.
- Twist a well-known phrase to make it yours, as in "You may get lost, but not in the crowd" (a hostel ad), or Churchill's repetition and the "only thing we have to fear is fear itself" pattern. Sam recommends a book of phrase patterns (recommended by HubSpot's Dharmesh Shah) that lists many reusable phrasing structures, including alliteration.
- His most successful ad for The Hustle: "My friends think I'm smart. I'm not. I just read The Hustle." He estimates about $10 million was spent on it and that it was "singularly responsible for the exit." It originally used Mark Cuban's face, drew a cease and desist, then switched to Ben Franklin on a dollar bill.

chunks.heading: Sentence-level writing rules
chunks.text:
- Write at a seventh-grade reading level. Check it at hemingwayapp.com. USA Today is fourth grade; the New York Times is seventh.
- One point per sentence. Where you would use a comma, consider a period.
- Start sentences with "and" or "but" to create rhythm.
- Vary length: short, medium, long, short. Good writing is like music, with rhythm that keeps attention.
- Warren Buffett explains complicated businesses like insurance in simple sentences. Sam analyzed his annual letters: average sentence length has fallen from about 25 words early on to about 17.
- Hemingway wrote profound things in simple language.
- Edit hard: write the first draft, then cut a third, and keep cutting ("killing your darlings"). Write with the eraser. Quote he shares: "write drunk, edit sober." Get the crap on paper first.

chunks.heading: Stories, the hero's journey, and objections
chunks.text:
- Use stories: "There's no such thing as too long, just too boring." A story has a beginning, a middle, an end and some tension.
- The Wall Street Journal "two young men graduated from the same college" ad ran for 28 years and reportedly drove over $2 billion in revenue. Sam copied it for a $300/year product at The Hustle called Trends, and says it made a lot of money.
- Hero's journey framing: the customer is the hero and the brand is the guide. The Wall Street Journal is the guide that shows the way.
- Handle objections inside the copy, like Eminem in 8 Mile naming every insult before his opponent can. Write lines like "I know what you're thinking. Who is this person? Why should I trust them?" Put them in the copy or in an FAQ.
- Get small "yes" nods early. Open on something the reader will agree with.
- Failed-solution framing (from another speaker in the episode, not Sam's own point): absolve the reader of guilt for earlier failed attempts.

chunks.heading: Worked ad rewrites
chunks.text:
- Sam says generic product-benefit ads ("the nightly drink for restorative sleep") are weak. For a sleep supplement, he would use proof (a before/after sleep score or a customer quote), or an educational ADA story:
  - Attention: "There's a scientific reason why after the age of 35, 75% of men wake up between 2 and 3 a.m." (he stresses he made up these facts for the example)
  - Interest: the feeling of waking up unsure why, and assuming it's just age.
  - Desire: it isn't your fault, here's the cause, here's the easy fix.
  - Then explain why other versions don't work, add social proof ("trusted by 100,000 dads"), and only then pitch the product.
- For glass food storage, he would make the shock visual: "Imagine storing your food in the toilet bowl", then claim that one-year-old plastic containers hold more E. coli than a toilet (he flags it as an unverified example and says he would verify the stat with research).
- For kids' clothes: "Would you put your kids' milk in a plastic cup and microwave it until the cup started melting? Of course not. But that's exactly what you're doing when you buy them polyester pajamas and put them in the dryer."
- Make numbers physical. "150 grams of fat" means nothing; showing the actual block of fat does.
- Bottom-of-funnel ads can still sell desire first and mention the price second.
- Use humor if it is part of your brand. Sam says it is one of the easiest ways to sell. The Hustle used funny headlines and a famous welcome email, written by funny people he hired.

chunks.heading: How to get good: copy work
chunks.text:
- Copy work is the top method he recommends. Hand-write great writing word for word, like learning an instrument by playing Jingle Bells before writing songs.
- Writing it out by hand matters because "you have to feel the texture," and physical practice improves retention.
- What to copy: top ads, classic American short stories, best standup jokes, famous SNL bits and TV scenes, or whatever is considered the best of the genre you want. He has copied Gatsby, SNL scripts and the Boron Letters.
- The same method works for any skill: he recreated Kanye beats, and for design he recreates websites he likes in Canva.
- His advice is about 3-6 months of one hour a day ("copy hour"), then combining what you notice from your favorites.
- He keeps a 5-year journal, writing one entry a day, and says writing things down changed his life.
- Reading outside business is also a source of ideas. He steals headline ideas from Thrasher magazine and other print magazines. Read fiction too.
- He says that he is "not that good of a copywriter", just better than most.
- Two-sentence summary of his story hook: a viral Instagram video (about 4 million views, roughly 10,000 follows) showing his father's one-room onion brokerage that sells about $10 million of onions a year became one of Hampton's best-performing ads. The video's 3-second hold was about 85%, and its average watch time was 35 seconds.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how he went from HustleCon conferences to a daily newsletter that reached ~2M readers and sold to HubSpot. He covers the audience-value math (CPM, niche, B2B), copywriting practice with AIDA, early Reddit/blog growth, selling ads, and why risk-derisking and confidence matter.

chunks.heading: Choosing a newsletter niche with the CPM math
chunks.text:
Sam says to do the math before writing a single issue, because most people pick a topic they love and discover it can't pay. The formula for the size of the opportunity is subscribers x sends per month x (CPM / 1,000).

His worked comparison:
- **UFC picks newsletter:** 50,000 subscribers, one send a week (4 a month), $10 CPM = about $2,000/month. "That's [ __ ]."
- **Doctor/heart-surgeon news:** 50,000 subscribers, 6 sends a week (24 a month), $1,000 CPM = about $1.2 million/month. He notes $1,000 is a high CPM; the point is the contrast.
- Two levers drive the gap: how often the topic produces news (news can go out 6 days a week, UFC cannot) and what an advertiser can earn from each reader.

How he values an audience:
- Value = number of people x how engaged/influenced they are x the price of what the advertiser sells.
- Example: 500 people who decide which supplies a top airline buys are worth more than 1,000,000 middle-America mothers earning $40,000. The airline contract is worth millions; 25-year-old guys who like comedy might return $500 on an ad.
- Brand advertisers just want exposure (his Toyota example). Direct-response advertisers want clicks and sales, so if they spend $10,000 with you they need to make at least $10,000 back.

Picking the niche:
- He uses an Ikigai-style overlap: what you're good at, what you love, what people want, and what people will pay for. "You want to find something right in the middle."
- Passion alone fails: "People don't pay for that [ __ ]" when the CPM is low (sports).
- For The Hustle he did the same math at the start: roughly 1 million to 3 million subscribers, about 26 sends a month, $50 per 10,000 sends, which pencilled out to tens of millions a year. He validated the audience size by looking at Wall Street Journal and Business Insider traffic (tens of millions a month) and trusting his gut that a million people wanted a daily business and tech email.
- His own preference today is B2B only, never consumer.

chunks.heading: Why B2B newsletters beat consumer ones
chunks.text:
Sam says that if he started a newsletter now, he would only do B2B.

- B2B readers spend more and advertisers pay more per reader.
- The content bar is low. "A lot of B2Boring... it's not that hard to be cool." Tech news wasn't a cool industry, so an occasional silly joke made The Hustle stand out.
- Acquisition is workable: B2B readers can be found and bought on LinkedIn. His guess is a subscriber for about $5 that earns about $5 a month in ad revenue (he hasn't run it recently and says so).
- Example he gives of the upside: a friend sold a boring HR-focused newsletter with about 1 million subscribers for roughly $500 million. The Hustle had 2 to 3 million subscribers and sold for tens of millions. His reason: the head of HR makes costly software-buying decisions.
- He calls LinkedIn "wide open" and a much easier channel than TikTok, YouTube or Instagram for this.

chunks.heading: Learning to write well: copywork and the ADA formula
chunks.text:
Sam's first requirement is "you have to be good... people forget this step." His method:

**Copywork**
- Hand-copy great writing word for word for about an hour a day, for roughly 10 months. He kept stacks of yellow notebooks.
- Sources: the "world's greatest sales letter" (a famous Wall Street Journal ad he found by Googling), classic books like Catcher in the Rye, famous newspaper articles, SNL skits (Judd Apatow did this).
- He annotated what he noticed, e.g. a period instead of a comma, then starting the next sentence with "and."
- His written steps: read and absorb; copy by hand 30 minutes a day with no missed days ("skip one day and you'll likely skip the rest"); keep a swipe file of writing you like; spend 3 to 5 minutes copying a favorite writer before any important writing.
- He still does the short warm-up before writing something important, choosing "today I want to write like this person."
- He credits it as the old way writing was taught in America, and says it was addictive because he could send an email and see ticket sales come in.
- Style comes from stealing from about five influences. His: Felix Dennis (How to Get Rich), Anthony Bourdain, David Ogilvy.

**ADA: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action**
- He prefers it to the school-taught thesis-and-three-paragraphs structure, which he calls unengaging.
- Example (drink more water): Attention is "Have you ever seen bodybuilders carrying a gallon of water at the gym?" Interest is a claim that water grows muscles. Desire is the before/after, "do this for a year and you'll look like this." Action is specific: buy a gallon jug, fill it at 8am, finish by 9pm.
- He uses it for everything: sales calls, copy, headlines, popups. The same structure applies to short-form video (hook, build, desire, call to action).

chunks.heading: Writing like a friend to build influence
chunks.text:
Sam says the thing that sold product was making readers feel they were friends with the writer.

- "The cool thing about a newsletter is you write it as if it's just me writing to you, not me to millions of people."
- Tactics: ask for recommendations, share silly bits of family life. His test of influence: email "I need a good book to read, reply with one." If only 3 of 10,000 reply, readers don't care about you.
- The Hustle's positioning: "your smart, no-nonsense friend who's going to send you free news every day."
- Shaan Puri's Milk Road copied this line for line for crypto ("your friend that understands crypto") and grew to 100,000 readers organically, then used paid ads. Sam's own growth ad was a made-up quote: "My boss thinks I'm smart. I'm not. I really just read The Hustle." He spent about $10 million or more running it on Facebook, and says it spread to many other newsletters. He credits some luck.

chunks.heading: Getting the first 150,000 subscribers without ads
chunks.text:
Sam's growth recipe for The Hustle's first year (roughly 100,000 to 150,000 subscribers in 12 months, 250,000 within a year per another point in the talk):

1. **Name the reader precisely.** His: a 26-year-old in New York, San Francisco or LA, working at one of a thousand tech companies, earning about $100,000.
2. **Go where that person already is.** For him that was Reddit, Hacker News and Facebook groups.
3. **Write long-form articles built around a headline (the ADA hook) for those communities.** Example: he paid a guy $2,000 to live on Soylent for 30 days and write it up, posted "I lived on Soylent for 30 days. Here's what happened" to the Soylent subreddit, and got about 50,000 visitors that week.
4. **Publish at volume.** Only about 20 to 30 percent of articles hit, but he churned out so many that it added up. He also used fake bylines (including a female author) and wrote all of it himself at first.
5. **Convert with a custom popup.** It read "Oh [ __ ] not another popup," then explained the blog existed to promote a daily business email, with "if you don't like it, I'll Venmo you a dollar." It brought in about 30,000 signups a month.
6. **Customize the "forgotten text":** the welcome email and unsubscribe page. His welcome email became famous enough that people blogged about it.

Where he'd go today depends on where the audience lives: Twitter for tech and business, YouTube for cars, LinkedIn for B2B. The principle is to build in the audience's existing home and funnel into the newsletter.

chunks.heading: Monetizing: selling ads, then hiring the seller
chunks.text:
Sam's ad-sales path for The Hustle:

- **First advertisers:** around 50,000 subscribers he found marketing managers on LinkedIn at companies whose founders had spoken at his events (35 of them). The pitch: "I have 50,000 subscribers, this is worth $1,500 to $2,000, do it for a grand and if it works keep going." Wealthfront bought and kept going.
- **Ceiling solo:** about $30,000 a month in ad revenue, doing the cold emailing himself.
- **After hiring a dedicated full-time ad salesperson:** about $70,000 a month within two months and $100,000 within a few months. "I'm not that good at selling advertising"; an organized specialist did better.
- **Make advertisers whole:** if a campaign underdelivers, run them again in a later edition. Production cost is near zero. His reason: repeat customers are the key, and an advertiser who doesn't profit churns. He later hired account managers to send results (clicks, signups) and call advertisers like HubSpot and Salesforce to iterate, treating it like enterprise sales.
- Same philosophy on his podcast: he doesn't want a sponsor advertising unless they will make a profit.

chunks.heading: What a solo newsletter can earn, and which model
chunks.text:
- Sam says that if he started again, by himself plus an assistant, he could do "at least three million a year." Plan: write 3pm to 6pm, spend the rest of the day on growth and business development, reach about 250,000 subscribers (he got there in one year), then land five or six advertisers paying around $50,000 a month each. Today ad networks make finding advertisers easier than when he cold-emailed.
- Friends do $2 to 3 million a year with themselves plus two others.
- Paid subscriptions: harder to start, easier to run. A friend does about $20 million a year in paid subscriptions, mostly one writer, over 10-plus years.
- The Hustle's own revenue: year 1 about $300,000, year 2 $2.2 million, year 3 $5.5 million, year 4 about $12 million, heading into year 5 on track for about $18 million. It had both an ad newsletter and a paid subscription newsletter. At the sale it reached about 2 million readers a day.

chunks.heading: Origin of The Hustle, selling it, and mindset
chunks.text:
- **From events to newsletter:** HustleCon's first event (July 1, 2014 era events) netted about $40,000 on $50 to 60,000 revenue; the second over $100,000. He worried a single rained-out day could kill a conference business. A newsletter of speaker stories had pulled in about 10,000 subscribers, and after reading Ted Turner's biography he did the daily-email CPM math. The Hustle launched April 19, 2016.
- **Speakers said yes through enthusiasm:** he told each of 10 prospects the others were interested, promised a car and to promote their company. "Sales is the transference of enthusiasm," and "it feels really nice to be led by a confident person."
- **De-risk, then go big:** he kept $1,000 in the bank as a flight home so every other outcome was upside. He hired people before he could fully afford them to force the business to work. He paid himself about $20,000 a year for the first stretch while keeping $2 million-plus in the business account, which he now thinks was low confidence and says owners often should pay themselves earlier.
- **Early near-disaster:** week two, a stunt where he plagiarized a bestselling romance novel to show a Kindle exploit drew a call from the largest romance publisher; they dropped it after he apologized in a blog post.
- **The sale to HubSpot:** its corporate development contact emailed about a "partnership." Sam replied asking directly whether they wanted to buy, then sent a Google doc of reasons not to buy him to surface problems early. Term sheet October 1, 90-day close, funds wired about early February. Due diligence was brutal for a small company (even receipts and NDAs for a $10 freelance logo). He says rumored prices were lower than the real price (mid tens of millions in his words). Strategic buyers beat private equity: HubSpot's logic was that converting 0.1% of a million-plus readers into $20,000-a-year customers justified buying the audience, which also earns higher multiples than a pure cash-flow buyer.
- Sam's rule of thumb: strategic buyers pay better multiples than private equity buyers who just want EBITDA.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how he grew The Hustle to 100,000 subscribers with zero ad spend, then scaled it with paid acquisition and ad sales. He also covers why he built Hampton as a forever business, how niche B2B newsletters monetize, and why depth beats breadth in learning.

chunks.heading: Why Sam started the hot dog stand and what it taught him about selling
chunks.text:
- Sam grew up in St. Louis, Missouri. His parents owned a fruit stand, which is where he learned entrepreneurship, though "back then they didn't call it entrepreneurship. It was just like making a living."
- In college he ran a hot dog stand called "Southern Sam's, wieners as big as a baby's arm". The work was hard and hot, and it pushed him toward online selling (eBay, then a couple of e-commerce stores) because he could make money from an air-conditioned room "in my sleep".
- Hot dogs are undifferentiated, so he read books on selling. His stunts included a free hot dog if you put your baby's arm in a bun with mustard and posted a photo on social media (matching the slogan). He also riffed with customers to get them laughing, which he compares to flirting.
- The insight that led him to copywriting: written copy can be written once and sold to an infinite audience, not just the people walking past his block.
- He left school and tried to join the early-stage Airbnb (then "airbed and breakfast"), which began his internet career.

chunks.heading: Differentiation beats being better
chunks.text:
- Sam's view: "It's a lot better and easier to be different than it is better."
- He corrected the idea of "sell what everybody is selling but say it better" to "say it different".
- His reasoning: business is mostly perception. He asks whether one car is really better than another, yet people perceive a Mercedes as higher quality.
- He says he learned the effects of differentiation from selling hot dogs.

chunks.heading: Hosting events and book clubs as a way to become the node of a network
chunks.text:
- Sam started events to meet friends. He read a book arguing that to attract friends and partners you should live an interesting life and bring others along with you.
- He ran a business book club, advertising it on Craigslist and in the San Francisco newspaper. About 2,000 people signed up to hear about it over a year, and he met his now best friends (including those at his wedding) and his wife's introduction through it.
- Running it took little effort: read one chapter ahead and lead the conversation. In return he got status and friends.
- He launched HustleCon, "basically like a TED talk for entrepreneurs", after selling a failed-ish roommate-matching app (a "Tinder for roommates", which he says was a much smaller market than Tinder itself). He ran the event to kill time until his next idea, knowing events make you "the node of a network".
- He says he is actually introverted and likes being alone now; the events were a means to get friends.

chunks.heading: Why he started The Hustle as a newsletter and how it grew
chunks.text:
- Three things converged: he liked writing, he saw newsletter founders on Andrew Warner's Mixergy (including Ben Lear of Thrillist), and media companies built on Facebook were losing reach as the algorithm changed.
- His thesis: "newsletters are like a pirate ship and every newsletter subscriber you get, it's like a little bit of a wind in your sails." Two to five writers sending ~1,500 words a day could reach millions of people.
- His math: with five or six million subscribers he thought a newsletter could make $100 million a year. Media execs he cold emailed called the idea stupid; he asked why it matters whether people read in the Gmail app or a browser, since "your attention's there or it's not".
- Growth: 100,000 subscribers in year one, then roughly 500,000, 1 million, and about 1.7 million by the sale.
- Revenue went roughly $300,000, $2.2M, $5M, $12M, then about $18M in the year he sold.
- Luck: there were only three companies doing it (The Hustle, Morning Brew under Austin Rief, and theSkimm), and advertisers started deliberately budgeting for newsletters, which got easier every year. All three founders reached the same insight at about the same time.
- He sold The Hustle to HubSpot at 31. His goal was $20M by 30 (based on a friend spending about $60,000 a month, which he calculated needed roughly $20-25M), and he missed by a year. He paid himself about $2,000 a month for the first years.

chunks.heading: Newsletter growth tactics: free first 100K, then paid ads
chunks.text:
- The Hustle reached 100,000 subscribers without spending "one cent in marketing", via blog posts that went viral on Reddit and Hacker News.
- Method: decide where your audience already lives, create content that gets popular there, and siphon readers into the newsletter.
- Example: because the audience was nerdy engineers, he paid a friend $2,000 to live on Soylent only for 30 days and wrote it up, aimed at the Soylent subreddit.
- Paid acquisition, later: first get to tens of thousands of subscribers organically to prove the content keeps people. Then calculate what a subscriber is worth, decide the payback window, and buy ads anywhere you can acquire a subscriber at that value. He says he and Austin Rief at Morning Brew took this seriously (Facebook ads) when almost nobody else did.
- He says newsletters are far more formulaic to grow than podcasts. For a new newsletter from scratch he estimates six months and about a quarter of a million dollars to reach 100,000 subscribers.

chunks.heading: Newsletter monetization and ad pricing
chunks.text:
- Roughly the first $15M of revenue came from ads alone. He thought ads could reach $40-50M but later said that was wrong and the number is higher, possibly $100M from advertising alone.
- The year he sold, he expected about $18M: roughly $12-13M from advertising and about $6M from subscriptions.
- He launched paid products at hundreds of thousands to a million subscribers, including Trends, which he priced at $300 a year and says was a pricing mistake ("I should have charged way more money").
- First ad: sold in June 2016, about two months after launch, for $30,000 that month. He offered the first advertiser (Chris Martinez at Wealthfront) "$20 per 1,000" with a money-back guarantee, and the $20 CPM stuck. Native ads (about 150 words) went for roughly $25-30 CPM, with cheaper units beyond that.
- At around a million subscribers he estimates each send was worth tens of thousands of dollars (he recalled about $45,000 and said he'd have to redo the math).
- Podcast lesson: when HubSpot bought My First Million it was about 300-370K downloads a month and earning about $10,000 a month in sales. Sam says his team specialized in newsletter ads and "did not know how to" sell podcast ads. The show now makes many millions a year.

chunks.heading: The order of media influence: podcast, YouTube, newsletter, blog
chunks.text:
- Sam's ranking of channels by influence: podcast first (you're in someone's ear for hours a week), YouTube second, newsletter third, blog fourth.
- His formula for media value: number of people x how influential you are with them x their buying power. Low influence over 10 million Midwest moms can equal a newsletter reaching 1,000 purchasing managers at Boeing.
- Podcasts are the hardest thing to grow ("like the hardest thing on earth"), but once you hold someone's ear 50 to 100 minutes a week you have real influence over them.
- He says he's a great writer, not a great podcaster; his co-host Sean is built for podcasting. Starting a new podcast from scratch under a different name in a new industry would be very hard; he calls podcasting "a little bit magic in a bottle".

chunks.heading: Playbook: a niche B2B newsletter to $100M (construction/HVAC example)
chunks.text:
- His claim: almost any business can reach $100M in revenue given enough time and the right model. B2B newsletters are more profitable than anything else he has done.
- Model to copy: Industry Dive, a B2B newsletter business sold to Informa for roughly $800M by his recollection.
- Steps for construction:
  - Daily newsletter, six days a week, aimed at decision makers who buy tens of millions of dollars of products.
  - Editorial philosophy: make a big industry feel small, like a high school yearbook. Name as many names and companies as possible, with quotes from people (e.g. a 500-person company owner in New Jersey), so readers see themselves and their peers and tell friends.
  - Target about $5M in revenue, then launch adjacent newsletters (plumbing, HVAC).
  - Layer on a paid community and a conference.
- Why ad pricing can be far higher than broad newsletters: vendors need to reach a hard-to-reach group. If an HVAC company buys about $30M a year of units, a vendor will pay a lot to reach that buyer. He gives the example of a friend's $100M HVAC business that he guesses buys $30M a year of air conditioning units. Pick industries where many vendors want to reach the buyers and Facebook ads don't work.
- Choosing a niche: "Which industries can I enter where there's enough people buying ads but it's really hard" to reach them any other way.

chunks.heading: Quick takes on other business ideas
chunks.text:
- Car wash franchise: decide who it's for and sweat every detail of the experience. His example is a family-friendly wash painted in bright colors, with toys and coloring books so kids can play while the car is cleaned. Expand through franchising and fund new cities by selling founding or annual memberships.
- Blue-collar roll-ups: he says it's a cool idea but "so much work". He'd rather build a newsletter to $100M, and jokes that he's romanticizing blue-collar work the way someone romanticizes hunting but wouldn't sleep outside in the cold.
- AI personal trainer app: the hardest of the group. Distribution is the hardest part, so he'd need a co-founder who is a fitness influencer with a large Instagram or YouTube audience (offering half the company), while he builds the product.

chunks.heading: Why Hampton is built to last, and the community gap it fills
chunks.text:
- The Hustle was built to sell. Hampton is meant to last "50 to 100 years" because "if you do it right, [growth] should compound", people at the top do the same thing for decades, he wants his two-year-old daughter to be able to work there, and he enjoys it.
- He thinks the wealthiest and most impactful people stay on one thing for many decades, and that huge growth compounds if you keep at it.
- The gap: YPO (about 30,000 members, more old-school and inherited family or real estate business) and Vistage (an estimated $800M a year in revenue, mostly blue-collar owners like plumbing or HVAC) exist, but he found internet-space communities borderline scammy or "broy". Nothing served young-thinking internet entrepreneurs who are past survival and thinking about thriving.
- The problem Hampton solves: after years with your head down you look up and have outrun your peers, so you make $5M, $10M, $20M, $50M decisions alone. "That's when mediocrity tends to creep in" because staff won't be honest, and a spouse knows your personal baggage but not your business.
- Standards: Hampton turns away more applicants than it admits. Rule from early on: "we will never trade off cool". People should join for utility (making more money, building a better business, feeling better), not because it's cool.
- Vetting: he and his co-founder have watched 100% of the recorded interviews of tens of thousands of applicants, and the team debates each one weekly, researching businesses to check they're legit. He thinks Hampton should tell that story better.
- Brand lesson: he started by trying to build Hampton without relying on his reputation, then realized that was "the stupidest thing ever". Leaning into his personality as a kind of "cult leader" increased engagement.

chunks.heading: Habits and advice: master few books and set goals in four categories
chunks.text:
- Read less, master more. Sam says he used to read one book over and over to master the techniques, which is a better way to consume information. He suggests sticking to three or four classics (such as Robert Cialdini's Influence) and reading nothing else.
- On breadth: "there's an overemphasis on breadth of knowledge and not depth", and it's far better to be an expert at a narrow thing than a generalist at many. Test: you could teach it back to someone.
- Goals: set them each year in four categories: family, fitness, finance and fun (add faith if religious). He reviews them with his wife once a month to check they're on track, with specific plans such as scheduling a tour of Gilded Age architecture or a trip he's always wanted.
- Good goals are time-bound, achievable and super specific. His analogy: a trainer can't help you with "I want to be fit"; they need to know if you want muscle, front splits or a fast 5K.
- Common failure: too many goals and not enough reminders. "Distractions are loud," goals let you "put blinders on", and focus and patience are underrated traits.
- Picking a spouse: he calls choosing a good life partner the best financial decision he made, because his wife kept him on track and helped him up "when I wanted to quit, which was often".

chunks.heading: Sobriety and facing fear in his 20s
chunks.text:
- Around 20-21 Sam developed an addictive personality problem with drugs and alcohol and used alcohol to cover insecurity, especially around women. He was arrested two or three times in about three weeks and spent time in jail. Airbnb rescinded the job the day before he started, over how he answered a question about convictions.
- It took about 12 months sober before he felt confident in his own skin.
- His view: alcohol is like beer goggles that blur reality, and sobriety forces you to face fears and consequences. Small acts like talking to a stranger sober build the muscle of confidence, and after a couple of years it "became like a high".
- Advice for young men: don't avoid fearful things, acknowledge the fear and do them anyway. Drugs and alcohol give fake courage and create a bad cycle.
- He notes that young men lack a clear rite of passage, so at 21-22 he felt like a boy who was supposed to act like a man.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how he built The Hustle's newsletter audience: do the email math, siphon traffic from subreddits with viral stunts, and obsess over headlines and welcome copy. He also covers hiring writers, copy work, memorable phrasing, and defining what a brand stands against.

chunks.heading: Sam's approach to copywriting: write colloquial copy, test phrasing live, and steal from the best
chunks.text:
- Sam separates two kinds of copy. Direct-marketing copy (Motley Fool style, 3,000 words that talk you down a slippery slope into a purchase) is one thing. "Colloquial copy" is what he's good at: it's "almost like designing a website on Photoshop and making it look good." He treats it as texture: landing pages "need to feel and read a certain way."
- He says copy matters more than design. Bad design plus good copy can still hit your outcome, good design with weak copy can't, and having both is ideal.
- He wants a brand that's "professional yet informal": cheeky and fun, but elite. His reference points are old Wall Street Journal and New York Times full-page ads, old Porsche ads, and Rolex campaigns, plus Felix Dennis (author of *How to Get Rich*), whose voice he describes as "Richard Branson and Mick Jagger had a baby."
- He builds a brand by mashing together things he's stolen: British racing green, 1970s-80s print-ad sophistication, and Dennis-style voice.
- To find the right phrase, he says phrases out loud on sales or Zoom calls and watches faces "like a comedian." If the eyebrows move, the phrase stays (e.g. "business group therapy"). If it doesn't land, he swaps it and tries again.
- He keeps the vision/pitch language consistent across hundreds of conversations, tweaking a word at a time. He says great leaders and CEOs tell the same story repeatedly, and that this is a form of propaganda: "you have to repeat constantly."

chunks.heading: Making phrases memorable (and why he now keeps "soul" in writing)
chunks.text:
- Sam is "obsessed with phrasing." He argues a rule or message only gets followed if it's memorable. Example from Hampton: instead of a long confidentiality sentence, the rule became "nothing, no one, nobody" (don't talk about anything to anyone).
- He notes that catchy phrases can override logic ("I might as well" keep waiting in line even when you don't want the thing). Good-sounding phrasing changes behavior.
- He studied *The Elements of Eloquence* (recommended by HubSpot CTO Dharmesh Shah) for rhetorical devices:
  - Using one word twice with two meanings ("forgive us our trespasses as we forgive them that trespass against us")
  - Antithesis ("not because it's easy but because it's hard"; "those who can, do; those who can't, teach")
  - Merism, pairing words for effect ("in sickness and in health," "hook, line and sinker," "ladies and gentlemen")
- He says he used to believe in cutting everything unnecessary, then realized "your writing needs to have some soul," and phrases like these supply it.
- He admires writers who use simple language for depth. Hemingway and Salinger write at about a fifth-grade reading level, and "he was sad" can carry a lot. He often checks writing with the Hemingway app.
- Dharmesh's experiment (Sam's account): he built a Zoom plugin to count laughs while he delivered a talk to groups of about 10 HubSpot employees, aiming for a laugh roughly every 90 seconds, and edited the talk to hit it. This year his goal was more memorable phrases.

chunks.heading: Headlines, opening lines, and "slippery slope" structure
chunks.text:
- A 1% click-through rate can become 10% with better headlines, so he says to spend real time on the headline. Early Hustle writers wrote great articles with weak headlines, and he compared it to a tree falling in a forest with no one to hear it.
- He thinks in headlines even while developing an idea: "what would the YouTube title be?" It helps him frame the hook.
- The first line matters just as much. On Facebook, people's eyes go headline, then description, then picture.
- He rejects "it's too long" as a diagnosis: the real problem is "your slope wasn't slippery enough." Make the opening slippery so people fall down the whole piece.
- Length rule he and Perell endorse: write under 500 words or over 2,000, since the middle is "no man's land." At The Hustle, Sunday stories were either long (2,000+) or short, and people wanted one or the other.
- He doesn't buy that attention spans are shrinking, only that people want payoffs faster (a laugh or insight every 60-90 seconds). He mostly doesn't believe in changing trends: "human nature is almost always the same."
- On a homepage: use a clear promise with a number plus a sub-headline that explains it, and make it falsifiable, concrete and visual. His advice on the Write of Passage page was to turn a strong testimonial into a bold claim and lead with it.

chunks.heading: Learning to write: copy work, the bottom fourth of a résumé, and editing
chunks.text:
- Sam learned to write through copy work: copying great sales letters by hand, with pen and paper rather than typing, for an hour a day for months. He compares it to learning an instrument by copying songs, then combining what you steal into your own voice.
- He still does it before writing. He'll copy 10 minutes of a book he likes (e.g. Anthony Bourdain, for boldness) to "get in the mode."
- He says the real writing comes in editing: "nine out of 10 times you write something and the first five paragraphs, just delete it." The first part is a warm-up and the workout is the edit.
- His motto is "Bold, Fast, Fun" (tattooed on his arm). Fast means speed and momentum, and putting stakes on a project by publishing or committing publicly (a shirtless "before" photo, money on the line, or a private blog that exists "on the internet" even if unshared, which he says gets around 100 search visitors a day).
- He captures ideas the moment they occur, using voice transcription on his phone while out walking, and never lets the epiphany go cold.
- He reads about a book a week, with 10:30pm to midnight for entertainment (history, Gilded Age 1880-1920, assassinations, thrillers) and a daytime half-hour to hour for "enrichment" (currently Berkshire Hathaway acquisitions). He uses Goodreads, where reviews are harsher so a 4.2 is world class, and he highlights on his Kindle and writes short notes afterward.
- On depth of research, he praises Nick Bilton's *American Kingpin*, where the author researched the wind, weather and Facebook photos to recreate a Glen Park scene, and he likes that his own neighborhood was described accurately. He also notes narrative nonfiction often smooths the facts into a cohesive story.

chunks.heading: The Hustle's growth playbook: email-first, then viral posts in the right subreddits
chunks.text:
- Sam started The Hustle in 2016 (he was experimenting with email from 2014). His thesis was that retention on a website is hard, since BuzzFeed-style sites must win every visitor every day, while email puts you in front of the audience for free. His back-of-envelope math: 1 million subscribers emailed daily at a 50% open rate is about 15 million opens a day... which he extrapolated to roughly $2 million a month. He says that arithmetic "changed my life."
- Early skeptics, including a digital media CEO, said it wouldn't make money. His answer: it doesn't matter whether someone is in Chrome or an email app, if you have their attention the ad works.
- The core metric was opens, not pageviews. Subscriber path: roughly 150,000 in year one, 500,000 in year two, 1 million in year three, 1.7 million at sale in year four, and nearly 4 million now under new ownership.
- Growth engine for the first 150,000: blog posts built to go viral in the specific subreddits where the target audience already lived. His strategy: "go to where the people who you want already are and siphon them off."
- Example 1: he exposed a self-publisher making about $60K a month by remixing sex-advice books with sexy titles and fake reviews. Then he published a plagiarized werewolf-Navy-SEAL romance novel (picked because romance had the most liquidity: most new books and most buyers) with fake reviews and reached #1 in its Kindle category, to show Amazon was negligent. A publisher threatened to sue, he explained the point, and they told him to take it down. Posted to the self-publishing subreddit, it went viral across other communities.
- Example 2: someone lived on Soylent ("Slim Fast for nerds") for 30 days, and it was posted in the Soylent subreddit.
- He did stunts like these roughly monthly, and the loop was blog post to Reddit to a pop-up to a newsletter signup.

chunks.heading: Conversion copy: AIDA, the pop-up and the welcome email
chunks.text:
- Framework: AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action). Example he gave: open with the guys at the gym carrying gallon jugs of water, claim water builds muscle faster, explain what that means for you, then tell them to buy the water.
- Hustle pop-up copy was written the way people talk in a bar: roughly "While you're here, The Hustle is a daily newsletter. We write these crazy blog posts every now and then. If you don't like it, we'll Venmo you a dollar." Tone matched the audience of a young male skew (around 60-70% young men) at the time.
- He calls the thank-you page and welcome email "the forgotten text," which 9 out of 10 companies leave generic ("Thanks for subscribing, click to confirm"). His welcome email instead said, in effect: when you entered your email a bell went off in our office, our head of operations ran outside and hugged a stranger, an employee started doing 15 push-ups to burn off energy... Then it thanked the reader and said the first email arrives tomorrow. This worked because the brand was a bit bro-y and could be obnoxious.

chunks.heading: Research tactic: use the Wayback Machine to see how winners started
chunks.text:
- Don't copy a company's copy as it is today. Go to the Internet Archive and look at what they said in the early days, because "it's not exactly fair to compare yourself to the final version."
- His method: find a news article announcing a funding round or milestone (WSJ, TechCrunch), then look at the site about three months before it. That shows the positioning that was working before they had resources and breadth.
- It also shows culture and tone the company had when it had to stand out, rather than the polished version (his Shopify example).
- He cites a mistake at The Hustle and Morning Brew: the original homepage was just a plain email box and it worked. Later, committees (people who hadn't looked at the early numbers) added complexity by copying open-menu media homepages like GQ.com.
- Counter-position against incumbents: the Ben Thompson / Barstool pattern of looking at how the establishment (ESPN, New York media) talks and doing the opposite.

chunks.heading: Hiring writers and building the team
chunks.text:
- Sam says he hired roughly 50 to 100 writers over the years, and of the 30 to 40 staff at the sale, about 30 became prominent in the newsletter space or run their own agency or newsletter. He says his approach was "buy her stock early before the market finds out."
- Many weren't writers when hired: Trung worked at an analytics company, Steph was a product manager (he found her through a personal blog post with the headline "To be great, just be good consistently"), and Zach Crockett was a blogger.
- Screening: look for people writing for fun, and read what he calls "the bottom fourth of a résumé" (what they studied, sports, hobbies). He asks for a story about it. His line: if you spent $200,000 on college and can't entertain him about a favorite class, he doesn't want to be around you.
- Onboarding: have new writers rewrite The Hustle's daily email by hand for a few weeks to absorb the voice, then let them go.
- Zach's pattern: every Sunday a long piece, "no deep cuts, hits only," with many hitting 2 to 5 million views.

chunks.heading: Brand positioning: know what you stand against (Hampton)
chunks.text:
- Sam says his mistake at earlier companies was being good at writing what the company stood for and bad at writing what it was against.
- At Hampton, the brand is deliberately masculine in the sense of attracting people aggressive about business growth and emotional growth, with no preference for men over women. He accepts that some will call it too masculine or exclusive and says "it's not for everyone."
- At The Hustle, he hired people who called themselves artists and found they were too slow, a lesson in defining who and what you're against.
- He prefers narrative written memos to presentations because writing forces clear thinking ("you don't have to think clearly to be a good speaker but you have to in order to be a great writer"), and he cites Amazon's six-pager as the model.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how he validates and launches businesses: research obsessively, then act within 24 hours and sell by hand before building anything. He covers why he bootstraps Hampton, how to grow an email list, and copywriting via copy work.

chunks.heading: Sam's origin story: fast action, plotting, and focus
chunks.text:
- Sam's college side hustle: he bought mypoisonivytreatment.com to learn SEO after getting poison ivy. He found Zanfel sold for roughly $50 an oz, and a commenter said it was basically the mechanic hand cleaner "Mean Green" (barrels for about $50).
- He repackaged Mean Green as "Itch Juice" with a Fiverr logo, selling for about $40 against roughly $1 of cost. It did $200-300 a day in week one and later $500-1,000 a day. He quit because he didn't want to build a poison ivy business.
- His rule: when he has an idea and momentum, he acts within 24 hours. He ties this to impulsiveness, OCD, and a habit of giving himself 3 seconds to approach a girl. Early results create dopamine and keep him going.
- He calls himself a "manifest cowboy" and uses self-hate as fuel ("you're soft, you can't pull this off").
- Plotting phase: before The Hustle, he spent about 12 months researching. He maps economics, who is winning, and where they are weak. He cold-calls bankers who sold companies in the space, founders, and ex-employees, and reads Glassdoor, Reddit and app reviews. He keeps it all in a Notion doc, then checks which idea fits his skills.
- He told Shaan (co-host) after Milk Road sold to take 6-12 months to plot with no timeline. Once you have an audience, getting customers is easy; building a product you want to run for 10 years is hard.
- After deciding, he goes all in and treats it like a 9-to-5 (longer in practice). He argues for focus, not juggling many things.
- With an audience he talks less about new ideas before they work: smart audiences copy you, early exposure risks reputation, and too many early customers is a problem. He avoids hyping tests because people read a launch as the next big company.

chunks.heading: How Hampton was launched and run
chunks.text:
- Hampton (joinhampton.com) is a vetted peer community for founders of digital-first companies, like YPO for internet entrepreneurs. Founders need at least $1M in revenue (average is about $30M, per Sam).
- The idea came from a monthly "business group therapy" with Sean, Siavash and Ryan Hoover. They discussed layoffs, what to do with money, and how to sell without looking desperate, things you can't Google or tell employees.
- Process: members apply, are interviewed, are placed in a group of 8 with similar-sized companies and industries, and meet monthly with a facilitator. An online community runs alongside. Example: during the Silicon Valley Bank scare, members got a heads-up and pulled money out.
- Launch: a Google Doc describing it, ending in a Typeform. He sent it to about 50 friends via Twitter DM, interviewed everyone who responded by phone, and with partner Joe Spicer hired executive coaches and wrote a curriculum.
- He and Joe recorded the interviews and hand-matched members into groups. They used his free HubSpot account (from selling The Hustle) and emailed Stripe links.
- It was manual at first and reached multiple millions in run rate before there was a website. Work started in summer and the site came in December.
- "Hand-to-hand combat": some days his calendar is booked 9am to 9pm with customer calls, and he won't build a website until there are sales.
- Why he built it: people said he could only build things because he had an audience. He did it quietly, without announcing it, to prove otherwise. He also had Tiger 21's founder on the pod and interviewed him publicly so everyone had the same info he did.
- Before Hampton, he had run Trends (trends.co), which had Hampton-like qualities, but he felt he got parts of it wrong.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping vs. raising money
chunks.text:
- Sam and Joe chose to self-fund. Before starting, they wrote out what success meant to each of them in a Notion doc (daily life, values) and aligned on freedom: "whatever the hell we want, whenever the hell we want," working hard without outsiders telling them what to do.
- His case: you can build more wealth by owning most of a company you grow at your own pace. A community product doesn't need to scale like software, so he didn't want to be forced to grow fast.
- Raising money still fits when you have "a machine that turns one dollar into five." Then you "fill up the dump truck with money." He cited Uber and Chewy beating Joe's profitable-from-day-one PetFlow.
- Exits are rare: the stars have to align. When The Hustle sold, the CEO had a bad accident a week later. He knows someone who sold a billion-dollar company and made $4M because of four partners.
- He thinks the odds are better with a company you mostly own that sells for $30-50M than a venture-backed one that needs a huge exit.
- He tells people the safest path to wealth as an individual contributor is to join a Series C company with 250-1,000 employees, good benefits and equity with 10x upside (Sarah's List on the pod). His wife joined Airbnb at about $18B.
- Founder pay anecdote: a friend sold a company for hundreds of millions, and just before the wire hit he had about $2,500 in his account.

chunks.heading: Distribution and growing an email list
chunks.text:
- Sam's first 100,000 Hustle subscribers came in year one from long blog posts he posted on Reddit, with about 3% of visitors signing up. Today he would start on Twitter plus the blog.
- Growth rule: aim to grow the list 3% per week (he cites Paul Graham). His team held a Monday "numbers meeting" for years, picking one metric, later two opposing ones (new customers and renewal rate), so none could be gamed.
- The Hustle reached about 3.5M readers (about 2M at sale). He estimates a list that size could make $40-50M a year from email ads alone.
- Paid marketing only after organic: he, the Skimm and Morning Brew began paid acquisition once they had hundreds of thousands of subscribers and understood CAC and LTV (about $2 per customer). Newer publishers do it too early, which makes a leaky bucket and false signals.
