- Paid marketing should wait until about 20,000-40,000 subscribers (a rough ballpark) for a mass-market email.
- List value is roughly subscribers x engagement/influence x spending power. 10,000 CTOs at software companies with 1,000+ employees beat 500,000 stay-at-home moms.
- Real influence shows when readers buy what you recommend, read your book picks, or show up to your meetups. Subscriber growth is easy to buy ("you need a tow, man? I'll get you a tow"), but retention for 3-4 years is the hard part, so get the content first, then the growth.

chunks.heading: Copywriting as the core skill
chunks.text:
- Sam calls copywriting the most important skill: "understanding what motivates people and then using the written word... to get them to do what you want."
- He says it applies to hiring, dating, fundraising for charity, and selling. He claims that given a plain text page versus a designer's fancy page, his words would win on conversion.
- Method: copywork. Print great writing (sales letters, in his case) and copy it by hand daily, the way you learn piano by playing other people's songs. Hunter S. Thompson did it with books, and Judd Apatow with SNL scripts. He says it imprints texture and flow.
- Agora case study: Bill Bonner's Baltimore publishing company has dozens of newsletters and does over $1B a year in revenue, per Sam (he is vague on profit). The funnel: free newsletter or webinar, then a $100 product, then a $2,000 product, and most money comes from the back end. Pages are about 4,000 words of long-form direct response with a small "buy now" link at the bottom. He says the company has been sued repeatedly for misleading claims, but the copywriting is worth studying.
- AI: he is unsure whether copywriters survive, but he says AI is a productivity tool and some humans will still edit. He fed the book *How to Get Rich* (Felix Dennis) to ChatGPT and asked it to rewrite his sales page as Felix Dennis, then iterated and stole the best lines.

chunks.heading: How Sam sizes people up and builds a team
chunks.text:
- He hires for "freaks": original thinkers who take the risky right option instead of the safe embarrassing-proof one. At The Hustle he told hires "let your freak flag fly."
- Authenticity check: he distrusts people who turn on weirdness in the interview. He asks what they read every morning, who they follow on Instagram, and which subreddits they use.
- The "bottom fourth of the resume" trick: ask about clubs or the major, e.g. "what was the most interesting class and why?" If they can't talk with passion about what they spent four years and $100,000 on, he passes.
- His admiration is for quiet operators: CB Insights' Anand (reportedly around nine figures in revenue on about $10M raised, patient for 10 years, low profile) and Dharmesh Shah of HubSpot, who funded HubSpot with $500,000, told Brian he'd be CEO, and still builds side projects like WordPlay and ChatSpot.
- He also admires John D. Rockefeller (honest dealing, left in his early 40s and let CEOs run things) and Rob Dyrdek.
- He says he reads fiction and history now, not business books.
- Biggest insight from HustleCon green rooms: successful founders are not 20x smarter, just braver, and they share the same anxieties. Surrounding yourself with a crew that expects success builds confidence (Jamaica sprinters, NWA, Basquiat/Haring/Warhol). It made him believe he can do almost anything that doesn't require genius-level IQ.
- He says he is not as interested in dinners with the older and richer crowd as in hanging around young builders, such as the AI scene in San Francisco, for new ideas.

chunks.heading: Ideas he sees working, and AI experiments
chunks.text:
- Brokerage businesses: asset-light marketplaces in industrial niches (e.g. bricks, aluminum, materials) where a national buyer wants one phone number and local suppliers fill orders. He says he has seen ones with $50M+ revenue and 20 or fewer employees. His dad brokers onions (to chains like Walmart and White Castle) with one other person. Look for national reach matched with local production.
- Small asset managers: a $100M fund at a 2% management fee is $2M a year before expenses, in his estimate.
- Jackson Greathouse Fall's Hustle GPT experiment (a $100 budget handed to GPT-4): he found it fascinating and sees AI as a co-pilot for business research and drafts, though he still edits.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr tells how The Hustle got its first 100-150k subscribers through Reddit and Hacker News stunts, why he surrounds himself with more successful people, and why he now builds for decades with Hampton. He also covers cold outreach, media versus product businesses, and how to pick a next company.

chunks.heading: Why Sam values being around more successful people
chunks.text:
- Early in his career he started a weekly book club in San Francisco called "the anti-MBA", ran it for two years, and used ads on Craigslist to recruit attendees. It put him next to people who ran real companies, such as the founder who now runs a PE firm.
- At HustleCon he told speakers to arrive hours early for a "mic check" (not a real thing at conferences). Speakers included the founders of ClassPass, WeWork, Poshmark, The Athletic, and the OkCupid/Match CEO. He stayed quiet, listened, and occasionally threw in a question.
- What he learned: "they are not 10 times smarter than me... but they're like 10 or 20 times more successful." The gap in success is huge, but the gap in ability is not.
- Seeing it up close demystified achievement. He compares it to putting on glasses after having bad eyesight.
- He calls this habit "collecting people": finding 20-22 year olds who are getting after it and giving them a shot, and spending time with people doing interesting things.
- His value in a room is as a connector. He brings powerful people together and lets them talk.

chunks.heading: How to get his attention (and how he filters inbound)
chunks.text:
- His inbox, and once his public phone number, drew constant inbound. He defaults to ignoring everything, since "usually people just want something that helps them and not you."
- Pitches that describe what you will do go to junk. What works is showing finished results: "I've already done X, Y and Z, here's the website and here's the results."
- "I'll work for free" backfires. He then has to invent work for you. He'd rather be told which problem to solve, with an example of the solution already built.
- His rule is "No New Friends." He assumes by default you're lying or selling, so you have to prove you're trustworthy.
- On second chances: "people don't change" and "the way you do one thing is the way you do everything." Late to meetings means sloppy. Lie once and he assumes you will again. He is very loyal once someone has earned trust.
- Example of the approach working: Michael and Simran won a viral-clips contest on My First Million (a $5K prize for making clips with a tracking hashtag), then built a short-form agency from it. They already had editors lined up and Sam's number, so they were ready when the opportunity came.

chunks.heading: Early Hustle growth: Reddit, Hacker News and stunt stories
chunks.text:
- With no social following, Sam posted on Reddit and Hacker News. The first month brought about 800,000 visitors to the site, and he says this still works.
- The first 100-150K subscribers came in year one. Method:
  - Write a piece likely to rank in a specific subreddit and post it in about five places.
  - Example: a subreddit with 50-100K people followed Soylent, so he had someone live on Soylent for 30 days. It drew 500K to a million visitors.
  - A strong pop-up converted about 3% of visitors (roughly 30,000 subscribers per hit). He could do this about once a month.
- Stunt articles in week one:
  - He wrote about a man who rewrote Kindle books on picking up women (via Philippines freelancers, clickbait covers, paid reviews) and made $60K a month. He promised readers the next week's follow-up, which was a signup incentive.
  - They did the same: picked the most liquid Kindle category (romance), plagiarized a book titled "Captivating Claire", and reached number one in a niche. Publisher Harlequin threatened to sue, so he apologised and removed the book.
  - A friend's account of microdosing psychedelics (2016) also went viral.
- Sam says the moment they knew they'd "made it" in media was a defamation threat from a billionaire.
- On clickbait ethics: tell the truth, but the best possible version. Compressing details that don't matter is fine. "Bait" means a fake duck; give them the goods. Audiences aged 20-30 have a high BS detector, so lying costs trust.

chunks.heading: Media businesses versus products, and what he'd do about it
chunks.text:
- Sam says it is easier to start with a product and add media than the other way round. He cites Car Wow (a marketplace), Hagerty (insurance) and Bring a Trailer as the best car content, made by companies that have money and "don't give a [___]."
- On media companies building tech products: possible but rarely done. The skills and cultures differ, and incentives conflict. Example: he would not offend a big advertiser if it cost his top ad salesperson (Katie, about $2M booked in a year). Promoting your own product also competes with ad inventory.
- Exceptions he names:
  - Craig Fuller (FreightWaves): enterprise software around $30M plus roughly $30M in ads. He also bought a flight magazine and built a residential airstrip community, using the magazine to sell homes.
  - Blockworks (information product with some data), and others. These are "exceptions to the rule."
- He does not think media brands are dead. Hearst and Fox endure, and Meredith (magazines) does about $2B a year, reaching Middle America. He pushes back on "this is the future" absolutes.
- On exits: media companies get bought because legacy players want the new thing on the new platform. When The Hustle sold he preferred a non-media buyer (he first thought WeWork, then HubSpot). He passed on Vice because it was all stock and a culture mismatch, and Vice stock later went to zero.
- Hustle sold in year four at about $20M revenue. Morning Brew, run by his now-friends and former rivals, is close to $100M a year. Sam notes they could have done it too, and that the business really compounds on a decade-plus timeline.

chunks.heading: Skills and low-lift paths for a young founder
chunks.text:
- His biggest regret is not learning design (or no-code tools like Webflow). With design he says he could mock up a landing page for a software idea, cold-call, and get pre-sales or at least commitments.
- He is not an engineer and hires most of what he builds, but he can write.
- Writing method, "copywork": copy great writers by hand. It was common practice until about 1920. Like learning music, you copy existing songs and then recombine what you notice. It works for comedy, novels and ads, and he does it regularly.
- Why media personal brands get outsized: the niche was small, so being a pioneer (newsletters, five years ahead) stood out, and eyeballs are required. Media is "sexy" and rich people want in (Bezos and The Washington Post). Most people also think they can write or make video, then find it hard.
- His belief: distribution matters as much as or more than product, and second-time founders learn that.

chunks.heading: Building Hampton for decades, not an exit
chunks.text:
- Goal at The Hustle: about $20M after tax by 30, a number a wealthy person once told him was "you're good."
- After selling he spent roughly two years "scheming" before starting Hampton. He used the Ikigai framework: what you're good at, love, the world wants, and will pay for. Too little of any circle gives you a hobby or a bad job.
- Core approach: build something that can last decades, because value compounds. He compares it to YPO and Vistage (founded in the 60s, sold several times, Vistage for billions). He believes peer and membership businesses hold up better than software, which must keep reinventing for things like AI.
- Brand lasting power: green and gold British racing green, Rolex and old Porsche ads as references, the name Hampton from a street he lived on. He likes products that stay unchanged for 100 years (the tuxedo, Rolex, E-Type Jaguar).
- Sustaining it: ask what people will always want. Connection with like-minded, high-caliber people, accountability, and feeling less alone. Same logic as Amazon's cheap, fast, wide selection.
- How Hampton works:
  - Applicants have a revenue threshold; no revenue means funding, or a prior exit. Digital-first. Some cities prioritised for density.
  - Five to six thousand have applied. All who fit on paper are interviewed; his partner Joe watches every interview and approves.
  - Members are matched into groups of eight with similar-sized companies, meeting monthly with an executive facilitator ("business group therapy"). There is also a member-wide digital community and industry sub-groups.
  - Average member revenue is about $25M a year. Examples include Andrew Wilkinson (about $600M company) and the CB Insights founder. Larger founders want to hear what's new from smaller ones, and smaller ones want next steps.
- Lesson from Trends, his earlier $300/year product: he priced too low. Big companies would pay far more (his example: a $30,000 subscription). Packaging for a different customer changes everything.
- Observation on growth: what got a company to $20M usually just needs a few small changes and another 5-10 years to reach $100M. Often founders just need more time.
- He chose to focus on one thing rather than spread across many projects, and he sees most peers as better off focusing. Having money changed his view: with a baseline secured, "the less I care the more easily it comes," and he thinks long-term.

chunks.heading: How to find your next business
chunks.text:
- Write down the life you want: money, revenue, how you work, who with.
- Build a Notion doc of 10-20 industries and business models you find interesting. Research them hard for up to a year, and call the founders, employees and customers for behind-the-scenes information.
- Pre-sell lightly: see whether customers would buy, without actually building.
- Treat it as "dating an industry": talk to many, then pick one and commit three to six months to a single plan, saying no to everything else.
- He calls this "plotting" or "worry time." You don't need the answer immediately.
- If you're just starting out, take whatever works for a first win and financial security.
- Timing: most opportunities don't need you to be first. If an idea still has room in 24 months, don't panic about AI-style hype.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr walks through the stages from $10K to $100M. Early on it's selling a service, asking for money and cold emailing. At the middle stages you need distribution, hiring and systems. Past $10M it's time and patience. He also covers copywriting, peers, intentional goals and integrity.

chunks.heading: The five levels of making money, and what changes at each one
chunks.text:
- **$10K:** sell a service, ask for the money, and charge more than feels comfortable.
- **$100K:** put your head down and repeat the same thing.
- **$1M:** the gap is fear and patience, not knowledge.
- **$10M:** the gap is people and systems.
- **$100M:** the gap is time (or capital and a great market).

Sam also covers copywriting, cold email and peer groups as cross-level skills.

chunks.heading: Level 1 ($10K): sell a service and ask for the money
chunks.text:
- The easiest first $10,000 is a service. Find two or three companies that need something, do it free for a testimonial and proof, then charge.
- Sam prefers products to labor. His own first $10K was a hot dog stand ("Southern Sam's Wieners as big as a baby's arm"), started at age 20-21 with $500 in supplies and a borrowed stand he paid rent on at month end.
- The most common blocker is asking. When the buyer goes quiet after you say "$10,000", sit in the silence.
- $10K is nothing to many businesses. Sam says you probably need to charge more than you think.
- For businesses, the pitch is simple: how does your skill make or save them money? Hustling to $10K this way is "very straightforward".
- The first dollar stays exciting at any wealth level. The fear before starting is the same for beginners and veterans; the veteran knows it's normal and moves anyway.
- He compares it to a cold plunge or a professional runner: it hurts the same, the pro is just used to it.
- To find customers, use your skill. Sam used forums and Reddit because he could write. A service provider could cold call Yelp listings: "If I called 100 people, I'm going to get two people that are interested."
- Sam's "ikigai" check for what to sell: what the world wants, what it pays for, what you're good at, what you care about.

chunks.heading: Copywriting, cold email and follow-up
chunks.text:
- Sam calls copywriting "without a doubt" the most valuable skill at any money level. It's getting what's in your brain into someone else's and moving them to act. "Copywriting is just sales."
- It also works if you're scared of people, because you can sell behind a keyboard.
- Books he recommends: Ogilvy on Advertising, Joe Sugarman's *Advertising Secrets of the Written Word* (he calls it the ad-a-week guide to copywriting), and Cialdini's *Influence*.
- He likes pre-internet direct-response writers because mailing letters was expensive, so they had to be good enough to get a stranger to write a check.
- Reciprocity example: he arrived 10 minutes early to buy a motorcycle off Craigslist and brought the seller a Coke. The seller asked $2,000, Sam offered $1,500, and he got it because he'd been nice.
- Cold email structure is AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action.
  - Attention: something that cuts through, e.g. "yes this is a cold email and it's totally out of the blue, but hear me out."
  - Interest: something specific to them, like an obscure old blog post you read.
  - Desire: what's in it for them.
  - Action: one specific next step, with an easy out ("if you're not interested, just say no").
- "Follow up or die." He emailed Pandora founder Tim Westergren 52 times before getting a yes. He treats silence as "he hasn't seen it yet", not rejection.
- Sam says five of his six groomsmen came from cold emails.
- Everything is a numbers game. Website conversion is about 2% at best, so plan for hundreds of conversations. His Mormon-missionary example is that door-knocking works through volume.

chunks.heading: Level 2 ($100K): don't overthink, then learn distribution
chunks.text:
- Up to roughly $2-3 million in a business, Sam says you put your head down and repeat the same thing. $10K to $100K is just doing it more times. "You can be a sledgehammer."
- He says every business can reach $10 million in revenue and almost every one can reach $100 million, though it may take long or need a model change.
- Getting to about $3-5 million is straightforward and he's done it seven or eight times. Past $5-7 million needs teams, systems and leadership.
- To reach about $100K a month you need distribution, meaning some reliable way to get customers: an audience, buying ads, cold calling, cold email, door knocking, conferences, networking.
- Selling at the high end of your market is about as hard as selling at the low end, so he says charge more than you're comfortable with.
- His first conference had $250-300 tickets plus a $2,000 VIP tier. Someone bought the VIP. He made roughly $50K profit in six weeks that summer and then took a six-week motorcycle trip.
- He says he's never been driven by money; he likes turning an idea into reality quickly. His own anecdote of an early sale: Wealthfront paid about $8-9K to advertise in his newsletter, which he got by cold email.

chunks.heading: Hiring, leverage and one-person businesses
chunks.text:
- After that first $50K he defaulted to hiring, accepting lower profit for long-run leverage. He quotes Rockefeller: "I would rather have 1% of 100 people than 100% of my own effort."
- Hire the thing you suck at. Founders should keep doing sales and marketing until about $5 million in sales.
- Once a company hits $5-10 million, he sees the CEO's job as: don't run out of money, recruit great people, and watch sales and marketing.
- Sam himself hires organized, detail-oriented "nerd" operators.
- Remote and overseas staff can be as talented as anyone, but he finds in-person co-workers add something.
- One-person businesses are possible. His Copy That course makes six figures a year and he hasn't logged in for eight months, but he doesn't find it fulfilling compared with relationships and teams.
- He says a great company is "a dictatorship" in decisions, though you listen to ideas and treat people well.
- He prefers a co-founder with the same values and goals but opposite personality. A partner levels you out, and he finds going solo lonely.
- Spotting a plus-talent hire: if they quit, would you say "have a nice day" or "please don't go"? He's had hundreds of employees across companies and about 8-10 "total killers". A killer tells you about problems you didn't know existed after solving them in ways you didn't know were possible.

chunks.heading: Level 3 ($1M): fear and patience, not knowledge
chunks.text:
- The one trait Sam sees across the many million-dollar founders he's met is overcoming fear and taking the first step.
- The common failure is impatience and no systems or hiring. He knows a talented friend who repeatedly builds businesses to $1-3M, then gets bored after about three years and restarts. Sam calls quitting a working business a consistent habit of losers.
- What you sell matters less than staying with it. His mother-in-law, a Haitian immigrant, started selling decorative throw pillows on Etsy at about 55. She did $200-300K in year one and passed $1M about four years later with around 4-5 employees, spending only about $100 a month on ads and working two or three days a week.
- A million in a year is possible. His own timeline at The Hustle: about $350K in year one, $2.2M in year two, $5M in year three, $7M in year four, $12M in year five, and a planned $18-20M the year it sold. He says he could now reach $5M in year one with that business.
- For getting to $1M the gap is fear, not knowledge. You can Google how to do it, and he says courses help (Neville Madhora's copywriting course, Noah Kagan's "Make Your First $1,000", from which he built a poison ivy product, Itch Juice, that made about $2,000 a month for a few months).
- Lack of focus is the real objection. "Think of A, then B. Don't worry about C and D, but dream about Z."
- Revenue is not profit. A friend at $18M in revenue had only $25K in the bank because growth means buying more inventory, so cash flow suffers in e-commerce.
- A million won't fix your emotional issues. He meets sad rich people.
- Pick a business you'd do for about 20 years, since business is rare in letting you choose your location, colleagues and culture.

chunks.heading: Level 4 ($10M): people, systems and goals
chunks.text:
- At $10M it's people and systems: the right people in the right seats, plus checklists. A VC friend (Jason Lumpkins) told him that once you hit $10M with the right systems, $100M is nearly inevitable given time.
- He thinks the market is big enough for $10M in almost any business, e.g. a laundromat via 100 locations, franchising, or licensing a lead system. He says you can often fix a stalled offer by repackaging it.
- Thresholds like $1M, $10M and maybe $30-50M each feel insurmountable and aren't.
- Sam sold The Hustle for about $20M-plus after setting that target at 24-25. He cites Felix Dennis, who regretted not stopping at about $20-35M, and the 3% rule.
- He says the goals he hit (a ranch, a Rolex) turned out dumb, but he's glad he hit them. His advice is to put your head down and achieve them, then figure it out. Better to drive fast in a direction than to overthink, like the pottery class that made 100 pots.
- To feel like it was real early, he put a large balance into a manual account in a budgeting app a year before.
- Pick explicit goals across family, fitness, finance and fun (faith if religious), "the total man". Examples: a quarterly fitness challenge, such as NFL-combine metrics like bench, 40-yard dash, broad jump and vertical, or a 21-minute 5K and a 300 lb bench in one hour, or a 50-mile run.
- With his wife and with his business partner Joe, he wrote down separately the life they each want at 30, 40 and 50, what they would and wouldn't do to get there, and how they define success. They compare notes and repeat the exercise every 6 and 12 months.
- Set an exit or success definition before you start, when you aren't emotional.
- Luck matters more than people admit, maybe about 80% of his own outcome.

chunks.heading: Level 5 ($100M): time, a hot market or capital
chunks.text:
- Sam hasn't built a company past about $50M, so he's reasoning from others. He thinks the difference is time, "it takes longer than you think". His podcast took about four years, not six months, to reach 100,000 downloads per episode.
- Some people compress it with a wicked market where "the ball's rolling down the mountain", or by raising large capital and hiring the best people, like Mark Lore (diapers.com, Jet.com).
- Staying power: he puts himself in situations where he can't bail, e.g. "burning the boats", and having people (hires, a producer) depending on him.
- Decision lesson from a founder friend: when something fails, ask "are you sure you learned the right lesson?" The real lesson may be not to start the new initiative at all, because new initiatives reduce productivity first. Double down on what already works.
- Most business decisions are reversible (Tylenol's recall/tamper-seal recovery); cap table mistakes are the exception.
- Sort criticism into constructive feedback (your mic is bad) and hate, and only act on the first.
- He says high integrity is the common trait of successful people he knows. His partner pays vendor invoices the day they arrive despite net-90 terms.

chunks.heading: Peers, environment and Hampton
chunks.text:
- Surround yourself with peers at your level or above. He says you don't need a mentor, "you could read a book".
- He cites a 1970s study (people around obese or unhappy people tended to become so) and MrBeast and friends working through YouTube together.
- Hampton's three C's: confidentiality, commitment, candor.
- He recommends being explicit in friendships: opt in, state expectations and goals out loud.
- Normalize success. Treat $100K as achievable and don't put money on a pedestal ("respect it, treat it mean").
- Hampton: 1,000-plus members paying about $15,000 a year, groups of eight meeting monthly with a trained moderator; applicants need $3M revenue, $3M funding or a $10M exit, with a four-step vetting and about 3% acceptance. He built it on the YPO model.
- Sam says he grows Hampton through retention and keeps churn low.
- He sets boundaries: he doesn't travel overnight since his kids were born, works 40-50 hours a week, and accepts he'd likely be wealthier otherwise.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains why he chose not to raise venture capital for Hampton, how he reverse-engineers a business from constraints (Ikigai plus email CPM math), and why aligning co-founders on lifestyle non-negotiables up front matters. He also covers prioritizing audience over advertisers, protecting community quality, and timing exits for liquidity.

chunks.heading: Antler interview: failing to raise money and bootstrapping instead
chunks.text:
- Sam tried to raise money for his first company (The Hustle) and failed. Investors called it "a lifestyle business." He was bummed at first, then thought: "that sounds awesome."
- He frames the choice by goal: if the main goal is freedom and making money for yourself, bootstrapping is "100% the way to go." If the goal is impact and buying a lottery ticket to go really big, raise venture capital.
- He says he is "anti-VC for me," not anti-VC. He supports VC-backed companies he invests in, but it doesn't meet his needs. He admits he may be "selfish": he cares more about his own lifestyle.
- He knows a founder who sold a company for $900 million and made $3 million after raising a lot and having four or five partners. The founder said it was worth it. Sam's takeaway: "then you just care about different stuff."
- He cites HubSpot, which bought his company, as an example of early dilution. By his recollection (he says he could be off by about 20%), HubSpot raised its first round at a roughly $5 million valuation and sold about $2 million of stock, so almost half the company went away right away.
- He says some of his friends sold VC-backed companies for hundreds of millions, while his own sale was "a rounding error" by comparison. He thinks he may have made more money than many of them. They may have more pride and street cred from building something huge.

chunks.heading: Cap table, growth pressure and why Sam won't raise for Hampton
chunks.text:
- Sam says there are maybe only one or two mistakes in business you can't undo, and your cap table is one of them. Taking venture money means "it's my duty now to get a return," which is not good for every type of business.
- For some businesses, growth can really mess you up. He wants Hampton to grow but says you have to be more careful about how.
- He believes VC "would destroy our company." He points to Chief, a similar women's network that raised a reported hundred million dollars. He says its idea, branding and CEO were strong, but taking that capital changed the constraints.
- Hampton will never raise money. Sam says people message to offer investment and the answer is no, so as not to waste their time.
- He is unwilling to pay the price venture capital requires. Raising money, he says, means "signing up for a commitment" and getting a partner, and people often partner without thinking hard. He compares quick partner picking to arranged marriage: it can work and also fails a lot.

chunks.heading: How Hampton got to $1M in revenue before it had a product
chunks.text:
- Hampton chose a business model that did not need outside capital. The constraint was: "we don't want to raise money, so what can we do without raising money?"
- Before it had a website, Hampton had about $1 million in revenue and roughly $800k to $1 million in the bank. The "site" was hampton.squarespace.com, essentially a Typeform. Sam invested zero of his own dollars.
- He messaged people like crazy and ran what he called a "zebra calendar": 20-minute calls with 10-minute breaks, so his calendar looked like stripes.
- They charged members up front. That made members more committed, and the cash was used to hire people to make the experience better.
- Sam's view: it is "a very easy thing to sell" but "a very hard thing to deliver," so the team works hard on delivery.
- Hampton's target is a big business ("I do want to build a big business"), but built without outside funding.

chunks.heading: Protecting the product: strict membership bar and customer acquisition
chunks.text:
- Hampton gets roughly 2,000 to 3,000 applications a month, and many are under $3 million in revenue. Sam says he doesn't remember anyone below that threshold getting in.
- His co-founder Joe watches 100% of interviews and turns down about half right away. Sam says it costs revenue, but the bet is that a tight bar improves retention and growth over the next 20 years.
- Sam's view on audience versus advertiser: the problem with ad-based businesses is that you start asking how to sell more ads, which pushes you to be safe and avoid saying anything wrong. It is tempting because it makes more money early.
- At The Hustle, LinkedIn and Goldman were advertisers (some seven-figure contracts) and he sometimes held back a joke because of that. In one case, the headline "SoFi more like so [ __ ]" ran after the SoFi founder did something sexual-adjacent, even though SoFi was an advertiser. It hurt, but they published anyway.
- He argues that prioritizing the audience ultimately makes more money. His example is Barstool, which was unapologetic toward one type of person, probably made little money for a long time, and then advertisers came once the audience was huge.
- Hampton's top acquisition channels, in order: (1) content he makes, mainly My First Million, (2) referrals, which he calls the biggest after media, and then (3) paid ads, which are "way down" the order. They had only just started buying ads.
- The Money Wise podcast, where high-net-worth people open their finances (income, expenses, portfolio), is another media asset for the company.

chunks.heading: Using spreadsheets of biographies and constraints to pick a business
chunks.text:
- In his 20s Sam read multiple biographies of a person and built a spreadsheet mapping their timeline: how much money they made and the inflection points. It gave him confidence about what is possible, the way seeing someone run a sub-4 mile does. He still does this.
- For new industries he reads about 50 interviews, then interviews early employees to get the real numbers, to understand "the physics of this business and how wealth is created."
- He used this to choose the newsletter business. His constraints at the time:
  - He could get about $25 to $50 per 1,000 email sends (he says $25 at the time, in his words "I think it was $25").
  - To hit his money-by-age goal, he needed a daily email, six days a week, for a niche with a $25 CPM and enough readers.
  - He then asked about his skills: he likes news, business and writing. Result: a daily business news email for higher-earning or aspirational younger people.
  - He projected roughly $100k in year one, $500k in year two and $1M in year three, and potentially $10M in revenue later.
- He says it is Ikigai and that he stole it: what the world wants, what it will pay for, what you're good at and what you love. He spent months on the exercise before deciding "daily newsletter, that's it."
- He once built a similar list for jobs: companies at Series B or C that pay well, have good parental leave, allow a normal-ish life, and whose stock could 10x. They interviewed and editorialized and sold access to the list, but "no one wanted it" (he says they may have executed poorly). He thinks the idea should exist, though it is harder to do now because companies like Lovable grow so fast.

chunks.heading: Lessons from 900 episodes: no single rule, design a rich life
chunks.text:
- After 900-plus episodes of My First Million, his main lesson is that there are an infinite number of ways to reach the end destination. Silicon Valley rules (focus, MVP, working hours) can work, and he can show dozens of people who broke all of them and still ended up in a great place.
- Biography examples: Andrew Carnegie said he worked 8 to 11 a.m. and that if you can't do a day's work in three hours "you're doing it wrong." Sam's point is not "don't work hard" but to read the full story: Carnegie put in years of work first. John D. Rockefeller grinded, then at 36 went into "semi-retirement" and still became the richest American. Sam Zell worked around 100 hours a week until he died.
- On strengths: he believes weaknesses mostly can't be fixed. It is easier to change your environment and build systems that show off your strengths than to fix a weakness.
- He believes in "a rich life," a concept from his friend Ramit Sethi: get very specific about your ideal day, finances and what a full life looks like.
  - He did this with his wife while dating (six months in). Each wrote, in specific detail, what their ideal setup, routine and location looked like in 5 and 10 years, what they would and wouldn't give up, and where they'd compromise.
  - Example: she wanted New York City (her parents live there), he did not. They compromised on Texas first, with summers in New York. They now live in New York, after years in San Francisco.
  - He did the same exercise with a co-founder before starting a company: define success at 5 and 10 years, what you will and won't do (for instance, no sacrificing family time, no venture capital), and agree on the rules up front.
- On his own first companies: he started at 24, and his opinions changed. At the hostel he wanted to hire lots of young, inexperienced people because it felt punk rock. Later he preferred efficiency and more experienced hires. He wishes he had set expectations earlier.

chunks.heading: Sam's non-negotiables and a view on exits
chunks.text:
- Hampton non-negotiables, set early and deliberately: he exercises every morning and has breakfast with his kids; no meetings before 10:00 a.m.; essentially no travel (he doesn't like flying or traveling alone). If a business opportunity requires him to fly, "either that opportunity is no longer going to exist or you can figure out how to do it without me." No venture capital.
- He says the first company is when founders say yes to whoever offers help ("whoever says yes, I'm into"). By later companies you avoid past mistakes.
- On what attracts investors or partners: he used the idea "treat them mean, keep them keen." Show a clear direction ("this is where I'm going, you in or out?"). He says that energy tends to attract people.
- On exits:
  - Timing an exit is "really hard," but getting it right can be the best thing ever.
  - He says many software founders who didn't sell around four years ago "probably should have." As an example he mentions Miro (reportedly bought for about a billion) and says it's not a great sign when a company like Bending Spoons is the one buying you.
  - Have a target price at which you say "mission accomplished" and take it. Selling for cash up front is rare, deals often have lockups, and he says cash in the bank is worth "like 10 times" the equity that could be. For private businesses, "take the money if that's your goal."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr tells Andrew Wilkinson how he went from a hot dog stand to The Hustle exit, MFM and Hampton. He covers why feeling inadequate drives ambition, why meeting successful founders removed his fear, hiring a CEO to run Hampton, and the narrow circle of trust and fixed routines he keeps.

chunks.heading: How Sam got into business and what drives him
chunks.text:
- Grew up in St. Louis, Missouri. His mom was a teacher and his father owned a produce business selling fruits and vegetables.
- His first business was a hot dog stand in college in Nashville. He then saw that the internet was a huge opportunity.
- He cold emailed the founder of what was then called "air bed and breakfast" (Airbnb) and asked for a job interview. He claimed to live in the Bay Area (he didn't), flew out, and got an offer. They then fired him the day before he started, because a background check caught that he had lied on his resume about a DWI.
- Stuck in San Francisco with nothing, he started a roommate-matching business ("Tinder for roommates") and sold it for about $50K.
- He then ran a conference, HustleCon, which made about $60K in its first 6 weeks and roughly $150K-200K in profit in its first 10 months.
- He used that success to launch The Hustle, a newsletter. People laughed at newsletters at the time. He sold it for tens of millions of dollars.
- Near the end of The Hustle, Shaan Puri recorded the first episode of My First Million and The Hustle became its publisher. After about 8-10 episodes Shaan asked Sam to join as co-host.
- His current company is Hampton, a paid community of founders, typically running about $25M revenue businesses, who are interviewed and vetted before joining. He splits his time between MFM and Hampton.
- He says he made enough money that he didn't have to work again, "but I didn't make enough money to please my ego." He also describes himself as an artist "addicted to launching stuff and the dopamine that comes with creating things."

chunks.heading: Why he builds: the hierarchy of motives
chunks.text:
Sam describes his drive as layers, like Maslow's hierarchy:
1. **Stuff:** He wants little beyond a big house where family can visit without annoying him because they have their own space.
2. **Time:** He wants to be a "time billionaire." Life is short and capitalism isn't going away, so "the best way to win is to have enough money that you could tell anyone to go [expletive] themselves and I could spend my time how I want."
3. **Rebellion against control:** His parents controlled the money ("you're in my house, I pay the bills, you're going to do what I say"), so he decided to acquire capital so he could do what he wanted.
4. **Insecurity:** He was insecure growing up (braces, girls didn't date him, felt bullied). Seeing peers like Andrew find a path early, he felt behind. He says he doesn't want to tear anyone's tower down: "I want to have a skyscraper just as big because I want to feel adequate."

He also notes that in school he was liked but never "the guy." Starting companies made him "the guy" in his own clubhouse.

chunks.heading: Demystifying successful people (the hustle con insight)
chunks.text:
- At HustleCon he hosted roughly 150-200 speakers from startups of the 2014-2018 era (Grammarly, Casper, Away, Warby-type names, The Athletic, OkCupid/Match).
- Backstage he concluded most were in the same ballpark of intelligence as him. In some cases he thought they were less smart. Only three or four people (he names Max from Grammarly) had clearly more "horsepower."
- They had the same fears he did. He describes the Match.com CEO as so nervous before speaking that Sam had to calm him down. Others agonized over firing someone, or over how to spend $100M just raised in order to live up to the valuation.
- His takeaway: "the people I admire are screw-ups and fearful just like I am." It was like going from bad eyesight to putting on glasses: "the world is clear, I can dominate this just like these guys do because it's okay that I'm a screwed up person."
- On social comparison: podcasts show prepared, polished versions of people. "Behind the scenes everything tastes like chicken." In his forum groups (about 24 people over 15 years), everyone has something driving them insane, most often people problems.
- He says the best people when they're jealous of someone ask "what are the cheat codes, how do I work backwards from what they did," instead of tearing the person down. Capitalism isn't winner-takes-all, since many people can create value.

chunks.heading: Running companies: delegating to a CEO
chunks.text:
- At The Hustle he was command-and-control. At Hampton he hired a CEO who runs the company day to day, heavily inspired by Andrew's model.
- Sam acts as the marketing department: the podcast and his personal brand drive growth, and he comes up with ideas that pounce on opportunities.
- He plans to launch more companies and hire more CEOs. He wishes he had done this sooner but lacked the confidence and was "too much of a puss to break the mold."
- He still works a "9 to 5." His workload is about 40 hours a week, sometimes 30, sometimes 90. The change is that he is no longer in charge of HR or budgets, and focuses only on where he adds significant value.
- He quotes the idea "there's no such thing as problems, there's only people problems," so having someone else handle them is a good life. He still has one: keeping the CEO happy and rewarded, but he works with him, not with the 20 employees or 50 contractors.

chunks.heading: Money, family, fame and who to trust
chunks.text:
- Parents' reaction over time: for about 5 years they told him to get a real job. After the exit (a headline said he sold The Hustle for a rumored $40M), they asked whether he had health insurance. Later came pride, then a kind of intimidation.
- His advice on money and family: tell relatives that the money isn't important, and "more likely than not you should always say no" to requests for money from family or distant family, even though it creates tension.
- He used to exaggerate prices to look cooler. Now he doesn't disclose what things cost, because it isn't important and he doesn't want people to feel inadequate.
- On fame: the podcast reaches millions per month, around 100 million downloads and YouTube views last year. He feels gratitude when approached but also discomfort for safety reasons, and because he doesn't want to be seen as a guru. "I'm just thinking out loud." He says the real ballers are the quiet people he talks about.
- Trust: he keeps about 5 friends who have keys to his house, access to his bank account, and a role in his kids' trusts, then another 10-15 people he'll share anything with. Everyone else gets a no. The house rule is "No New Friends." He was deliberately rude to one new friend for 6 months because he assumed the man wanted something, then apologized once the friend proved himself.
- He uses excuses (covid, pregnancy, the baby) to decline invitations rather than a flat no.

chunks.heading: Health, routines and habits
chunks.text:
- He had a drug and drinking issue after college, was a college athlete, then got fat and "lumpy" for 6-7 years. After selling the company he spent about 3 years on fitness, lost around 30 lbs, and learned nutrition from his wife. He says girls still don't care. Shirtless posts mostly draw men.
- He took an SSRI for 10 years and no longer does. He credits better eating, much more exercise ("like a dog that's worn out at the end of the day") and a stable, supportive wife. Anxiety is about 50% when the home front is good. He still takes lorazepam for flying due to claustrophobia.
- Typical day:
  - Wakes 7:00-7:30, no alarm.
  - Lifts weights 5 days a week. On non-lifting days he does a cold plunge. On lifting days he also takes a 1-hour walk.
  - Plays with the baby until 9:00, then decaf coffee made with a Comandante grinder and an AeroPress.
  - Podcast days (2-3 a week): prep 9-11, record about 1.5 hours.
  - Lunch at noon, usually a meat and a carb such as chicken and sweet potato.
  - Works 1-5 with breaks every 30-50 minutes to see wife and baby.
  - Gym at 5:00 for about 1.5 hours, dinner and baby time, then Legos with his wife from 9-10 with the TV off.
  - Bed at 10:00, reads 10-11.
- He does mostly the same things every day: same food, similar exercise, similar reading. He is a homebody who has honed in on what makes him happy.
- Tools and products he recommends:
  - **MyBodyTutor** (about $300/month) for diet coaching via texts/calls and a fitness coach (about $350/month) who writes his workouts and sets a quarterly athletic goal.
  - **Ninja Creami** for protein ice cream. One pint is about 300 calories and 65g of protein: a cup of milk, a cup of almond milk, two scoops of protein, frozen overnight. He says most Americans eat too little protein.
  - **Fiv** app plus a Garmin heart-rate strap to stay in his target heart-rate zone with audio cues instead of a watch.
  - **Opal** (and Freedom) to block social media. He is only on Instagram before 9 a.m. and after 8 p.m.

chunks.heading: Reading and learning
chunks.text:
- Reads about a book a week, for entertainment rather than self-improvement. Mostly history, lately some novels. He reads only on a Kindle Oasis (glass screen, side handle for reading in bed) and not audiobooks.
- Process: highlights on the Kindle, researches what to read on Goodreads, and the next morning looks up topics on Wikipedia for context and reviews his notes. He pulls shocking facts for the podcast and Twitter.
- He reads for about 60 minutes a day. If a book doesn't hook him by about 10%, he drops it. A 350-page book is about 7 hours.
- Books he rereads: *Carnegie* by David Nasaw, *Mastery* by Robert Greene (it changed his view from "generalists are awesome" to "you need a skill set"), and *Titan*, the Rockefeller biography. He admires Rockefeller as honest, loyal and confident.
- With Shaan on the podcast, the chemistry comes from 600 episodes together and from "Bro moves," such as always guessing under when asked how much something cost, to set each other up.

chunks.heading: People and sources he's inspired by
chunks.text:
- **Jack Smith:** built Vungle, sold it for $850M at 28, still dresses like a bum, writes to prisoners, and buys thoughtful gifts based on things you mentioned.
- **Laird Hamilton:** admired for carving a path and living what Sam sees as an ideal life.
- **Rob Dyrdek:** impressed him by tracking his time minute by minute and making bold declarations. He bought land for $12M with only $13M and figured out the rest. Sam likes "people that call their shot."
- **Business Untitled** podcast (Mike Novogratz and David Bartov-style hosts, per his description): he finds it better than All-In, with only about 3,000 YouTube subscribers.
- **Baller Busters** on Instagram, which investigates get-rich-quick gurus.
- **Penske Media Corporation / Jay Penske:** owns Variety, Rolling Stone, WWD, Deadline, Hollywood Reporter, Robb Report and Dick Clark Productions, plus a stake of about 30% in Vox Media. He calls him one of the best digital media operators, quiet and profitable, and wants him on the podcast.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains why he sold The Hustle to HubSpot and what he changed building Hampton. He covers prioritizing brand over finance early, charging more, launching businesses to an audience, and the real difference between an audience and a community.

chunks.heading: Art vs. business: why Sam says he is an artist, not a businessman
chunks.text:
- Sam says he is an artist. His art is "pouncing on an opportunity and putting my texture" on it: launching, driving hype, and turning a non-thing into a movement people buy into.
- He enjoys the zero-to-one stage. Around $10M a year in revenue, the work shifts to spreadsheet optimization (moving a conversion rate from 1% to 2%, allocating capital, hiring to a plan). A manager can do that, and he got no joy from it.
- He did not know the difference between revenue and cash flow until about four years into the company. He finds tax strategy and financial analysis boring and says to "just pay someone to do it."
- He tried reading Warren Buffett and talking to hedge fund people, and found hunting for loopholes in numbers dull. He prefers building brands and convincing people something new is worth buying.
- His decisions often make no logical sense at first and only look sensible a year later.
- Brand work is the part to nail early. Operations, finance and tax mess "figures itself out," but "the brand [stuff] doesn't figure itself out." Brand is rare and can't be bought, and more people can fix operational mistakes than can build a brand.
- Early-stage advice:
  - Don't form an LLC first; use your own social security number to collect money.
  - Don't buy a domain; use a free URL like "my product.squarespace.com."
  - Don't collect domain names. Get a sale, a customer or someone who likes the idea before doing any admin.

chunks.heading: Origin: blogging, Airbnb, and building The Hustle
chunks.text:
- Sam sold sports equipment on eBay in high school, worked for Mike Wolfe of American Pickers in Nashville ($10 an hour), and ran a hot dog stand called "Southern Sam's wiener as big as a baby's arm."
- He ran track at a Division I school but quit in his junior year.
- He saw Airbnb ("air bed and breakfast") in 2010 and wanted to work there. He blogged on Tumblr and emailed the CEO ideas to get noticed. He got an interview and a job offer.
- The day before he started, Airbnb rescinded the offer because he had lied about a criminal record (a DUI and a fight from his college addiction issues). He was left in San Francisco with almost no money.
- He kept blogging, sometimes five articles a day, and used the blog to start a TED-style conference. He got his customers to the conference through the blog.
- He then realized email was more powerful than the blog: the bigger his email list, the more conference tickets he sold. That led to The Hustle, a daily tech and business email.
- Early on, he got conference speakers (founders of WeWork, Casper, Away, Grammarly and others) into the green room and let them talk. They complained about the same insecurities he had.
- From this he concluded that:
  - top founders have the same self-doubt as everyone else and are scared but act anyway;
  - luck is real;
  - most are in his intelligence ballpark, and a few are smarter;
  - many are in roles they didn't want but are too nervous to hire someone to replace them.

chunks.heading: Selling The Hustle to HubSpot
chunks.text:
- Sam's personal goal was $20M after taxes by age 30, which would let him spend roughly $600-700K a year for life. He was inspired by Felix Dennis's book *How to Get Rich*, whose lesson is to sell out by about 35 and avoid becoming a "punch drunk boxer" who never quits.
- He sold in part because it was 2020, with Covid and the George Floyd riots, and he thought the world might end. He had also been sick, paid himself little, and felt basically poor.
- In 2019 he hired a banker, who lined up about 10 potential buyers. None were interested.
- In October a HubSpot corp dev person emailed him cold. Sam replied that he didn't want to waste time and asked whether they wanted to buy or not.
- He then sent a three-page Google doc listing every risk (revenue, projections, what could hurt the business) and said to call him only if none were deal breakers. None were.
- Process and timeline:
  - Letter of intent in the first month.
  - Term sheet at the start of the next.
  - Then about 90 days of diligence.
  - Close in February.
- Mistakes and lessons:
  - He had no banker and said his price first, and HubSpot accepted it right away. His lesson: "huge mistake, don't say the first number."
  - Diligence is brutal for the seller, with "the most painful 90 days." A $30-40M deal gets the same scrutiny as a multi-billion one because it is big enough to matter.
  - HubSpot's team said backing out after taking the deal up to their board would embarrass them. He had assumed they would walk or copy him.
  - Secrecy mattered because HubSpot is public, so he couldn't tell anyone.
  - He had just hired a CEO who hadn't started yet and had to tell him he was taking the deal.
- After the sale: he got cash and stock. He recalls the stock going from about $350 to about $850 a share while vesting, and he has not sold any. He still hosts the My First Million podcast, which HubSpot pays him well to do, and he promotes his own things on it.
- On money and happiness: "it kind of does" make you happier. Having money removes the stress of not having any, but happiness plateaus quickly. People adapt, and it's "never enough" even for billionaires.

chunks.heading: Hiring a CEO, hiring practices, and culture
chunks.text:
- Stepping aside was easy once done. He feared everyone would quit or think he was soft, and the opposite happened.
- He says a good CEO often loves the admin he hates, so hiring one is the right move. Not every founder has to run the company.
- On culture: he once thought it was a weak word and now says it is important. Know your values and don't let in people who aren't on board.
- At Hampton he screens out entitlement and complaining about non-issues early in interviews.
- He uses the line "get on the pirate ship": those aligned with the values come aboard, and everyone else gets sailed past.
- Turnover is fine. Someone leaving after a couple of years is acceptable.
- A mistake he made at The Hustle: he told the team he wanted to create 10,000 jobs, then realized he didn't want that and lacked the nerve to say so. He tried to appeal to everyone and lost the juice.
- A strong leader holds the line on what the company stands for. Dave Portnoy at Barstool does that, and the people who are into it become more committed.
- He hated hard conversations early on and avoided them partly because he was young and lacked the tools.
- Hampton strategy for people:
  - Hire few, overpay, and aim for 5-10 year tenures instead of the roughly 18-month Facebook average.
  - He believes the business can reach $100M in revenue with about 50 people.
  - As a "collector of people," he hires the best and puts them in the right seat, because even a great hire takes 3-6 months to ramp up.

chunks.heading: Raising money, risk, and being "offensive" vs. "defensive" with capital
chunks.text:
- "Should I bootstrap or raise?" is a bad question. Raising is rocket fuel and fits only if you want to build a rocket.
- Venture-backed growth math he cites: "triple, triple, double, double," meaning triple annually twice, then double twice. Example: $500K in year one, $1.5M, $4.5M, then toward $50M in about 6-8 years.
- Institutional money means expectations: an exit in about seven years, and you are one of a hundred bets where the firm wants 10-50x. Small seed money from friends and family is different.
- Raising money feels good while you do it, but afterward you carry expectations. This is why he prefers not to raise.
- Many founders who raise hundreds of millions earn only salary. One friend raised $50M, sold in an acqui-hire after five years, and made only about $125K a year in salary.
- Bootstrapped companies can take a long time to throw off cash. He guesses around 6-10 years before an owner can take a meaningful dividend, and restaurants take 8-10 years. Digital products can be faster.
- Be "offensive," not defensive, with capital. When his money was all in the business, he wouldn't let the bank balance fall under $1M and pulled back ad spend even when Facebook ads were working.
- His friend Austin Reef (Morning Brew), who has a finance background, treated it as capital allocation: put money into a machine that turns $1 into $1.50 as long as it works. Morning Brew spent harder when its customer acquisition costs improved, and Sam says that is when they pulled ahead.
- Now that he has money, he is looser and makes better decisions. His analogy is dating: when you don't need it, you do better. His attitude is: "if this works great, if it doesn't, I'm fine."

chunks.heading: Hampton: pricing, positioning, and the audience-led launch
chunks.text:
- Hampton is a peer group for founders. Members are put into groups of eight at similar business sizes who meet monthly, like group therapy.
- Membership requirements:
  - At least $2M in revenue, or $5M raised, or a prior business sold for at least $5M.
  - A founder or CEO.
  - A digital-first business.
  - An interview, and "you can't be an [jerk]."
  - Average member revenue is about $25M, and the ideal range is $10-20M.
- Inspiration: Vistage, around since the 1950s, which Sam says sold to a PE firm for over $1B after about $400M in revenue and $150M in EBITDA. He argues community businesses run themselves once empowered.
- He used ikigai (what the world wants and will pay for, what you're good at, and what you love) to pick the business. He deliberately chose a business people dismiss, as they did newsletters, and plans a billion-dollar company without selling early.
- Pricing lesson:
  - First-time founders price too cheap because they want everyone to afford it, then can't afford to acquire customers.
  - His $300-a-year Trends subscription at The Hustle would need about 100,000 customers to reach $30M, which is nearly impossible.
  - Social apps need huge user counts, and only about seven are sustainable. Meanwhile, thousands of enterprise companies you have never heard of make hundreds of millions selling products that cost tens of thousands of dollars to a sales force.
  - Higher price lets him fund a better service. He tells would-be consumer app builders to map out how they'll reach 10 million users.
  - Higher prices attract buyers who want quality. He would pay $45 for a good protein.
- Launch:
  - He built it privately for about six months with one other person, at hampton.squarespace.com, and reached millions of dollars in revenue without his audience, to prove he could.
  - When he announced it on Twitter and his podcast, about 5,000 people applied.
  - The podcast gets roughly 150,000-200,000 downloads per episode, and YouTube adds more. Most of his time now goes to content because the audience builds the brand.
  - Paid ads are limited to bidding on the word "Hampton" on Google.
- He favors launching real businesses to an audience instead of selling ads: "more people should build audiences and sell real products." He cites the Kardashians and Rihanna as examples.

chunks.heading: Audience vs. community
chunks.text:
- Sam says the terms differ tactically and are often confused.
  - Audience: one to many, like Nick posting videos or Sam hosting a podcast.
  - Community: many to many, in a specific physical or digital location.
- Test: stop creating for a month and come back. A community should have more content and interaction when you return, growing exponentially. An audience-led brand fades with its creator, as Casey Neistat's relevance did.
- A community helps you scale and sell because it doesn't depend on your name. People ask what happens if you leave.
- You don't need a community. If you are an audience company, be great at that.
- A community is like a marketplace and needs liquidity: enough people posting and consuming. Typical contributor rates are about 0.5-1% of active users.
- A forum on your own website is hard because few people will visit. Meeting people where they already are lowers friction. His Facebook groups see 10-15% poster rates. Slack suits professional communities, and he says Discord suits Gen Z.
- Reddit is a great community company but failed at media. The New York Times is an audience company with weak community-building.
- Community managers are a different skill set than content creators.
- He praised Nick's decision to pause building a Reddit-style forum inside his app.

chunks.heading: Real estate, renting, and ownership
chunks.text:
- Sam bought a 20-acre property in Fredericksburg, Texas, Marathon Ranch (marathonranch.com), as an Airbnb-style short-term rental. He intended a fitness hotel but settled on a simple gym with a squat rack, dumbbells and a ping pong table.
- Real estate bored him because results take about six months to show and it rewards patience and spreadsheets. He hired a manager for 20% of revenue, which he calls a lot, and visits about twice a month.
- He says buying a primary home that doesn't cash flow is not a good investment. It is a store of value that grows with inflation at best, and early mortgage payments are mostly interest. Buy if it makes you happy, but treat it as an emotional decision, "just like you do with a car."
- He rents, splitting time between Brooklyn and Austin, and prefers calling a landlord to fixing things. He owns one nice car and says things can start to own you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam argues ideas matter for people who actually ship, and that you vet them with quick back-of-envelope math plus lots of cheap research, not spreadsheets. He shares his research stack (Companies House, SimilarWeb, annual reports, Web Archive), how he cold-emails mentors, and why fear makes companies boring.

chunks.heading: Sam's stance on whether ideas matter
chunks.text:
- Sam splits people into those who do stuff and those who talk about stuff. When people DM him a launch idea, he replies "Awesome, send me the link when it's live" and doesn't read the idea.
- For talkers, he says ideas are irrelevant. Turning what's in your head into something you can see and touch (he calls it "manifesting") is a skill you build with reps.
- For people who already ship, ideas matter. One to three degrees off course early can mean a big gap later, like a rocket.
- He learned this from Kevin Ryan, who was an early employee at DoubleClick and later its CEO. Ryan funded about five ideas a year with $300,000 and had roughly two good ideas a year. The companies that came out of this include MongoDB, Business Insider, Gilt Groupe and Zola.
- Ryan's logic for raising money on a good idea: if you picked the right idea, you've built a cash machine where $1 in returns more than $1, so you pour money into it.
- Sam adds that you need to get quick at spotting patterns, because testing a bad idea costs hours of your life.

chunks.heading: Finding the "spark plug": learn the mechanics of business models
chunks.text:
- Sam compares business knowledge to the "How Stuff Works" books. If you understand how an engine works, you know it needs a spark plug, so an idea without one should be abandoned.
- Good songs share structure (a chorus, an interesting melody, a bridge). You don't reinvent the structure; you add your own texture within the rules. Business ideas are similar.
- Every day he makes "a really small sketch of how a thing works" for whatever he buys or visits. He checks SimilarWeb on any interesting site, even a Topo Chico or a mattress company, and runs this on about five companies a day.
- He sees this as curiosity plus obsession, and says it also normalizes success: the more you see how things work, the less complicated they look.

chunks.heading: Back-of-the-envelope validation instead of spreadsheets
chunks.text:
- Sam calls detailed financial modeling early on procrastination driven by fear. He fights the urge himself and says he has to "bully myself" out of it.
- Kevin Ryan taught him that you only need back-of-the-envelope math.
- His example for The Hustle:
  - Several people told him a high-quality newsletter audience can earn about $25 per 1,000 sends (he says "per 1,000 cents").
  - Business Insider reportedly had 80M monthly visitors for tech news, so a million interested people seemed plausible.
  - 1M readers at $25 per 1,000 is $25K per send, times 30 days, which he put at "around 10 million a year in revenue".
  - If it can make $10M, he figured he could find a way to $50M or $100M.
- His first check is who else is in the market and how big they are. A company at $1B proves the idea is physically big enough.
- He doesn't need a first-mover: Salesforce already existed when HubSpot started, and the point is that a market is big enough to pursue and you figure out the rest along the way.
- When a partner proposed building a revenue-model spreadsheet for a side project, he said he didn't care. His view is that models become necessary at roughly $30-50M, when executives need targets, and before that they can hurt you.
- Modeling is useful to avoid downside in a big business. If you're trying to maximize upside, it's mostly a set of assumptions that won't capture the crazy thing that works.
- Even so, he says new ideas still need assumptions (is 3% conversion too high, is 1%?), which you get by researching how others do it, not by building a model.

chunks.heading: Sam's research toolkit
chunks.text:
- **Companies House (UK):** private UK companies above a revenue threshold (he says about $20M, possibly $10M) must file income statements, free and public. He found a VPN review site that owned several VPN companies. The company, Compare Tech, had about $15M revenue and $13M profit with 3-4 people and almost no marketing cost, and was acquired for about $150M roughly six months after he researched it. Lesson he took: search traffic in a rising market can unlock a lot, and a VPN with 5-6 people is probably a commodity.
- **SimilarWeb (browser plugin):** treat traffic numbers as directional only (divide or multiply by 2-3). He looks for four signals:
  - monthly visits above about 3M
  - traffic source (direct and search are interesting; social is less so)
  - time on site
  - which sites refer traffic
- **annualreports.com:** read the S-1 or annual report of public companies. Example: Tech Target owns about 31 niche sites (CIO-type sites) that sell leads from webinars and white papers to software vendors, with about 3M monthly visitors. The filing explains exactly how the business works and what's possible at that traffic.
- **Web Archive:** go back to a company's first months and see how it positioned itself, then pair that with news from each year. His example is Pandora, which started as software so Best Buy could recommend CDs in store kiosks, then became one of the first iPhone apps. He builds a timeline in a sheet and looks for the platform jump that drove growth.
- Other sources he lists:
  - Facebook Ad Library, to see successful advertisers' positioning and targeting
  - Moat, for banner ads
  - SEMrush, for search ads
  - Jungle Scout, SEO-style data for Amazon
  - Glassdoor, to read what employees say about churn, management and the business
  - newspapers.com, for press on pre-internet companies
  - LinkedIn profile searches, e.g. "HubSpot LinkedIn sales quota" to find typical quotas, or "The Hustle writer articles" to see how many pieces writers produce
  - reviews: Google "[company] reviews", Reddit, Amazon, Etsy and iTunes app reviews, to learn a product's strengths and weaknesses

chunks.heading: Example: turning SimilarWeb research into a tested business (erotic fiction)
chunks.text:
- Sam read that Crunchyroll sold for about $1B. He put it in SimilarWeb and saw a "similar" site, Literotica, an ugly, 1999-looking site for erotic stories.
- SimilarWeb showed about 60M monthly visits and an average 17-minute session. His reasoning: even with only banner ads, that's a big business.
- To test his research method, he built a one-story site:
  - hired a writer on Fiverr for an erotic story and another Fiverr freelancer for an audio version
  - offered part one to read or listen to
  - ran $500 of Facebook ads
  - the end of the page offered $5 per month for part two and new parts monthly
- In one night he collected $500 from the $500 in ads, then refunded the buyers because it was only a test.
- He handed the project to a trend subscriber, who sold it about six months later for $500,000, after about $150K in revenue and a team of around five writers.
- He still thinks "Audible for erotic stories geared towards women" could be fairly big.

chunks.heading: Building a network by persistent cold outreach
chunks.text:
- Sam found Kevin Ryan's email by typing "Kevin at [his incubator's domain]" into Gmail. He sent about 30 emails before getting a reply.
- Early emails were short updates: what he was building (The Hustle, partly inspired by Ryan's Business Insider), progress so far, and an invitation to point out mistakes. After about seven he got one line: "you're on the right track."
- When he told Ryan he'd be in New York, Ryan gave him 30 minutes. He says he flew there just for that meeting.
- He still cold emails and DMs people all the time, often asking for nothing and only complimenting them. Over time he built a reputation as a doer, which attracts other doers (he cites Dharmesh Shah).
- He keeps outreach casual, sometimes just messaging "what's up?" without a reason.
- He says he sends a few well-chosen one-line questions to people with perspective he lacks and gets a lot of value from a short reply.

chunks.heading: Keep new things weird and low-stakes; don't operationalize early
chunks.text:
- Sam's advice to a $300M/year company that wanted a newsletter for non-converting customers: don't hire a team and operationalize it.
  - Hire one competent writer and send a weekly email to about 10 internal people.
  - After 3-4 weeks expand to about 30 people, then 50, including the CEO.
  - Don't act on all the feedback, since everyone complains about something.
  - After a couple of months, launch to customers.
- His reason: a hired writer who is nervous will write how she thinks she is supposed to write, not what customers want, and can feel she'll be fired if it fails. You need to remove consequences so she can take risks.
- At The Hustle he celebrated attempts that failed and used the phrase "let your freak flag fly". His rule was that you won't be in trouble for swinging and missing, but you will be for not swinging.
- He says boring companies are often the result of operationalizing too early and scaring employees.

chunks.heading: Everyone is afraid, so the real blocker is fear, and learn from direct marketing
chunks.text:
- Hosting HustleCon gave him a view into 150-200 founders, including WeWork's Miguel McKelvey, Classpass's Payal Kadakia, Casey Neistat, ThredUp, Zapier and The Athletic's founder. Backstage they confessed fears: avoiding firing a bad employee for two years, doubting profitability, and the grind of renewals.
- His takeaway: most people are only a few percent smarter than he is. The difference is they act while still unsure. Feeling afraid is normal and shouldn't stop you.
- He distrusts people who make their work sound complicated. If he can't understand what someone does, he reads it as their problem, not his.
- He learned marketing on the Warrior Forum and in affiliate and black-hat SEO circles rather than from an MBA. He says you can learn from even unethical operators.
- He cites ClickFunnels as a company whose product is inferior to HubSpot's but whose direct-response marketing is very effective. He recommends combining direct-marketing skills with startup-style product focus and hiring.
- Long-form copy often outperforms minimal copy. He points to Hey.com, Basecamp and Apple's Kindle page, which is roughly 3,000-4,000 words. His reasoning is that with a new product you need many words to explain it, and a 1% conversion rate could rise to 5% if a few more people read.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how he reverse-engineers successful businesses, builds from a narrow niche, and uses staged goals and stakes to scale. He covers newsletter and podcast content tradeoffs, the founder growth stage shift around $10M revenue, and how Hampton plans to scale through trained local moderators.

chunks.heading: Sam's path into media and why email newsletters worked
chunks.text:
- After moving to San Francisco, Sam cold emailed the Airbnb founders and got a job offer. They fired him the day before he started because he hadn't disclosed a pending DUI during the interview process. He calls the firing warranted ("lying by omission").
- He joined a startup that did "okay," then a second one where he was killing time looking for a big idea. He started a conference called HustleCon.
- He read Dale Carnegie-style books as a kid ("how to make people like me") and was drawn to salesmanship. His friend Neville Madora showed him a video on the power of copywriting, which convinced him written words could persuade at infinite scale.
- Newsletter insight: he noticed internet-marketer friends sold large amounts relative to the size of their email lists. He then saw an interview with Ben Lear (Thrillist) describing their newsletter-era numbers (the interview was from roughly 2008-2010; Sam watched it in 2014) and concluded it would still work.
- He started a blog of viral stories, getting about a million visitors in month one. Two early viral posts: a recap of Pandora CEO Tim's story of going 2 years unable to pay full wages (told live at one of Sam's events), and a story about a friend buying LSD on the Silk Road for medical use.
- The math he used: if a million people sign up and he emails them 5-6 days a week, it should be far more lucrative than chasing site traffic.
- Early on he had to convince advertisers that newsletters mattered; a friend told him a newsletter could never make more than $1 million. Sam's counter: in an email app on your phone, nobody cares whether it's Chrome or not.
- He says the playbook still works. More competition makes attention harder, but tooling is far better than when he had to duct-tape WordPress together. He hears that ad rates have since come down.

chunks.heading: Headlines, copywriting and writing for your target reader
chunks.text:
- Sam starts any piece with the headline, sub-headline, first sentence and image in mind, in that order. Readers drop off sharply after the top, so he obsesses over it.
- Each sentence should be "a slippery slope that drags you down to the bottom." He admits this is manipulative but compares it to a good fiction book keeping you on edge.
- He writes for his target person (basically himself), uses jargon and doesn't dumb things down, and assumes the reader is smart. Non-target people can consume it voyeuristically.
- Analogy: Nike's ads show ripped pro athletes, but most buyers aren't ripped. Appeal to the ideal customer; others will watch anyway.
- He cites Shane Smith (Vice): the best way to get through someone's "[ __ ] detector" is "don't [ __ ]."
- Insider jokes and inside baseball make core fans love you more: "cults have rituals, put them in your content." Don't fear that some readers won't get it.
- Pure-utility content is a strong position but harder to do.
- On AI writing: he doesn't use it for writing. He uses it for research and ideation, for example finding studies and story hooks (the "Michelangelo effect" story, and a study showing you tend to resemble the people you grew up around) for copy about why groups matter. He says it's bad at long-form sales copy and journalistic writing, and that AI writing is an instant turn-off when he reads applicants' work.

chunks.heading: Content strategy: serve your taste, accept the tradeoff with views
chunks.text:
- On My First Million (about 850 episodes, millions of monthly listeners), Sam says podcast downloads are very consistent month to month, only slightly higher each time, while YouTube views are highly variable.
- When the team chases views, those are typically episodes he hates doing, and view counts "go through the roof." Episodes he loved often get little traction.
- They tested it deliberately for a month or two: chase numbers, then not, and compared the revenue difference. His default is 80% do what they want, 20% serve the listener.
- YouTube is driven by thumbnail and title ("get rich doing this") and it is "easy to appeal to the lowest common denominator."
- Sam's rule on the audience: don't dumb it down for the broad audience, write for the target person. He doesn't track audience breakdowns closely ("the analytics are pretty [ ] and I just don't care").
- He doesn't push "everyone should be an entrepreneur." He says most entrepreneurs fail, and the show's message is that there are a million ways to get done what you want. One example is "Sarah's List": companies with 500+ employees, good maternity leave, pay, and stock options with 10x potential, for his wife's career.
- He had his mother-in-law, a Haitian immigrant in her 50s, on the show. He told her the basics of Shopify when she wanted to start a pillow business; she built the site in 2 weeks and the business now makes millions a year. He says he enjoyed that interview as much as Ray Dalio's.

chunks.heading: Advertising independence and editorial integrity
chunks.text:
- Sam is not against advertising but does not want it to be the main way he makes money.
- Example: at the Hustle, an advertiser (SoFi) had a CEO who got into trouble over sexual misconduct. The Hustle's headline was "SoFi, more like So [ ]," and they ran it even though it cost his salesperson commission. He says he hated having to choose between ad revenue and telling the truth.
- He notes subscriptions have the same issue: he knows which stories drive subscribers and could game them. His view is that "everything's gameable," so be aware of it and try to stay true.
- This is a reason he prefers revenue models (subscriptions, events, community) that don't depend on advertisers.

chunks.heading: Building Hampton: studying old communities and the business model
chunks.text:
- At the Hustle he launched "Trends," a paid research product on deconstructing businesses.
