He didn't remember the exact numbers but says it reached roughly $4-5 million a year in subscription revenue with about 3 people, at about $300 a year. A companion Facebook group reached about 20,000 members in a year and people said the community was better than the newsletter.
- After leaving, he studied older community businesses: YPO (founded around 1958), Vistage (he says roughly $600-700 million a year in subscription revenue), and World 50 (Fortune 500 executives, hundreds of millions in revenue). Their longevity (30 to 60+ years) convinced him to build a community business that could last 50-100 years.
- He used the "ikigai" framing: what you're good at, what you love, what the world wants and will pay for.
- First attempt targeted VPs of marketing, which he calls stupid and which failed. His partner pushed him to try CEOs, and it worked.
- First format: 8-person core groups with a moderator meeting monthly on Zoom. As Zoom fatigue and post-COVID demand for in-person grew, about 20 months ago they pivoted to in-person groups in each city. They now have 18 chapters.
- Hampton requires at least $3 million in revenue to interview; the average member does roughly $20-30 million. He bootstraps and has raised no money.
- He says Hampton's main member sources are people who've heard him mention it and member referrals. They spend very little on ads.
- He made a deliberate decision early that Hampton "can't be the Sam show." He's been to few of the chapters. His advice: you can fix being the central figure once you reach about 20 employees, but you must get over thinking no one can do it as well as you and over the fear of letting go.
- His partner Joe is CEO of Hampton. Sam says he is "not a very good CEO."

chunks.heading: Scaling Hampton to a billion in revenue: the moderator model
chunks.text:
- Sam says the way to a billion in revenue is more chapters through trained moderators.
- About 90 moderators currently, mostly with executive-coach backgrounds, paid to run groups. They are conveners, not coaches: they draw people out ("last month you said this, give us an update"), handle scheduling and enforce group norms (some groups fine members $100 per minute late), and help organize retreats.
- Plan: let applicants become moderators, put them through a 10-day training, then send them to their own city (the example list included Berlin, Paris, Birmingham, Alabama). Hampton has marketing that already generated about 100,000 applicants to join.
- It isn't legally franchising, though he says it works like one: the brand stands for something, moderators are trained, and there is give and take on local flexibility.
- He believes this could produce hundreds of new moderators per year and tens of thousands of members, with a built-in global ecosystem (a member in Atlanta flying to Hong Kong has a local network).
- Scope is "tech enabled": an HVAC company counts if it uses technology, but not someone who owns 10 apartments in Miami. He isn't in the real estate business and rules out physical spaces like a club.
- He thinks the same model should be done for other industries (for example dentists), noting groups for religions and new moms already exist.

chunks.heading: Studying winners and the A-B-C goal method
chunks.text:
- Sam's core skill, in his words, is studying people and reverse engineering them: "I'm going to steal that from you."
- Process: become a historian for roughly 6 months. Find the first employees and current employees of comparable businesses and interview them about everything that made them succeed and what dragged them down. Then copy the winners, avoid the losers' mistakes, and do it in your own niche with your own taste and style.
- He describes it as like Nike versus New Balance: similar products with small differences that change everything.
- He says this raises the odds of winning above reinventing the wheel, though the plan isn't guaranteed (he avoids the word "playbook" because unknowns will pop up).
- Example of studying events: he recommends studying Bisnow (sold for about $60 million in 2016, bought by Morning Brew; hosts 2-hour 9-11 a.m. events and real estate newsletters across markets; he estimates it may now be around $60-70 million in revenue).
- The ABC method: set a Z goal (for example $50 million in revenue in five years), work out the growth rate and attributes needed, then only focus on the next step (B) of roughly 3 to 6 months. When you reach B, set C, then D. Don't worry about later steps.
- Example B goal: go from $2 million to $3 million a year by spending more on ads to get subscribers and hosting 50 events. A different profit-based version works too, he said. Make profit the goal if that's what you want.
- Analogy: to bench 300 lb, you talk to trainers, eat 200g protein a day, lift 3 days a week with 5x5 near failure. It's not guaranteed, but far better than random gym time.
- Staying on track: build systems with stakes (hire a large team so you get dragged toward the goal even on days he complains; posting a shirtless photo monthly to lose weight). "Discipline is not nearly enough."
- Constraints: "constraints are key when you're starting a company."

chunks.heading: Hiring, management, working hours and company-stage lessons
chunks.text:
- Sam says his strength is hiring good people and letting them do their own thing. At the Hustle he had about 30 employees at the sale; he says roughly half became "newsletter millionaires" or ran their own newsletter businesses. They were good at finding outcasts and empowering them.
- He says he's not a good manager: he ranks high on neuroticism, thinks nothing is good enough and wants everything better immediately, and wears people thin. He needs someone as a buffer. He says kids and success have made him more patient and less caring in a good way.
- Working hours: about 40 hours a week (10 to 5 or 6) but thinks about work constantly. He doesn't believe in 996. His view is that people claiming 60-70 hour weeks mostly work in sprints or waste time. He says having kids made him "way less ambitious" and he doesn't like that feeling.
- The messy middle: he says the hardest stage of business is between roughly $1 million and $10 million in revenue. It's where you're hiring a real team but still constrained.
- Hampton data point: he reviewed about 5,000 interview transcripts of applicants (those with $3 million+ revenue). Between $3 million and $10 million, founders talked mostly about money problems. After $10 million the talk is about hiring and scaling problems. There is a distinct drop-off at $10 million (possibly as low as $5 million), which he ties to a CEO moving from "what/why" to "who."
- Current Hampton weaknesses he names: branding and copywriting ("ironic given that's my thing"). What's going right: the pivot to in-person, strong hires, and a strong executive team.

chunks.heading: AI's effect on agencies, his AI use, and media predictions
chunks.text:
- Sam rates himself an intermediate AI user; his team and business partner are far more advanced (his partner sends him AI-built dashboards). He uses Claude daily, has made a couple of Chrome plugins, and lets new tools go into his workflow.
- He thinks agencies are the biggest near-term winners: agencies have been easy to start but painful to run since growth meant adding more people and client services is hard. AI changes margins because fewer, more talented people can do high-quality work, so he expects agency valuation multiples (public and private) to rise.
- His personal setup: "Ari," a fictional AI persona (styled after a young Jackie Kennedy) who reads his texts, Slack and email plus news he cares about and prints a personalized newspaper each morning. He has made other personas with different political takes. The printer breaks about half the time.
- Business idea he offers: an all-AI New York Times, a physical paper or newsletter produced by AI personas that eventually do their own scoops. He acknowledges many will hate it.
- Luddite history he told: weavers in England (about 300,000 to 400,000 artisans) smashed steam-powered machines; destroying them became a capital offense. They signed letters as "General Ludd." He says refusing AI means you'll get left behind if your goal is to get rich, but you may choose a happier life. He adds, "I just don't think your emotions matter that much" if you set a goal to build a company, though "not using AI" could itself be a marketing angle.
- He is glad his own business is human-driven (events, groups), and says he picked it for durability, not AI reasons. He was always nervous about depending on Gmail changes at the Hustle ("a newsletter is like a pirate ship, every email is more wind in your sails").
- On the OpenAI-TBPN deal: he thinks it was great for John and Jordy but "stupid" for OpenAI, and predicts OpenAI will give the company back within two years, after which the founders "win twice."

chunks.heading: Corporate media inside a company, and how a startup founder should get attention
chunks.text:
- Sam says starting a funny or opinionated media company inside an organization is nearly impossible, because employees don't want to get fired and the voice gets sanded down. Successful ones need a powerhouse opinionated person with free rein.
- HubSpot bought the Hustle largely because they couldn't build a media program themselves. Its CEO Brian Halligan told Sam that if anyone ever tried to censor him, he should text Halligan directly, and nobody has ever told Sam not to say something. Sam says the Hustle (now HubSpot Media) and My First Million drive large amounts of lead generation and revenue for HubSpot.
- Advice for a startup founder who wants attention: pick a super niche, narrow field (probably one you think is too small), and share about it every single day. Make it jargon-filled and esoteric; once you build that nucleus it's much easier to expand.
- Be specific about who you appeal to and who you don't. Have an enemy and be willing to "piss that person off." Define the audience narrowly across demographics and psychographics and only appeal to that person.
- Example: Derek of Die, Workwear, who posts hyper-niche menswear content for about 15 years, grew huge, and got a lift when Elon bought Twitter.
- Media people he admires: Lenny and Newcomer, practitioners who are niche and don't answer to anyone. He notes writing is harder than people think ("just cuz you've always thought about running doesn't mean you can run a marathon"), and says to just start writing a few posts rather than dreaming about it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle grew to nearly 2M subscribers, what due diligence on the HubSpot sale was like, and how he hires and hands off. He gives concrete advice on paid newsletters: charge more, bill annually, and use a long-form sales page as your homepage.

chunks.heading: Sam's experience selling The Hustle to HubSpot
chunks.text:
- HubSpot cold emailed Sam in October. The deal was announced on the last day of January, about 90 days from first contact to close.
- Sam had received buyer approaches for a long time. Early on he took them seriously and prepared; later he sent a one-pager listing why a buyer should and should not buy The Hustle, plus the pricing expectation, then "if you want to talk, call me." He says most people don't do this and HubSpot liked it.
- Due diligence was painful. He had a spreadsheet with about eight tabs (real estate, IT, revenue and P&L, daily email, trends and others), each with roughly 150 questions. He estimates he gave them 500 to 700 items, including things like aging accounts receivable by year for five years.
- His support was thin: one finance person (Edie), an outside law firm, an outside tax firm, and himself. He had to do much of it in private because employees couldn't be told.
- He notes founders and CEOs push to close fast, while the people doing the work need to button everything up carefully.
- He declined to disclose the price. His reasoning: he thinks it's weird that anyone can Google the HubSpot CEO's salary and share sales, and the CEO agreed. He won't confirm or deny press reports of the figure.
- Why he sold: he had raised a little angel money and felt a duty to return it to investors, and the deal let him hit a personal goal of making enough by about 35 to live lavishly and leave a large sum to his children. He says he now never wants to sell anything again and wants to own things forever.
- A serious illness (Lyme disease with facial paralysis) made him want enough wealth that an emergency wouldn't ruin him.
- He structured the business early so that employee profit sharing was nearly impossible to reverse later, and wishes he had set it up differently.

chunks.heading: How The Hustle ran with Sam hands-off
chunks.text:
- Just before the sale he had made an offer to a CEO hire, which he rescinded when the HubSpot offer came.
- His operating pattern: start something, then hand it off. He sold the first $150,000 of advertising himself, hired a salesperson, and never sold again.
- He sets revenue targets with the sales team and growth targets with the growth team, then leaves them alone. If a team struggles, they ask for help and he drops in with introductions, creative ideas, or his personal brand.
- For new products he locks himself in a room and does it nearly alone. For Trends he took the first $50,000 in pre-sales on Gumroad and personally called customers to ask why they bought. Once it showed signs of working, he handed it to more skilled operators.
- His view: most people are bad at starting things, so use the few who are good at it for new stuff and put others on running it. He says a company that gets ADD can be ruined, and that he'd be bad at day-to-day operations.
- On hiring: early on you can only afford a $40,000 person who is smart but unskilled, or driven but inexperienced. Once bigger, hire people who have done the exact job before. He recounts Andrew Wilkinson's advice: "just go find someone who's already done this before," like hiring a mechanic who is a good mechanic rather than a good electrician.
- He enforces a rule that no one writes in his name without his approval, e.g. a re-engagement email sent as "Sam".

chunks.heading: Growing the list to nearly 2M subscribers
chunks.text:
- Scale at the sale: close to 2 million subscribers, tens of thousands of paying subscribers, and about 900,000 opens on a recent send.
- Email's advantage: with a known unsubscribe rate (e.g. 5% a month) you can compute churn and LTV and therefore what you can spend to acquire a subscriber. He says you can't do that on a website.
- A media executive he admired once told him the business would never exceed $2 million a year and that they should do video instead. He disagreed.
- Acquisition is as important as content: "people think if you have good content, you're going to make it. Acquiring users is as important as the content."
- Paid acquisition got harder: Facebook subscribers cost about $1 four years earlier and about $3 to $4 at the time of recording.
- Co-registration (co-reg) is a major channel, with about 100 websites. Example: after someone submits a job application, the site offers "do you want to sign up for The Hustle too? Just click here" using the email it already has. Product Hunt does the same, listing The Hustle or Trends with a one-click signup.
- Co-reg requires building tooling, unlike Facebook which is plug and play.
- At higher spend (tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars a month), he negotiates quality-based pricing: pay $1 per lead only if the subscriber is a power user, e.g. opens at a 75% rate over the first 10 days. This guards against bot signups.
- Daily-newsletter peers he cites: The Skimm and Morning Brew. He says there was no playbook and they figured it out themselves.
- He says copying them isn't the right move; try something that seems silly now and may be normal in a few years.
- For solo creators like James Clear, tactics aren't that different. The main difference is that the founder-operator life is miserable: he was writer, growth marketer, admin and accountant at the start, and a daily email is very hard. A sellable asset requires interchangeable people.

chunks.heading: Subscription pricing and paid newsletters
chunks.text:
- Trends at the sale had over 15,000 paying subscribers, and was on track for close to eight figures. He originally planned a company with advertising bootstrapping a later product, inspired by Nathan's "billion dollar blog" idea.
- Trends came from his research on which products to build: friends loved the research and asked for more, then a Facebook group where members shared their own research showed community plus research was the product.
- Financials: on track for about $20M to $22M in 2021 net cash receipts, with advertising roughly $14M to $15M. Ad revenue was over $1M a month.
- A Black Friday campaign drove about $800,000 in a day, around 3,000 customers at a price he describes as about $200 to $300 (he says "200" then does the math with 300).
- Reason for subscriptions: advertising-only media limits what you can say, because advertisers can pull their ads.
- Renewal rate on Trends is very high; he says they undercharge. They tested tripling the price and conversion stayed the same.
- His advice for paid newsletter creators:
  - Charge much more. Most charge too little (e.g. $4 a month). The difference between $99 and $299 a year likely won't change conversion, and likely not $299 to $499 either. People value what they paid more for.
  - Prefer annual billing only. Churn on content is higher than software, and monthly at $9 to $15 is rough. If you offer monthly, make it very expensive (e.g. $50 a month vs $250 a year) as an anchor.
  - He never offered monthly on Trends. He spoke with The Information, The Athletic, The New York Times and Motley Fool, who mostly push people to annual.
  - Make your homepage a long-form sales page, not a freebie-heavy page. Only The New York Times can get away with that. No freemium; they use a $1 trial.
  - Require an email to reach the checkout page. Conversion is around 3%, but about 10% to 12% will give an email, and nearly all would-be buyers still proceed. That builds a lead list to nurture with free value.
- He says to study the scrappiest commercial operators, ethically: Agora (about $1B a year selling newsletters, though sued over a diabetes cure book), Motley Fool (he guesses around half a billion in sales a year) and James Altucher. Ask why they win, and apply the tactics to a high-integrity product.

chunks.heading: Email promotion tactics and where email is going
chunks.text:
- "Accidental send" Black Friday email: an email styled like an internal Gmail thread where Sam tells the team the Black Friday sale is ready and he thinks the discount is too big, sent to the full list from his personal address. Tens of thousands of people hit the site, he got about 10,000 replies, and it was a record sales day. He says the idea was borrowed from Chubbies or Brooklinen. Even friends called to say it was sent to the whole list by mistake.
- An earlier version in 2014/2015: they accidentally resent the previous email, then followed up with a screenshot of a Slack exchange where he threatens the writer's job; it got their highest open rate.
- His metaphor: "Email is like your pirate ship, and every new subscriber is a little bit of wind in your sails."
- His predictions: an email client such as Hey or Superhuman could gain enough traction to change how we use email. He expects richer email, with purchases, video, swipe, and live video inline. He thinks a news outlet like The New York Times might not need a website, and breaking news (e.g. election results) could go out in real time rather than at 8am.
- He notes AMP for email exists but nobody uses it.

chunks.heading: Learning to write through copy work
chunks.text:
- Method: copy great writing word for word, by hand. He compares it to learning an instrument by playing songs before writing your own.
- He copied Hunter S. Thompson, J.D. Salinger's Catcher in the Rye (simple language, interesting storytelling), and long-form advertisements to learn copywriting and selling.
- He says Judd Apatow wrote out Woody Allen scripts and Saturday Night Live sketches word for word.
- He prefers handwriting because it's slower than typing, which forces attention. After enough of it, you start noticing why a piece works: opening lines, sentence rhythm, simple words for complex topics.
- Breaking a pattern like Ryan Holiday's one-sentence introductions can be learned by writing a segment out 10 to 30 times.
- General principle: remove emotion and decision fatigue from learning a skill by copying what already worked. He applies it to training (hires a coach to write a plan, sprinter training, 5x5 lifting) and eating (a personal chef, 1,800 calories a day).

chunks.heading: Launching a local newsletter and growing it
chunks.text:
- For Nathan's Boise newsletter, Sam says a $25,000 budget is fine and "badass."
- Growth tactic: publish a listicle every 3 days such as "You know you're from Boise if..." and "The eight stereotypes of Boise," ideally as an infographic.
- Proven earlier on a roommate-matching iPhone app launched in Boston, Manhattan, Chicago and others: infographics of the stereotypical roommate in each neighborhood, naming as many local vendors as possible (they share) and gently making fun of the neighborhood (its residents share). He had never been to Boston.
- He thinks this would grow faster than asking other creators to promote it to their Boise subscribers, which he says is a lot of work for them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr talks with Ryan Holiday about setting a $20M goal at 24 and hitting it by 31, why he still wants more, and why success never feels like arriving. He also covers investing in the business machine, email newsletters as a business model, buy-it-for-life, and getting sober. Mostly mindset, with a few sharp business lessons.

chunks.heading: Setting a money number, hitting it, and still wanting more
chunks.text:
- At 24, Sam asked a rich person what he spent. The answer was about $80-100k a month, while Sam was spending roughly $3,000 a month in San Francisco. He asked himself what sum would let him spend that much without ever running out, and settled on about $20 million.
- He set a goal of having roughly $20M post-tax, liquid, in index funds and bonds by age 30. He sold his company at 31 for around $20M and doesn't regret selling.
- He still wants more, though not for lifestyle reasons. He grew up without much money and is "always afraid of running out." He calls that a personality defect.
- He compares goals to bench pressing: he did 295 and wants to see if he can hit 300 in two or three weeks. He gets a rush from seeing progress.
- Selling gave him "less of a chip on my shoulder." It proved he was decent at the trade of business, and he describes it as a nice chapter, not an arrival. He says the old rage at ex-girlfriends and doubters is "awesome fuel," though it is hard to turn off.
- He paid himself $20k in year one, $20k in year two, about $50k in year three and about half a million in year four. For the first two or three years in San Francisco he was on Obamacare. His conclusion: "people who say money doesn't make you happy, it definitely makes you happier."

chunks.heading: Arriving isn't real: insecurity among the very successful
chunks.text:
- At his Hustle events, Sam would bring speakers in two hours early and sit quietly backstage listening. The founders and billionaires there complained about avoiding firing someone for a year, whether a $100M raise would pay off, and stage fright before 3,000 people.
- The lesson was that he could be insecure and still be good at his job. Insecurity is normal and doesn't go away. "Arriving is not the reality"; the destination keeps moving.
- Meeting many successful people showed him they are often in the same league on IQ and ability. A few are on a different level (he named Grammarly's Max as someone whose brain "has more power"). For most, the gap is choosing a path, timing, genre and luck.
- He believes that with 10 dedicated years in a craft or sport you can get surprisingly close to your heroes. That belief shifted his sense of what he could do, and now the question is which game he wants to play (for example, not the high-stress Wework-style raise-money game).
- Luck is real. "Work hard and you're lucky," and he dislikes bootstrap talk.
- Hampton, his CEO group, ran a wealth survey of members spending anywhere from $10k to $200k a month personally. Both groups reported similar happiness, and both said the spending didn't feel like much. Takeaways: most people don't know what they're doing, most aren't happy, and things aren't what they seem.

chunks.heading: Fear of being taken advantage of, and owning things instead of being owned
chunks.text:
- Sam is paranoid about being taken advantage of. When Scott Galloway asked him on the podcast what he'd made from his sale, he choked up partly out of that worry, not necessarily shame.
- At his ranch he hides his Tesla when a vendor comes to fix the driveway.
- His stated aim: "I own my things, they don't own me." He remembers his dad flipping out over a dented car and doesn't want to be like that.
- He has soured on possessions. He has owned nice cars and found them a burden (a $2,500 set of tires, dead batteries, special insurance), plus the chain of an assistant to manage it, a bigger house to store it, and junk haulers to clear it.
- In 2024 he was getting rid of nearly everything, selling items on Facebook Marketplace (a workbench for $400 and an old Xbox for $100) and enjoying it. He was moving into a furnished rental with only his clothes.
- He plans to sell his house and rent until he finds a home he'd keep for 50 years, instead of rushing a purchase.
- On "reduce, reuse, recycle," he says to drop the recycle part. Waste-management owners he interviewed told him most of it goes in the garbage.

chunks.heading: Buy it for life, and building slower
chunks.text:
- Sam is into the "buy it for life" movement (a big subreddit): rather than the $50 version you keep replacing, buy the thing that can last decades. His example was a convertible Amish-style crib that grows from infant to full-size bed.
- He applies the same slowness to work. He has been trying to build companies and projects more slowly: "what are you rushing towards?" He used to rush and is glad he did, but now asks why you'd hurry through something you enjoy.
- He reads for interest, not to learn. He read self-help heavily between ages 20 and 28, and now reads only what he finds interesting, with learning as a by-product. He thinks speed reading is a scam.
- His fitness is goal-driven. He picks a new goal each quarter, such as a bench or squat target, the splits, or an ultra marathon. His NFL combine attempt, with a 4.6 forty, 33-inch vertical, 107-inch broad jump and 16 reps at 225, was about 70% of his best. He says it was average for a wide receiver. He was a Division I track and field athlete and believes fast-twitch vs slow-twitch muscle is largely inborn.
- He theorizes an ultra is easier than a fast marathon because success is just not dying, but says he hasn't tested it.

chunks.heading: Newsletters as a business model
chunks.text:
- Sam asks whether the email newsletter is one of the greatest business models ever, if set up right.
- He cites the Hustle: about 4 million subscribers, a team of three writing it, and revenue of around $1 million a month on the way to roughly $20M in the year it sold. It had 30-40 employees at sale, partly because monetizing required accounting and other staff.
- Growth cost was small relative to scale: he says they spent about $400,000 in the month before the sale on growing the list.
- The model he likes: an input of a few writers produces millions of impressions daily, and you can write better when you write to a subscriber base instead of an unknown audience.

chunks.heading: Marriage, a pointed direction, and dependents instead of psychedelics
chunks.text:
- Sam spent ages 20 to about 23 or 24 intoxicated daily. He went to jail more than once, slept on the street and on buses, and expected to end up homeless or a criminal.
- He quit cold turkey at 23 or 24. A seizure and hospitalization came first. After a false start he locked himself in a room for about six weeks, with a blood pressure machine to monitor himself.
- Two things pushed him to quit: watching Oasis play to 100,000 people and realizing he could have that kind of impact but was a "loser" sitting intoxicated, and coming home after 24 hours in jail to a dog who had messed the house.
- He doesn't crave alcohol now and drinks non-alcoholic beer. He knows he is prone to addiction (nicotine pouches, formerly sugar) and calls himself a "better not" person.
- His view on relationships: "the best life hack on Earth is who you pick." He uses an image of a car with its back wheels jacked up and spinning. A good partner helps you point it in the right direction, then you pull the plug and go.
- He says if you can't commit, that may mean you have the wrong person. As an alternative to psychedelics for people lost at 40, he suggests having a kid, a dog, or employees, anything where others rely on you, so the question changes from "I am lost" to "I need to provide."
- On psychedelics, he has taken shrooms only once recreationally, is reluctant to mess with brain chemistry, and respects veterans who say it helped. He doesn't think they should be pitched as a cure-all.

chunks.heading: Heroes are flawed, and Twitter vs the blog era
chunks.text:
- Sam looks for people who are "mostly awesome." He names Lars Hamilton, Rob Dyrdek and HubSpot's Dharmesh Shah, admired for family-first lives, loyalty to spouses and a positive outlook. He also names Rockefeller, whom he sees as mostly honest and a good husband and father.
- He notes that heroes like Teddy Roosevelt and LBJ had ugly flaws. His line: "all great men are bad men," because achieving anything on a large scale means making decisions that leave a lot of people unhappy.
- On Twitter, he defends it as a place to find smart people. He gives the example of a thread by Die Workwear on how postwar Japan blended American fashion with Japanese craftsmanship, which led him to read a whole book on the topic.
- He also says it addicts successful people. He tells of friends with money or fame (he named hockey player Chris Pronger, whom he helped get started) who got hooked on wanting more audience, and he warns them they don't need it.
- He prefers the 2005-2015 blogging era, with blogrolls and long, nerdy, in-depth posts, and still reads Hacker News daily. He says you can't hide bad ideas in writing, which is why Amazon requires six-page memos.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how he and co-founder Joe Spiser tested demand with a public tweet, personally called every respondent, and sold group spots through a Stripe link before building anything. He covers co-founder alignment, designing groups around fast vulnerability, selective admissions, and why hiring a CEO too early backfired.

chunks.heading: Sam's origin story and the Hustle path
chunks.text:
- Sam is from Missouri and lived in San Francisco for a long time. He bootstrapped a newsletter business called The Hustle and sold it to HubSpot for tens of millions of dollars at age 31. HubSpot also got the Trends product and the podcast.
- He says The Hustle's goal was to be popular, so people know him more for that than for his actual success.
- He credits The Hustle partly to what he learned from Andrew Warner's Mixergy. He watched about 10 interviews, contacted the interviewees, "triangulated everything" and found his business that way.
- He says the first sale was "so much luck" and calls planning on a repeat of that luck "a pretty crappy plan." The longer the timeline, the less luck matters.
- Newsletters were seen as a joke when he started. He had the same experience with Hampton: serious operators don't take it seriously yet.
- He admits he got newsletters wrong in one case. When Tyler (Beehiiv) was building newsletter software, Sam told him it was a stupid idea. His reasoning was that he was already an investor in Kit (ConvertKit) and thought the market was too small for two.
- Before the first win, Sam describes the first five years of starting businesses as being "a loser." Google and an accounting firm wouldn't hire him.
- He credits a few decisions in his 20s for making the rest of his life easier: marrying the right woman, giving up drugs and alcohol, and getting his health in order.

chunks.heading: How Sam started Hampton and got it to roughly $1M ARR fast
chunks.text:
- Hampton is a peer network for founders and CEOs. The average member runs a business doing about $25M in revenue.
- He and cofounder Joe Spiser first tested the idea on VPs. Sam tweeted a form asking who wanted their VP in a community and got about 200-300 replies. He interviewed about 60 of them and "no one wanted it."
- Joe pushed for CEOs instead. Sam thought it was "a horrible idea," then tweeted a generic version (a dinner in New York for CEOs), got another ~300 replies and called them. This time they said "Take my money. I'm in."
- They reached about $1M in revenue in two or three months with no real website. The site was a Squarespace page with a logo saying Hampton and a link to a Typeform.
- Distribution in the first six months was purely word of mouth and Sam's network. They worked on it for ~10 months before announcing publicly.
- He wrote a Google doc explaining the product and sent it to about 100 friends, saying "I am not selling you." He says he never tries to convince a friend to do anything.
- He called all ~300 respondents and interviewed 100% of them. At the end of an interview, if it seemed the person wanted in, he flagged it to Joe. Joe set up Stripe and found facilitators on the back end.
- Sam told accepted members "give me six weeks" and he'd build their group. His calendar in that period was stacked 20-minute calls with 10-minute breaks, and he bought a wind-resistant headset to take calls while walking.
- Division of labor: Sam did the talking, they collaborated on thinking, and Joe did the making.
- Sam says he can "blunt force most anything to like 5 million in revenue" through his network and brand, and the real challenge after that is making the product good enough that people stay and refer.

chunks.heading: Hampton's onboarding, product and group design
chunks.text:
- The original onboarding: a Stripe link, payment, then weeks later an announcement email introducing each group. Sam wrote about why those eight people were together and "played it up" so everyone sounded amazing.
- Members went into a Slack, where Sam posted every day for a long time to set the culture.
- Groups started online because members were still traveling after COVID. Later members wanted in-person meetings, which Sam calls a big pivot. Digital is easier to manage but "way less good of a product."
- Each member is placed in a core group of eight people with similar sizes and types of businesses and similar-ish personalities. The group meets monthly. Facilitators moderate and are hired by Hampton.
- Beyond the core group there are hundreds of events and a network-wide community.
- Sam and Joe interview applicants and approve or deny all of them. Joe watches 100% of the interviews and clicks thumbs up or down. Sam will deny someone who is financially qualified if there is an energy or culture mismatch or something "shady."
- Sam says he turns down a lot of money this way, and it makes paid ads harder because "money is not just money."
- Sam's stated goal: "get eight amazing people in a room every single month and let them have the best conversations." He calls the business simple but "incredibly hard."
- Competitors and comps he cites: Vistage (sold about 1-2 years ago for roughly $2B, maybe $200-300M a year in profit, as he recalls), World 50 (nine figures a year in profit) and YPO. Vistage was founded in the 1960s and YPO in the 50s/60s, so he thinks the model can last 50-70 years.
- The moat is large, but he calls it a pain in the ass, logistics-heavy and "a very hard business."
- Vistage-style models are franchise-like: a moderator recruits about 18 people and earns on the 15th-18th. Sam says he's open to that but that the goal of this type of business is not to control everything. You build a framework and let customers' energy shape each group.

chunks.heading: Culture: speed to vulnerability
chunks.text:
- Sam and Joe are blunt and confrontational and wanted core groups to be "confrontational with love."
- Early exercises included net worth reveals, where members break down their whole net worth for the group. It makes people uncomfortable but he calls it effective.
- He compares the meetings to group therapy. The joke (which he says is not a joke): "how fast can I make a grown man cry?"
- The key idea is speed to vulnerability: the sooner someone breaks down, the sooner they can be built back up.
- He likes that it shows successful people have flaws. Seeing admired peers be vulnerable makes him feel normal and empowers him. He says this goes back to hosting HustleCon speakers backstage, where he learned that big names are "mostly normal like me, but they still have the courage to move forward."
- Hampton is testing a formal "point of view" for the company, with a team member (Jory) sitting in on meetings to take notes in a room used as a lab.

chunks.heading: Picking a co-founder: the alignment doc
chunks.text:
- Sam compares choosing a co-founder to marriage. With his wife he mapped out finances, lifestyle, kids and work expectations before marrying, and he did the same with Joe.
- He wrote about eight questions in a document, and he and Joe each answered separately, then met for an hour to review each other's answers.
- Questions included:
  - What does a win look like in 5 or 10 years?
  - What am I willing to put in emotionally, in time and financially?
  - What am I unwilling to do?
  - What values do we care about?
- Where they aligned: they want to win but also have fun ("winning without fun is silly"). Keep teams small, hire amazing people and give them lots of responsibility. Go big, meaning hundreds of millions in revenue, even billions, over decades. No venture capital, no plan to sell, and family first (e.g., dinner with family).
- They refused to build soulless or slimy products that make money without delivering value to the customer.
- The real difference was motivation. Sam says his comes from feeling inadequate and wanting to prove himself ("like a high school girl who wouldn't go out with you"), and he still feels that need. Joe's is pure passion.
- Sam says "I've done a lot of dumb things in my life. That thing was amazing," and he shared the questions publicly (searchable as "Sam Parr co-founder discussion").
- He first met Joe by emailing him after reading a Business Insider article, and said he'd be in New York the next day. He wasn't. He flew out after Joe agreed, and Joe invested $25,000 in The Hustle. Sam notes that people who do this to him now get told not to fly, because it's too much pressure.

chunks.heading: Lead generation and growth channels for Hampton
chunks.text:
- Early leads came almost 100% from Sam's Twitter forms and his network.
- Current sources: his podcasts (My First Million, plus the newer Moneywise), referrals and Twitter/content. He says My First Million has been "so lucky" and will eventually phase out, so the product has to be good enough to be referred.
- Paid marketing started recently at about $10k a month, sending traffic straight to the homepage, with a join page for tracking. He calls it "not that sophisticated."
- At The Hustle he says he bought roughly $10 million worth of ads and let a team handle the rest, and he describes Facebook's targeting as good enough to "do it for you."
- Sam says Hampton can't grow for growth's sake: throwing people in "will ruin it."
- His current big goal is 10,000 members meeting in real life every month. Hard part: if five people sign up in a city this month for a core group, he needs three more. Decentralization is key.
- Hampton grew faster than he wanted. He says "I would like to grow even slower" and doesn't disclose revenue because he doesn't want members to think it's about money. He wants the company to last forever and deliver value.
- He sees AI making in-person meetings more valuable over the next 10-20 years, and Hampton as a base for that bet, with a 5-10 year commitment.

chunks.heading: Hampton's event tiers
chunks.text:
- Sam lays out a ladder of in-person events, from cheap to expensive:
  - **Coffee hangouts:** a member visiting another city messages that city's members through the portal and the chapter lead helps organize. Example: a 20-person coffee hang.
  - **Evening experiences:** curated events like a sauna and cold plunge session at Other Ship in NYC, with a founder talk and group screaming.
  - **Adventures:** golf at Pimrod (a self-organized group that now goes yearly), rally car racing, lobster diving and a possible zero-gravity jet flight.
  - **Retreats:** multi-day trips like a health and wellness retreat in the mountains for about 15 members, spouses welcome.
- Both member-led and Hampton-organized versions exist. A member who owns a hotel can offer an at-cost deal for 20 Hampton members.
- Hampton's volume lets it get bulk deals. He says they ran about 300 events like these in the last 12 months.

chunks.heading: Building community yourself: do life with people
chunks.text:
- Sam's community origins: he ran a business book club called the "anti-MBA," posting on Craigslist and Reddit. His first attendee, Sieva Kazinski, is now one of his closest friends, is in his Hampton core group, and has invested in his companies.
- In San Francisco he organized meetups constantly. His philosophy at the time (while single) was "I'm going to do dope stuff and bring people along with me."
- He was part of Founders Dojo (an office run by a friend, Dave, with free seats given to a hand-picked group). Alumni included Moiz Ali (Native), Roman (Raycon) and many others. He remembers an office full of degenerates having fun, with marathon 24-hour livestreams on Meerkat.
- His advice to young people: get in the mix. "Do life with them." Bring people with you to whatever you do, and be the one who organizes the cool thing (his example: book a group-buy winery trip and tell three great people to come).
- Early in life, the goal should be quantity of relationships. Later, he says, you keep a tight crew. His own rule at home is "no new friends."
- He has moved his family to New York to live near a Hampton core group member (Austin Reef of Morning Brew), because he wants to raise families together.
- Andrew Warner took him under his wing and "changed my life." He met Sean Puri (his MFM cohost) and Ryan Hoover in the same era.

chunks.heading: What Hampton changed in how Sam works, and the CEO reversal
chunks.text:
- A core group practice: box breathing, to calm down before reacting to bad news or an email.
- He learned from a core group member (Val, who runs nine-figure companies) to stay unrattled: take bad news in, then ask what you can and can't get over.
- From Austin Reef he learned to rely more on intuition than data: "does this feel good, am I proud of this." Examples: he may know he can raise prices or optimize the funnel and choose not to yet, because he wants to treat customers like adults and not beg them.
- He originally installed a CEO because he was a bit intimidated by the opportunity and wanted to hand it off. He now thinks that was a mistake: "abdicating instead of delegating."
- He also thinks it was too early, because digital core groups turned out not to be the answer and people wanted in-person. He argues the person who can change fast is the one who would be fine if the company died, because it wouldn't hurt them financially. You can't ask a hired CEO to have that attitude.
- Joe is now CEO and Sam is president, a right-hand role. Sam went back into the business in March.
- Hard parts of coming back: working a lot, editing the team (he says he can do it but hates the pain it causes, "like working out"), and relearning systems like HubSpot, which had changed since he set it up.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how he thinks about building paid communities (Hustle Trends, Hampton). He separates an audience from a community, says to launch where people already are, seed it with a leader posting daily, scale slowly and meticulously, and charge more than you think. He backs it all with simple back-of-the-envelope math.

chunks.heading: How Sam defines a community versus an audience
chunks.text:
- Sam says "audience" and "community" get used interchangeably, and he thinks that's wrong. A blog or a Twitter following is an audience.
- His test: with a Creator or audience-builder at the center, you have an audience. A community is "a bunch of different people interacting without an audience Creator."
- The quit-posting test: if the creator stops creating content for two or three weeks, do more conversations happen while they're gone than when they were there? If not, it's an audience, not a community.
- He says the Hustle was often called a community but "that's not a community."
- He thinks "community" is an overused, ambiguous word (corporate teams say "we need Community"), so people dismiss it as silly and don't treat it as a serious business category.
- That dismissal is the opportunity. He likes finding ideas people write off that could be worth hundreds of millions or billions. He expects people to take community seriously in about five years, once numbers are released.
- A real community has its own culture and can organize against its owner. Example: the NYT Cooking Facebook group (he puts it at roughly 100,000 members) revolted after a policy change. He calls that "the sign of a good Community" because it's "its own thing" that's "incredibly hard to own and to like dictate."

chunks.heading: Spotting ideas early: do the math on paper
chunks.text:
- Sam says he picks unfashionable categories by running simple arithmetic rather than following sentiment.
- Newsletter example (the Hustle, launched 2016): a CEO told him it would never pass $2 million a year in revenue. Sam's math was roughly 4 million subscribers leading to about $60 million in revenue, using known ad rates, with extra newsletters on top.
- Writer-leverage math: about 3.5 million subscribers and roughly 2 million unique daily opens, which he approximates as about 60 million reads a month (assuming about 30 sends; he says they send about 27). That ran on three writers. BuzzFeed had about 60 million monthly uniques with about 150 writers.
- Why a daily newsletter beats a blog: a blog must acquire new readers every day, while a daily send creates a habit and readers return.
- Proof point: he says competitor and friend Morning Brew is at about $80 million in revenue, so the prediction "kind of came true" even though he sold early and wasn't the one who pulled it off.
- His summary: "the math is the math and that doesn't lie." It sounds stupid because nobody is taking it seriously.
- He says the Hustle, theSkimm and Morning Brew each reached a similar conclusion without knowing each other, then success pulled in imitators. He predicts the same cycle for paid communities.

chunks.heading: Hampton: the business, the numbers and the $100M math
chunks.text:
- Hampton (joinhampton.com) is a community for CEOs of companies above a revenue threshold. Sam calls it "a business Therapy Group."
- Origin: running the Hustle was lonely. He couldn't show fear to employees (not knowing how to make payroll, dreading firing someone). He had peers for this in San Francisco, but most founders don't.
- Format:
  - Small groups of 7-8 CEOs with similar types and sizes of business, matched from a waitlist.
  - Monthly three-hour sessions with an executive facilitator.
  - A digital community for all members.
  - About 150 dinners this year, plus retreats.
  - He says non-CEO roles (COO, a Chief of marketing-type role) might come later.
- Group size: he says he "just made it up." Seven still works if someone is out, and it feels like a round table of eight.
- Timeline: work started in June (about a year before the talk). It reached about 300 members through DMs and word of mouth, with no mention on the My First Million podcast despite its big audience. It was announced publicly about six months before the talk.
- Why he didn't build in public: he was embarrassed and didn't want to fail. He also wanted it big enough to be hard to copy before announcing.
- Why he waited to announce: he wanted to perfect the product first. "You can't just like throw a ton of people in there at the same time."
- $100M math: about 10,000 paying members gets to $100M. He says they are already in the thousands of members (the transcript is ambiguous on exact current counts). His reasoning is that 10,000 CEOs obviously exist who would sign up, so it's "a very easy math thing."
- The name: he grew up on Hampton Avenue in St. Louis. He names LLCs and projects after streets, and he likes the old-Rolex-ad look of British racing green, his favorite Jaguar color.
- Members run it too: he asks well-known members (including founders of public companies) to serve as local "social chairs." The pitch: "Do you want to be more popular and thought of as a thought leader?" Hampton gives them a budget and a spoon-fed discussion playbook to host quarterly dinners in their city, and these chairs greet and onboard new members.
- He says members aren't there to see him: the product and community are good enough that he's "one of the least successful people in the community," and Hampton champions members, not him.

chunks.heading: How to launch and seed a community
chunks.text:
- Start where people already are, at the lowest friction. His examples:
  - Facebook Groups were his starting point.
  - Slack for white-collar or tech people. He says he never thought this would be true.
  - Discord for young guys or Gen Z.
  - WhatsApp for international audiences.
- He says his team's CTO Dharmesh at HubSpot disagrees and prefers owning the platform, though Dharmesh acknowledges that's very hard. Sam's view: getting people to visit a dedicated site or app multiple times a day to comment is "the hardest thing ever," and he doesn't think he or most people could pull it off.
- You need a leader who acts as the "cult leader," embodying the rituals and culture and setting tone the way a CEO sets company culture. This is hard in big companies because nobody wants to risk looking stupid or saying something inappropriate.
- The leader must be in the group constantly. Sam checks roughly three times an hour, and now has a trained community manager but still keeps his "finger in the pulse."
- Seeding example (Trends, the Hustle's paid community, launched around 2018):
  - Trends was about $300 a year, with a weekly newsletter deconstructing businesses.
  - He created the Facebook group two days before launch, as an afterthought.
  - He posted in it every day for about a year.
  - He asked smart friends to post content he wrote for them, daily, to create initial traction.
  - After about six months people started commenting on their own and it developed its own culture.
  - He says it reached roughly 20-25,000 members at one point and now has thousands more; he isn't sure of the current number.
- Start the group as a "dictatorship" and let it evolve into more of a democracy. Hampton has core rules, for example members can't talk about what's discussed in their core group, and anyone who does is removed.
- Needs a "shtick": something that differentiates the community, even a small twist. Examples he gives: developers who are "a little punk rock," or "the most helpful developer community" that replies thoughtfully to everything.

chunks.heading: Scaling a community without killing it
chunks.text:
- Don't pour a lot of people in at once. Community is more like an event than software: with software you can add users and fix on the fly, but a community that grows too big too fast "sucks" and has "no soul."
- He cites the HubSpot event itself, which he says reached 28,000 attendees one year and was scaled back because the experience got worse.
- Be meticulous about who gets in, and "indoctrinate" them with the norms: how to behave, how to give, how to take.
- Hampton's structure for scale: chapters, where each person mostly interacts with a cohort of roughly 300, plus ways to interact with the whole network.
- Large communities can still work. Reddit's sub-communities each have their own culture. He says delaying growth is the hardest part, since you want to grow fast to make more money.
- Fear of damage: he worries daily that someone will say something bad, because he thinks a spoiled community is almost impossible to recover. "If you have a dead community, in my opinion just kill it and start over."
- FOMO is, in his words, the second or third most important thing about community. Hampton creates it with "Adventures" such as rally car racing, mountain biking and Lobster diving in Miami two weeks before the talk, with spouses invited so the whole family is bought in.
- Adventures are partly about raising energy: he cites a book saying exciting dates create dopamine and attraction, and applies the same idea to bonding members.

chunks.heading: Monetizing communities: charge more, not ads
chunks.text:
- If community is the business itself, charge money. He says paid is "a significantly better route than advertising." He also says to charge more than you think, because the revenue lets you provide a better service.
- If you already own a product (like HubSpot) a free community is fine.
- His Trends mistake: pricing at $300 a year was "really stupid." It meant he needed tens of thousands of members and a small staff to earn what Hampton already earns, and he couldn't afford certain services.
- Pricing rule of thumb: for something job-related, where one conversation could earn someone more money or advance their career, charge much more. That ROI justification also makes people value the community more. For a casual giveaway-style group (the stay-at-home-mom giveaway communities he mentions), something like $50 a month could still be fine.
- Example he cites of a micro-community: a guy who reviews high-end CCTV cameras and sells memberships to large casinos, about 1,200 members at roughly $1,000 a year, around $1.2 million a year, with essentially no competition. His take on the appeal: unlike the newsletter he had to write six days a week, a community doesn't require making content constantly.
- Newsletters and communities pair well: a strong audience builder already knows what people want and how to evoke emotion.

chunks.heading: Where community is going: paid niche professional communities
chunks.text:
- Prediction: newsletters had a boom, and communities will follow. He expects many paid communities for niche professionals, possibly going public.
- Example: Doximity, a paid community for doctors, which he says is valued at about $4-5 billion and doing hundreds of millions in revenue (he says he butchers the name and gives these figures from memory).
- Other niches he lists: orthodontists, dentists, lawyers, any profession.
- Why people want them: a safe space to ask things you can't ask your spouse or look silly asking in front of coworkers. He says social media got so big that people no longer feel safe sharing, so micro-communities will boom over the next five to ten years.
- Corporate takeaway: if your boss says "do community," focus on meticulously letting people in and teaching them the culture, not on a big launch or the software.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how copy work trained his writing, why long-form copy and simple stories convert, and how he writes cold emails with attention, interest, desire, action plus heavy follow-up. He also covers going viral by angering a segment, and hiring by reading people's writing.

chunks.heading: Cold email: the AIDA formula and why follow-ups do the work
chunks.text:
Sam's cold email framework is AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action.
- **Attention:** a headline that stands out. For a speaker pitch he would leave the subject line blank, because "no subject" grabs attention.
- **Interest:** a short story or personal hook. His example: "Hey Tim from Pandora, I'm hosting this event in Oakland, which is right by Pandora's office. I'm going to have 3,000 people there, and you're going to talk in front of all of them."
- **Desire:** name the other speakers (or the people he is talking to about coming), "those are all ballers."
- **Action:** one specific ask. "All you have to do is say yes and I'll take care of everything else and you just have to show up. Are you in?"

His view of fear and volume:
- "You're 50 cold emails away from everyone on Earth." That means one initial email and 49 follow-ups. "The follow-up is key."
- To get over the fear of annoying someone, he asks "do you want to win or not?" He compares it to approaching someone you want to marry: if you want it, you have to do it.
- "No one cares about you. They only care about themselves." If you look foolish, they will most likely forget it.
- He thinks we will look back in 50 years and say "I can't believe you could just do that."

chunks.heading: Cold email follow-ups and expected close rates (HustleCon speakers)
chunks.text:
Sam used cold email to book speakers for his HustleCon conference.
- Follow-up emails were mostly event updates: tickets sold (for example "we've sold out of a thousand tickets already"), other speakers confirmed, and "I'm holding a spot for you." The ask stayed the same: say yes and reply.
- Expected results: if he asked five people, he would "for sure get one" speaker.
- A yes or no usually came "by email three."
- He once emailed the Pandora contact about 30 times. Some nos turned into yeses on the spot because the updates showed momentum ("all right, screw it, I'm in").
- He has not used physical cold mail but would. He thinks catalogs for e-commerce and clothing brands are very effective, and Hampton has considered it.

chunks.heading: Copywriting: copy work, rhythm and plain language
chunks.text:
Sam learned copywriting while running a hot dog stand in college, after finding Neville Medhora's blog. The technique that mattered most was "copy work": copying great writing word for word, the way schools used to teach children to write. His analogy is learning piano, where you learn simple songs and then see patterns well enough to write your own music.

What he copied:
- Ads from the 60s and 70s that ran for decades, on the logic that long-running ads were successful (some were 10 pages long).
- Powerful blog posts, books such as Catcher in the Rye, and SNL sketches. He copied anything he felt was timeless.

What he learned:
- **Rhythm:** a short sentence, then a slightly longer one, then a long one that lands the point.
- Use a period instead of a comma where possible, and make sentences more direct.
- Avoid adverbs.
- Write simply. He cites Hemingway and Stephen King (*On Writing*) as simple writers, roughly at a fourth-grade reading level. The goal is developing a voice, not memorizing rules.
- In lightning-round answers, beginners should follow formal copywriting rules strictly. He writes headlines as a near-full sentence and leans toward curiosity.

chunks.heading: Long-form copy and storytelling
chunks.text:
Sam argues long-form sales copy still wins and has not gone away.
- Examples he points to: hey.com (Jason Fried), Amazon product pages (thousands of words, hundreds of images and reviews), Apple product pages, and a roughly six-minute deodorant video ad.
- **Reason one (logistics):** a buyer has many objections, and the page must answer every one so they are confident the product fits their needs.
- **Reason two (emotion):** "storytelling is the easiest way to make people feel something."
- Claude Hopkins example (Pepsodent toothpaste): "Rub your tongue over your teeth. Do you feel that film?" A simple demonstration story taught people to want toothpaste.
- Popcorn example: saying movie popcorn has a large number of grams of fat means nothing; showing a baseball-sized clump of fat makes the point. Sam notes he made the numbers up for illustration.
- A story can be short, even just a name. His examples:
  - The Anti-MBA Book Club, a free monthly book club in San Francisco with an expert on each book, started because he was envious he did not go to Stanford.
  - Sam's List: "Yelp for accountants." He asked his 400,000 Twitter followers for accountants they love, got 400 suggestions, called all of them, then published the database. The story is "I can't find an accountant, so I did the hard work for you."
- Write the way you would explain it to a buddy at a bar, and put those words on the site or in the name.
- Sam's List is a small business, roughly $300K this year by his estimate. He funded it with a small amount of money and gave half the company to the operator, Kimmy.

chunks.heading: Writing first, building second
chunks.text:
Sam uses copywriting as a product-selection tool. He often thinks in reverse: instead of building a product and asking how to sell it, he asks "what can I write that will sell?" and then builds that.
- A line with a high conversion rate tells you the idea is sellable.
- Writing forces clarity. He believes Amazon has people write a memo describing a product before building it for the same reason.
- **Trends pre-sale:** he pre-sold about $60,000 of Trends before the product existed. The first landing page was on Gumroad and brought in about $10,000. The copy told a plain story: what the product will do, the full price he would charge later, a lower early-adopter price, a first version sent to buyers, a no-questions refund ("just hit reply and say not for me"), a free subscription forever if they love it, and a note that he might call for feedback.

chunks.heading: Going viral: make some people angry
chunks.text:
- His rule: "If you want to go viral with content, the goal should be to piss off a certain type of person." Some people love it and some are angry, which is "oftentimes" what virality needs.
- Peloton's husband-buys-wife-a-bike ad is his example of outrage that probably helped.
- **Hustle launch article:** he plagiarized a romance novel, uploaded it to Kindle and made sales, to prove a scammy acquaintance's claim of making $60K a month this way. Middle-aged romance novelists were angry at a young Californian guy. The article got about a million views and about 30,000 new Hustle subscribers.

chunks.heading: Building The Hustle: newsletter math and bootstrapping with events
chunks.text:
- **Why newsletters:** he did it years before newsletters were popular and was laughed at. He tells people he said it would become a $100 million a year company and thinks he sold too early.
  - Business Insider told him about 80 million monthly visitors, roughly half for tech. So a TAM of at least a million subscribers seemed realistic.
  - A Thrillist founder shared newsletter ad prices. A million subscribers and six sends a week implied he could make about $30K a day.
  - Facebook was cutting organic reach and marketers like Noah Kagan relied on email. His view was that email is the main thing and everything else is the afterthought.
- **Growth:** roughly 0 to 100K subscribers in year one, 100K to 500K in year two, 500K to 1M in year three, then to about 1.5M. It felt steady, not fast, at the time. Growth came in spikes from viral articles.
- **Operations:** the company ran tightly, with known acquisition cost per customer and known customer retention.
- **Events funded it:** he started HustleCon between ventures, and it made roughly $400K in the first 12 to 18 months by his recollection. After about a year of the newsletter he dropped the event, using about $500K saved from conferences to bootstrap the newsletter. He found the events business itself horrible.
- **Fundraising:** he tried to raise venture capital, and it ended up with a crowdfunding round. He regrets it because he did not need the money, and says "thank God no one invested" before he sold. He recommends fewer investors over more, and VC over crowdfunding if someone does need money.

chunks.heading: Choosing projects, hiring and focus
chunks.text:
**Project selection**
- He calls project selection the most important thing when starting a company. He says it is "an art" with no math behind it.
- He sets an outcome ("if in 10 years I get to this spot I'll be happy") and checks whether the TAM and math get him within one or two multiples. If yes, he continues; if not, he does not.
- For Hampton he knows it is possible because other companies in the space are multi-billion dollar companies.

**Hiring**
- He says hiring is his core skill, more than operating. He sets clear performance expectations early, then lets people collaborate on the plan and gets out of the way.
- He uses "the bottom fourth of the resume" (education, hobbies, interests). He wants the person to entertain him and show passion and clear thinking: "if they studied four years of philosophy and can't tell me their favorite course, then they're a loser."
- He finds people through their writing, such as a blog, and does lots of outbound even though each job listing now gets about 500 applicants.
- His outreach is simply "I love your work." His goal is to "buy stock in people before it's matured" and give them a platform. He tells hires to stay three to five years and promises support if they move on.

**Time and structure**
- He says he has one company, Hampton. Sam's List runs by Kimmy with a half stake. He hosted Moneywise (Hampton's podcast) for its first year and then hired a host.
- My First Million takes Monday and Wednesday, 12 to 2 with 2 hours of prep from 10, and the rest of his time is Hampton.

chunks.heading: Bunk SF, tooling and skills Sam wishes he had
chunks.text:
**Bunk SF (roommate matching)**
- Mechanic: get a landlord's permission to host a party in a three-bedroom apartment, invite about 100 loosely vetted people (similar age, work, neighborhood and budget), and match them into groups that then find their own place.
- Acquisition: post a $1,000 one-bedroom Craigslist ad framed as filling an empty $3,000 three-bedroom. It brought thousands of applicants a day until Craigslist shut it down. He says Airbnb grew similarly. Sam calls it a hard, dumb business because the customers have no money.
- Craigslist's old office later became The Hustle's first office.

**What he would do differently**
- He would learn to code and design. Even with tools like Replit and Cursor, he says you still need to be technical.
- He wishes he had paid attention to Photoshop or front-end design in high school, because good design matters to copywriting.
- He says he has good taste and sets direction for Hampton's branding by drawing and making a deck of colors and feelings, but cannot finish the details himself.

**Lightning round**
- Headlines: curiosity.
- Communities: growing slowly can make them last forever if done right.
- Clicks vs. connection: he can get anyone to click, but prefers connection since clicks don't convert.
- Paid or value commitments: paid.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr traces his climb from $10 hot dogs to the Hustle's sale to HubSpot, showing how each larger deal came from delivering more value. He covers copywriting, pricing mistakes, selling to early advertisers, negotiating an acquisition, staying focused, and cutting friction when starting.

chunks.heading: Building a business: start with tiny deals and climb the deal ladder
chunks.text:
- Sam's early sales were deliberately casual. His hot dogs sold for about $5 in the afternoon and $8-10 in the evening ("drunk people"). His roommate-matching service took about $300-400 per room, on an honor system: find a place, then call and pay if it came through us.
- His lesson: "it's about value given." A hot dog is worth an afternoon, a roommate is worth a year, so you take a small fraction of a much bigger value and the price is higher.
- He undervalued himself for a long time. He sold his first startup (a roommate-matching app) for a job and bonuses worth about $100K, and says he only realized this year that big companies badly need people who move fast and ship, which they struggle to do.
- He says he is still a poor negotiator and has other people (including his wife) negotiate for him.
- Deal sizes climbed in steps. At the Hustle he started selling a $1,000 sponsorship, then his team sold tens of thousands, then hundreds of thousands, then multi-million-dollar deals. The bigger the deal, the longer it takes: many meetings, jargon, RFPs, becoming an approved vendor. He calls enterprise sales hard and process-driven, unlike the casual early deals.

chunks.heading: Getting the first sponsors and underpriced early deals
chunks.text:
- His first sponsors (Lawtrades and Wealthfront) paid $1,000 on a "street style" deal: "just give me a grant, and if it works you advertise again; if it doesn't you've only lost a grand."
- He had to Google what an invoice was and numbered his first one "0035" so it wouldn't look like his first.
- Early on he told advertisers he'd send their message to 50,000 people and to pay whatever was fair after seeing the clicks. After roughly 10 clients he moved to $25 CPM, with past results as proof. The range he later found was about $20-30 CPM.
- His view: this is mutually beneficial. Early publishers are underpriced, so smart advertisers and media buyers should find small audiences early and buy a year of ads, then ride the growth.
- Growth timeline: Hustle Con was decided May 1 and run about six weeks later (mid-June), making about $60K profit. He lived off it for roughly 8 months, then ran it again and made roughly $200-300K profit. A newsletter written about the speakers built an email list, which became the media company. By the third event he was doing $300-400K in revenue (about half sponsors, half tickets). The newsletter went live around April 2016 and reached 100K subscribers in about a year.
- Hiring plan: costs were about $25K/month, so he sold $30K/month of sponsors to create $5K of profit, enough to hire a salesperson. That took him about two months. The salesperson took ad revenue to about $100K/month within two months.

chunks.heading: Trends: copywriting and pricing lessons from launching a paid community
chunks.text:
- The Hustle's ad business reached roughly $500K-$1M/month, but Sam disliked it. Sponsors limit what you can say, and his teammates carried quotas, so criticizing a company could cost them money.
- Two to three years in he launched Trends, a paid subscription research community. It took off, and he pre-sold about $50,000 from a single Word document that explained it.
- On copywriting: he calls it the most important skill in business and life. It means understanding what motivates people and persuading them, whether to buy, to agree with you, or to like you. Trends sold on copy alone.
- On pricing: he charged $299, which he now calls a mistake. His rule: "299 is no man's land." Charge either about $99 (impulse buy) or $1,000-2,000, because someone willing to pay $299 would likely pay far more.
- He says he would run Trends differently if he owned it now; HubSpot doesn't care about its revenue. He suggested to HubSpot that they drop the price to $99.
- Trends Guides: a higher tier priced roughly $2K-$10K/year, which Sam describes as a Gartner-style model. It gave buyers niche research on one specific business model (e.g., how the Hustle does X) plus access to a peer community. They pre-sold tens of thousands to $100K. It was mostly the same as selling the $299 product, except buyers needed approval.
- He says he could build a research business into nine figures in revenue and plans to launch one eventually. He doesn't regret selling to HubSpot given his information, mindset and goals at the time.

chunks.heading: Selling the company: cut to the chase and disclose the bad up front
chunks.text:
- He sold the Hustle to HubSpot for more than $20 million. He also holds a lot of HubSpot stock.
- His mistake: when asked for a number, he said these companies sell for 2.5-6x revenue, so buyers naturally start at 2.5x. "Right when I said that I was like [expletive]."
- What he did well: when a corporate development person emailed about partnering, he asked directly whether they wanted to buy. If yes, he said, he'd email them everything wrong with the company, since they likely already knew the good, and they could walk away if any were a deal breaker.
- They said none were deal breakers. He sees this as taking their later negotiating leverage ("we just found out...") off the table and making them say no fast. He compares it to dating in your 30s, where you ask about kids on the second date.
- He made up this approach himself.

chunks.heading: Studying other builders, speed and long time horizons
chunks.text:
- On Ted Turner: small companies have only two advantages over big ones, speed and focus. Turner moved fast, was an outsider (a Southerner in Manhattan), and clawed his way up from billboards to a radio station to a local TV station to CNN (about 25 years, then about 10 more for CNN to work).
- His takeaway: willingness to dedicate 30 or 40 years to something is itself a competitive advantage.
- Why he researches other businesses obsessively: to avoid repeating common mistakes, because "you are the average of the five people you read and think about most," and because seeing what's possible normalizes it. His example is Roger Bannister's four-minute mile, followed within months by others. Living in San Francisco around huge successes made big outcomes feel like "do I want that" rather than "can I."
- He says founders who claim they don't do research usually do more than they realize. His example is Gagan Biyani, who knew competitors' revenues and positioning in detail.
- He also does it because it's fun and inspiring.
- He hunts for talent early: the Hustle hired many nobodies, about five of whom are now "big shots," and several had no Twitter when hired.

chunks.heading: Focus: say no, track one number
chunks.text:
- At the Hustle there was no company Twitter page for roughly the first two years. The weekly "numbers meeting" covered one question: did the email list grow 3% this week? If yes, why; if no, why. That was the focus for about four years.
- He cites Herb Kelleher at Southwest: asked about adding salad, Kelleher asked if it would make them a cheaper airline, and when told no, said no. Sam's version: "you just say no all the time."
- His view is that the first big pile of wealth almost always comes from one thing, roughly 80/20. Focus on that, get enough money to never worry again, then explore.
- After the sale he shifted to exploration mode: a year of focusing on his body, the podcast and angel investing, then following whatever seems fun ("like a dog catching a smell"). He plans to "go to war" again eventually and is reading and plotting now.
- He still runs small side experiments to stay sharp, such as an $89 copywriting course (Try Copy), which sold about $20K at first and about $1K a day later. The method was "copywork" and the landing page was aimed at a 4% conversion rate. He launched it with no tweet, from Facebook group posts, on a Gumroad page with no custom URL.

chunks.heading: Tools don't matter: reduce friction and keep momentum
chunks.text:
- He has "a disdain" for people who say they can't start without a certain tool, domain name or camera. "I think that those people are losers and that's a loser attitude."
- His Try Copy course made $20K on a Gumroad page with no custom URL. He says ConvertKit versus Mailchimp, or iPhone versus a fancy camera, "matters not one single bit" for nearly everyone starting.
- His rules: use your phone (it's friction-free) and pursue an idea within minutes. If a domain setup takes 20 minutes, use a generic name instead. He picks zero friction and momentum over polish.
- Tool choice can matter if you already know the company will be big, but even then you can usually switch later.

chunks.heading: Growing a podcast and the 50-person cold outreach challenge
chunks.text:
- My First Million is at about 2 million monthly downloads, which he says is likely top five among business podcasts. He doesn't fully know why it worked.
- What he thinks would work: buying ads on other podcasts, spending a lot, and doing it with many shows. But you only retain listeners if the show is good. Podcasts are the hardest medium to grow because you "can't hide bad" with three hour-long episodes a week. He credits his co-host Sean's talent.
- He says copywriting skill carries over to podcasting because both are about influencing people.
- His challenge: make a list of at least 50 people you wish you could be in a room with (to learn from, do business with, befriend or date). Use a spreadsheet with columns for name, email and Twitter handle, then "messaged" (repeat about 8 times) and a mark for no reply or replied, with notes. Find emails with an email finder plugin.
- Cold email and DM them, follow up every two days, and don't stop until they tell you to go away. Replies sometimes come on the eighth attempt.
- His goal is usually just to get on their radar, not a specific ask. Under 30 is a big advantage because successful people like to help young hustlers. Send flattering updates on what you're working on, e.g., "I don't even need a reply, but I'll send you an update every couple of weeks."
- Results he cites: after about 6-8 months, people say "I'm in town, want to hang out?" He emailed the founder of Pandora about 50 times before getting a reply and now has dinner with him and their families. He did the same with Kevin Ryan (Gilt, Business Insider, MongoDB).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr's 2014 breakdown of hosting Bootstrap LIVE, a 3-hour meetup. He explains landing a "whale" speaker first, standing out with a handwritten letter, getting a free venue by appealing to the host's interests, selling tickets through free channels, and the actual P&L.

chunks.heading: How Sam planned and ran Bootstrap LIVE, his first conference
chunks.text:
Sam and his friend Teri hosted Bootstrap LIVE, a 3-hour meetup on bootstrapping (growing a company without outside capital). It was their first event, and Sam notes it was inspired by Noah Kagan's post on making $100k from tech events. He wrote it up in 2014 as a "how we did it" account, not expert advice. The event sold out at 120 tickets two days before it ran.

- **Purpose:** "to learn about the early days of bootstrapped companies," specifically the first $150k in sales.
- **Plan:** they knew how many tickets to sell, where to advertise, and who they wanted in the room. They sat down for a day, wrote the plan out, then "executed like crazy."
- **Mindset:** "Be ignorant, confident and over work." Because they rarely attended meetups, they didn't know most events are bad. They over-prepared and sweated the details.
