- **Credit and caveat:** the event was meant as a test, with profit secondary. Sam says he'd raise prices or add sponsors and a special dinner if profit were the goal. They skipped sponsors so no one would tell them how to run it.

chunks.heading: Landing a "whale" first to create credibility
chunks.text:
Sam's first step was establishing credibility, since ticket sales, PR and other speakers all get easier with it. They chose Andrew Warner of Mixergy as host: a talented interviewer with "a TON of clout." Sam had hung out with him a few times but they weren't close.

- **Make yes easy:** before asking Andrew, they built the Eventbrite page with speakers, schedule and location. They had no other speakers or venue yet. They listed them anyway, "knowing once we got Andrew we could get the other stuff."
- **Stand out:** popular people get constant requests, so they sent a handwritten letter and a $50 bottle of scotch. The letter spelled out "very, very, very clear" how the event benefited him.
- **Deliver in person:** they found his work address and Teri hand-delivered it. Andrew said yes on the spot.

chunks.heading: Choosing and recruiting speakers
chunks.text:
Sam says landing great speakers was key. He wanted accomplished founders who were real experts, had a good story and were nice and fun, not "the VP of marketing of some silly company, a self-proclaimed expert, or someone bragging about being a 'growth hacker.'"

- **Lineup:** Chris Herndon (Apartment List), Nikhil Arora (Back To The Roots), and Neville Medhora (House of Rave, AppSumo, NevBlog).
- **Cold outreach:** the email to Neville was "funny and straight to the point," and it was the first time they had ever spoken. Sam also called him to convince him to come.
- **Accommodation as a perk:** Sam offered to cover accommodation, which meant Neville slept in Sam's room while Sam took the couch. Neville joined the Anti-MBA book club that week.

chunks.heading: Keeping speakers happy
chunks.text:
Sam's goal was to make it so easy that guests "simply had to show up, sit down, and have a conversation (but in front of 120 people)."

- Printed Apartment List's and Back To The Roots' job openings on the back of the programs, since both were growing fast.
- Wrote a detailed itinerary for Andrew.
- Emailed every speaker the questions in advance.

chunks.heading: Getting a free venue
chunks.text:
Sam calls this "pretty freaking easy." Most offices love hosting meetups.

- They cold emailed a few co-working spaces and all said yes.
- The key was appealing to the venue's interests: "NO ONE CARES ABOUT YOU...THEY ONLY CARE ABOUT THEMSELVES."
- The pitch: 150 entrepreneurs in one room would help the space land a new client or two.
- They picked Geekdom SF in SOMA. The venue also supplied free beer and pizza.

chunks.heading: Selling 120 tickets with almost no ad spend
chunks.text:
Ticket sales were the hardest part, but the event sold out two days early. Weeks before selling any tickets, they spent a few hours writing down every place to advertise. Apart from $50 in Facebook ads, all promotion was free.

- **Free listings:** Startup Digest and The Fetch, where anyone can post.
- **Free tickets in exchange for promotion:** Ryan Hoover and The Bootstrappist.
- **Friends and cold asks:** Jason Evanish retweeted it; Web Wallflower was cold emailed by a friend; Neville emailed his followers without being asked.
- **Word of mouth** sold the most tickets. "If your event is awesome people will find out."
- **Timing:** Sam says most events sell 90% of tickets two days out, but they sold the majority two weeks before.

chunks.heading: The numbers: $1,940 revenue, $1,090 profit
chunks.text:
**Ticket revenue**
- Early bird: 60 x $19 = $1,140
- Regular: 20 x $25 = $500
- Late buyers: 2 x $50 = $100
- Discounted: 20 x $10 = $200
- Free: 20 x $0 = $0
- Total: $1,940

**Costs**
- Neville's flight: $250
- Andrew's scotch: $50
- Facebook ads: $50
- Professional videographer: $500
- Total: $850

**Profit: $1,090.** (Sam's headline in the post says roughly $2,000 in sales.)

- The videographer was a deliberate investment: they expected to host more events, and good video should help future ticket sales.
- Profits were reinvested, like a bootstrapped business, to fund flying in the next guest.
- A commenter noted the math ignores the value of their time; if it took weeks, they effectively paid themselves below minimum wage.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2015 essay on writing that gets people to act. Sam's core rule: write like you're talking to a 5th grader, using short words, short sentences, and short paragraphs so each sentence earns the next. He also lists the books, courses, and tools he used to study persuasion.

chunks.heading: How Sam writes copy that gets people to act
chunks.text:
- The goal of every piece of writing is to move the reader to act on what you want.
- He believes a good piece works like a "spell": the reader keeps reading because they want to, and rarely notices it's working.
- Sam doesn't call himself a great writer: "My grammar sucks. I am notorious for typos. But I am better than most."
- His edge is studying people: "I study humans and what makes them tick."

chunks.heading: The core rule: write like you're writing to a 5th grader
chunks.text:
- Use words with only one or two syllables.
- Use short sentences.
- Use paragraphs with only a few sentences.
- Aim for a 5th grade reading level, and use the Hemingway App while writing to check it.
- He frames this as a cheap, easy-to-copy tactic: it takes little work and works on most readers.

chunks.heading: Every sentence has one job: earn the next sentence
chunks.text:
- "The point of the first sentence is to get you to read the second sentence. And the point of the second sentence is to get you to read the third sentence. And so on."
- A well written email, blog post, or book creates a slippery slope, and the reader "melts away into the copy."
- Short sentences and short paragraphs keep the slope smooth, because each step is easy to take.
- He applies this to emails, blog posts, books, and sales copy alike.

chunks.heading: Make the writing do something to the reader
chunks.text:
- Sam opens the essay by telling the reader their reaction (to the headline, to the sentence about their reaction) is "all on purpose."
- The hook is intrigue: people scroll slowly and keep reading because they are curious, not because they are forced.
- He argues people are mostly blind to persuasion working on them, and they enjoy it anyway.

chunks.heading: Sam's five-step learning list for copywriting
chunks.text:
1. Take Neville Medora's Kopywriting Kourse.
2. Read *On Writing* by Stephen King.
3. Read *The Adweek Copywriting Handbook*, even if you don't write books or sales copy.
4. Read *Influence* by Robert Cialdini. He calls it "the greatest and most useful book I've ever read."
5. Use the Hemingway App while writing, aiming for a 5th grade level.

chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: - Sam wrote this in 2015 in his early 20s on his old blog, The Anti-MBA, and keeps it up for nostalgic reasons.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2014 essay where Sam Parr summarizes Made to Stick into six principles (simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, story) with examples from his own campaigns. Useful as a basic messaging and content framework, especially for finding the core, naming people to drive shares, and appealing to self-interest and identity.

chunks.heading: Making ideas stick: Sam's six-principle checklist (from Made to Stick)
chunks.text: Sam wrote this in 2014 as a cheat sheet of the book *Made to Stick*, mixing the book's six principles with his own examples from marketing work at ApartmentList. The principles: Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Story. He keeps the post up "for nostalgic reasons" from his early-20s blog, The Anti-MBA.

chunks.heading: Simple: find the core, then share it
chunks.text:
- Sam says to trim everything that isn't 100% needed and find the single most important thing, "being careful not to bury the lead."
- He borrows the military's "Commander's Intent": instead of detailed plans, state the goal (e.g. "take the bridge"). He used this at a meetup: he built a huge itinerary expecting changes, but made clear to the host that one specific goal held no matter what happened.
- He recommends the journalism inverted pyramid: most important point first, then supporting points, then details. It forces prioritization.
- The shared core should be compact and imply priorities so others can make decisions with it. Examples he cites:
  - A newspaper editor's motto "names, names, and names" kept reporters focused on local stories.
  - JFK's "put a man on the moon and return him safely by the end of the decade," versus the corporate version ("international leader in the space industry through maximum team-centered innovation...").
  - Southwest's "We are THE low cost airline" settles decisions like skipping dinner on flights.
  - Disney's "cast member" label tells even sweepers they're "on stage."
- Sam applied "names, names, names" to ApartmentList's Typical Roommates Infographic and Holiday Gift Guide. They deliberately named popular companies, and the people mentioned shared it most (each named company retweeted it).

chunks.heading: Unexpected: break the audience's patterns
chunks.text:
- Getting attention is step one; keeping it is step two. Humans think in patterns, so break them.
- Sam's process:
  1. Find the core message.
  2. Find what's counter-intuitive about it, and why it isn't already happening naturally.
  3. Deliver it so it breaks the audience's "guessing machines" on that counter-intuitive point, then help them rebuild a better one.
- His warning: "The key to be unexpected is to avoid gimmicky."
- Example: a minivan ad that starts as a normal feature tour, then a speeding car hits the van and the screen reads "Didn't see that coming? No one does." It turns a car ad into a safety ad. He also points to Old Spice's Soul Patch Flavor campaign going viral on Facebook.

chunks.heading: Concrete: make it sensory
chunks.text:
- Sam calls concreteness the easiest of the six traits to accept and implement. Something is concrete when human senses can detect it, and people "love real ideas."
- Examples he uses:
  - Abstract: movie popcorn has 20g of fat. Concrete: it has more fat than a bacon-and-eggs breakfast, a Big Mac and fries lunch, and a full steak dinner combined.
  - Michael Phelps's 12,000 calories a day is forgettable; a photo of the food is not.
  - An oral rehydration therapy promoter pulls out a packet and tells Prime Ministers it costs less than a cup of tea and can save hundreds of thousands of children.
  - Airbnb modeled each office room after a popular listing so investors, politicians and employees would feel that the site is fun and safe, rather than being told, countering the "couch surfing is for pothead hippies" image.

chunks.heading: Credible: five ways to earn belief
chunks.text:
When you lack a true authority, Sam lists these:

1. **Anti-authority:** a dying smoker makes the anti-smoking case. A nonprofit that trains homeless people had a former homeless person drive prospective donors and employers, revealed later.
2. **Concrete details:** messages must have "internal credibility." Vivid details boost believability (a lesson from urban legends).
3. **Statistics:** use them to illustrate a relationship, not as isolated numbers. People should remember the relationship more than the figure. Don't decide first and then hunt for supporting numbers; let statistics shape your view, then share the pivotal ones. He calls Priceonomics "AMAZING" at this, citing their San Francisco rent piece.
4. **The Sinatra Test:** "If I can make it there, I can make it anywhere." A founder who has sold one startup finds the next raise easier. An Indian entrepreneur building a FedEx-style delivery service couldn't win contracts despite guaranteeing on-time delivery, until he solved film piracy deliveries and delivered flawlessly. Sam's takeaway: "Do small favors for people to build credibility before asking for something BIG."
5. **Testable credentials:** invite the audience to verify the claim themselves. Wendy's "Where's the Beef" ads claimed rivals had more bun than burger, which any customer could check.

chunks.heading: Emotional: make people care
chunks.text:
- Sam's framing: the aim is not pushing tearjerker buttons but making people care, because "feelings inspire people to act." Build empathy for specific individuals.
- Three tactics:
  - **Associations:** link something people care about to something they don't. Watch for old associations that have become diluted. His examples: young kids avoid Facebook because their parents are on it; an anti-smoking ad ties cigarettes to big corporations, so smoking = "The Man," which isn't cool.
  - **Self-interest:** always speak to the reader, using "you" not "people." "No one cares about YOU...they only care about themselves." Don't say "we sell the BEST plant seeds in the world"; say "this seed will give you the BEST lawn in the world."
  - **Identity:** people decide by asking who they are, what situation this is, and what people like them do. Self-interest includes intangibles like self-esteem and duty. Examples: an anti-smoking ad built on not wanting kids to smoke; an anti-littering ad that shows littering hurts America and a crying Native American man rather than "the environment."
- He includes a teacher's answer to "why learn algebra?": "Never. You will never need it. But then again why do you lift dumbbells?" Algebra exercises your mental muscles, a means to an end. Sam flags it as combining surprise, analogy and a higher-plane appeal (learning, self-actualization).

chunks.heading: Story: collect them, don't invent them
chunks.text:
- Stories make the listener mentally simulate the idea, which burns it in. Sam says the hard part is creating one, so "always be on the look out" for them, write them down, and save them. Most good stories are "collected and discovered, rather than produced de novo."
- Subway's original campaign was "6 under 7" (six sandwiches under 7 grams of fat) until they found Jared, who lost 245 pounds eating Subway. Sam contrasts the resonance of his story against the tagline.
- Three classic plots he lists:
  - **Challenge:** underdog, rags to riches, willpower over adversity (Jared; *The Pursuit of Happyness*).
  - **Connection:** a relationship that bridges a gap of race, class, religion or similar (the Mean Joe Greene Coke ad).
  - **Creativity:** a mental breakthrough or an innovative attack on a long-standing problem (Mentos commercials).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2014 Sam Parr essay on using the reciprocity rule in negotiation. Give a small, unrequested gift before you ask for something, and the other person feels indebted. He shows it with a Coke on a motorcycle deal, a free speaking slot, and tipping and donation data.

chunks.heading: The gift-first principle (reciprocity rule)
chunks.text:
- Sam's rule: "If you want something from someone, do them a favor or give them a gift first… even if they don't ask for it."
- He grounds it in Robert Cialdini's *Influence*. The receiver feels obligated to repay, and this holds in every human society.
- Unexpected, unasked-for gifts still trigger the obligation.
- Small favors can produce outsized repayment. Owing someone feels bad, so people over-repay to relieve the guilt.
- Sam adds a caveat: give because it's the right thing to do, not only as a tactic. Don't become "an evil genius" with it.

chunks.heading: Winning a negotiation with a $1.99 Coke
chunks.text:
- Sam bought a Honda motorcycle on Craigslist listed at $2,200. He had just sold another bike for $1,800 and showed up with only $1,800 in cash.
- Before the meeting he stopped at Walgreens for two Cokes (one regular, one diet). He told the seller he'd bought a drink for him because they were on sale.
- He emailed the seller beforehand, and the seller called him right away to set up a viewing.
- Sequence: gift first, then a 30-minute test ride and inspection, then the price talk.
- He opened low: "I have a budget of $1,600." The seller said that was too low and claimed other buyers at $2,200.
- He countered at $1,800 and showed the cash: "I've got cash here now and most people on Craigslist flake anyway."
- The seller replied: "Well, since you brought me something to drink, I guess I can do $1,800." Result: $400 off.
- Sam doesn't claim the Coke alone caused it: "does it really matter?" He'd pay $1.99 even if it only raises the odds by 30%.

chunks.heading: Why a small gift works on skeptical counterparties
chunks.text:
- Sellers arrive expecting a fight. They anticipate "lowballers, tire-kickers, and flakes."
- A random passerby isn't expecting to be screwed, but a seller is. So a small kindness catches them off guard.
- Sam's version of the tactic: be nice and disarm them before the price conversation starts.
- He pairs it with credible buying signals: cash in hand, a clear budget, and a quick close (the "most people flake" line).
- Sam says he has bought hundreds of things off Craigslist, and the negotiation is always the hardest and most uncomfortable part.

chunks.heading: Using a gift to land a free speaker
chunks.text:
- Sam got Andrew Warner (founder of Mixergy) to speak at his Bootstrap Live conference for free.
- He first sent a bottle of scotch and a handwritten letter, then asked if Warner would speak.
- The ask came after the gift, not with it.

chunks.heading: Evidence Sam cites that reciprocity moves behavior
chunks.text:
- **Restaurant tips**: one piece of candy with the bill raised tips 3.3%. Two pieces raised them 14.1%. Delaying the second piece for emphasis raised them 23%.
- **Donations**: the Hare Krishna Society hands out free flowers (about 5 cents each). When the person says thanks, the giver replies "And we accept donations so we can continue good works." That usually brings in a dollar or two.
- Sam's takeaway: a cheap, unrequested gift followed by a clear ask converts far above its cost.

chunks.heading: Playbook Sam implies
chunks.text:
1. Give something small and unexpected before the ask (a drink, a handwritten note, a bottle of scotch).
2. Let some time or real interaction pass (a test ride, a conversation).
3. Make your ask with clear, credible terms (a stated budget, cash on hand).
4. Do it because it's good practice, not just manipulation.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2017 reading list from Sam's old blog naming the business books that shaped him. His emphasis falls on perseverance, networking by being interested in others, and copywriting and persuasion as the core skills of business. Light on tactics, but it shows what he values.

chunks.heading: Sam's pick for the best business book ever: "Titan" by Ron Chernow
chunks.text:
- Sam calls Titan, Ron Chernow's biography of John D. Rockefeller Sr., "seriously, without a doubt, the best business book I've ever read."
- He likes Rockefeller as "dynamic, inspiring, and rich (both figuratively and literally)": the richest man ever, thanks to Standard Oil.
- The traits he admires: loyal, disciplined, "confident yet humble, and ruthless." Rockefeller would crush other people's companies without a second thought, then be home for dinner, and he never cheated on his wife.
- Favorite quote, on perseverance: "I do not think that there is any other quality so essential to success of any kind as the quality of perseverance. It overcomes almost everything, even nature."
- Sam also wrote a 3,500-word history of Rockefeller and Standard Oil for The Hustle.

chunks.heading: Strategy and power: "The 48 Laws of Power" by Robert Greene
chunks.text:
- Sam recommends it as a book that is "unapologetic about giving you the tools and tactics to succeed in the ruthless world of business."
- It runs over 400 pages. Greene spends hundreds of pages on the 48 laws, giving a historical example of each and how to use it today.
- Sam wrote a cheat sheet and summary of the book on his blog, and says it is still one of his most popular posts.
- Greene's framing, which Sam quotes: you're better off following the teachings of Moses, Jesus or Buddha for long-term happiness, but many people live by very different rules. Most of them eventually self-destruct, yet they can do real damage to your personal and professional life on the way.
- Sam's takeaway is that you need to understand how power plays work, mainly to defend against people who use them.

chunks.heading: Networking: "How to Win Friends and Influence People" by Dale Carnegie
chunks.text:
- Sam first read it in 7th grade and revisits it every year or so. He says it "has changed my life more than any other book of all time."
- Written in 1936, it is one of the most popular non-fiction books ever and arguably the best-selling business book.
- Favorite quote: "You can make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you."
- Practical reading: to build relationships, lead with genuine interest in the other person rather than pitching yourself.

chunks.heading: Copywriting: "The Adweek Copywriting Handbook" by Joseph Sugarman
chunks.text:
- Sam's claim: learning to communicate with the written word is "hands down, without a doubt, no questions asked THE most important skill any business person can have." The skill is copywriting.
- He picks Sugarman's handbook as the best on the subject because it is simple, easy and fast, yet comprehensive enough to cover the basics. His line: it "covers everything you NEED."
- The standard he takes from the book: copy should be so compelling that the reader cannot stop until they've read all of it, "as if sliding down a slippery slope."

chunks.heading: Sales and persuasion: "Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion" by Robert Cialdini
chunks.text:
- Sam's logic: copywriting is the most important business skill, so learning how to influence others is essential.
- He says nearly every book, paper or study on persuasion after 1984 cites Influence. It is well researched, thorough and easy to grasp, and "the standard" on salesmanship.
- Favorite quote: "Embarrassment is a villain to be crushed." Sam highlights it as a reminder not to let fear of looking foolish stop you from selling or asking.

chunks.heading: How Sam picks business books
chunks.text:
- The blog he wrote this on (The Anti-MBA) started as a book club where he blogged about his favorite books, mostly business or "business-y" ones. He pushed this reading list as a substitute for getting an MBA, an idea he also wrote about at The Hustle.
- His list maps one book to one core business skill: biography and perseverance (Titan), strategy and power (48 Laws), networking (Carnegie), copywriting (Sugarman), sales and persuasion (Cialdini).
- He says copywriting and persuasion are the most important skills. He also picks short, practical books for the basics rather than exhaustive ones.
- He wrote the post in 2017 in his early 20s and keeps it up for nostalgic reasons.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2017 essay where Sam Parr lays out his process for deciding on a risky move like quitting a job for a startup. List the worst-case scenarios, build a contingency plan for each, and only then weigh the upside. Writing it down shows that downsides are usually smaller than they feel.

chunks.heading: How Sam decides whether a big career bet is worth the risk
chunks.text: Sam has studied risk-taking for about seven years: which bets to make, when to make them, and how to protect the downside. He says he is "far from being GREAT at it," but his process has served him well. He wrote this in 2017, in his early 20s, after watching people who wanted to leave cushy, boring jobs (to join a small startup in SF, or start their own company) get risk analysis badly wrong. His claim: most people are "HORRIBLE at measuring risk," and let emotions stop them from doing what they want.

chunks.heading: The downside-first process
chunks.text:
Sam's method is to write things down and map the outcomes. The steps:

1. Write out the exact risk being decided.
2. List the possible worst-case scenarios.
3. For each one, ask whether you are willing and able to be happy if it happens.
4. If not, write a list of solutions that make that scenario "nearly impossible."
5. Only once you are comfortable with every downside and confident you can execute the contingency plans (while living a life you are willing to live), look at the upside.
6. List the positive scenarios the same way. If you like the upside, even a little, and can live with the downsides, "the solution is easy: do it."

He admits the process "isn't unique" and is "just common sense," but argues the process itself is what matters.

chunks.heading: Worked example: leaving a big company for a 5-person startup
chunks.text:
Sam's sample decision: leave a 5,000+ person company, where you have been an accountant with little impact for 5 years, to move to San Francisco and join a 5-person startup with a product you love and a role with real impact.

Worst cases he lists:
- The company tanks after 3 months and you are laid off.
- You hate SF and want to move home.
- You embarrass yourself in front of friends and family who said you'd fail.

chunks.heading: Turning each worst case into a plan
chunks.text:
**Company tanks after 3 months**
- Savings of $30k, spending under $3k a month, gives 10 months of runway.
- Take a $1,200 apartment with roommates, accepting a worse place.
- During runway, Uber or restaurant work is the fallback, which he says would make you unhappy.
- The better fallback is an accountant job at a large company like IBM or Intuit, which he says pays about $100k and isn't hard work. Start networking with their recruiters now, just in case.
- Test: "I'm comfortable with the above plan and know I can execute on it."

**You hate San Francisco**
- You will probably know within 3 months, leaving about 7 months of runway plus job earnings, and enough to get home.
- Ask your parents ahead of time if you can move back in for a few months.
- Tell your current employer your real motivation, end on good terms, and confirm you could rejoin.
- List companies you like in your hometown and make contact now, so a job is realistic within the 7 months.

**Public embarrassment**
- Sam notes that failing in front of people can be crippling, so you should plan around that rather than ignore it.
- Don't post on Facebook, Instagram or other networks until you are happy in SF and it is working.
- Tell only your employer, your parents and a tight circle of friends.

chunks.heading: Filtering out unrealistic worst cases
chunks.text:
Sam's second technique is to list the truly worst outcomes, even unlikely ones, and go through them:

- "I'll run out of money and be homeless and hungry": not likely, so skip it.
- "I won't have a job": the IBM fallback already covers this, so it isn't worth considering.

The point is to stop fears that are already handled, or improbable, from driving the decision.

chunks.heading: Why writing it down works
chunks.text: Sam says most people let emotions hold them back from what they really want. Writing things down and mapping the outcomes typically gives people comfort. It also shows that "the downsides typically aren't that bad and the upside is worth the risk." For the upside he lists things like being happier, becoming rich, having no regrets in 50 years, learning about yourself, and meeting new people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr summarizes the book The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing (which he rates 9/10) law by law. The core theme is positioning: win by being first in the customer's mind, owning one simple idea, sacrificing breadth, and defining yourself against the leader rather than copying them.

chunks.heading: Law of Leadership: be first in the customer's mind
chunks.text:
- Sam summarizes *The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing* and rates it "a 9/10 book".
- He holds that being first beats being better. The first brand in a customer's mind "almost always wins, regardless of product quality".
- Example: IBM dominated early computers because it was first, not because it was better.
- Being first to market is not enough. What counts is being first in the mind. If customers don't think of you when the need arises, "you've already lost".
- Example: Hertz was top of mind in rental cars, so Avis had to position itself around "we love being number 2".

chunks.heading: Law of Category: invent a category when you can't be first
chunks.text:
- If you can't be first in a category, invent a new one. Customers remember the category leader, not the runner-up of the same type.
- Example: Charles Schwab wasn't the first brokerage, but it was the first discount brokerage and dominated that category.
- Law of Division: over time, broad categories split into subcategories, and each becomes its own game with its own winner. The computer category split into desktops, laptops and tablets, each with distinct players.
- Law of Duality: most markets eventually become a two-player race, and everyone else fights for scraps (Coke and Pepsi).

chunks.heading: Law of Perception: marketing is perceptions, not products
chunks.text:
- Sam's framing: "Marketing is not about products…it's about perceptions." The best-perceived product wins, not the best product.
- Example: people consistently prefer Pepsi in blind taste tests, yet Coke still dominates.
- Law of Focus: owning one simple word or idea in the customer's mind is power. Brands that try to mean too many things mean nothing. FedEx owns "overnight" and no one else comes close.
- Law of Exclusivity: two brands can't own the same word in the prospect's mind. If someone already owns it, pick a different hill to die on. Volvo owns safety.

chunks.heading: Positioning when you're not the leader: ladder, opposite, attributes, candor
chunks.text:
- **Ladder:** your rung in the mental hierarchy determines your strategy. Don't act like #1 if you're #3. Lead into your spot. Avis embraced being #2 with "we try harder".
- **Opposite:** if you're not the leader, don't copy them. Be the opposite. 7UP became "the uncola" against Coke.
- **Attributes:** you can't beat a leader at their own game, so pick a meaningful opposite attribute. If Coke is classic, Pepsi positioned itself as youthful.
- **Candor:** admitting a negative makes the message more believable. It disarms skepticism and builds trust. Avis said "we're number 2" and then followed with "we try harder."

chunks.heading: Brand discipline: sacrifice, line extension, and perspective
chunks.text:
- **Sacrifice:** winning requires saying no to customers, features and markets. "You have to give something up to stand for something." Domino's gave up menu variety to win on one promise: delivery in 30 minutes or less.
- **Line extension:** trying to be everything to everyone ruins the brand, and stretching a name across many products weakens its identity. Launch a new brand instead. Heinz failed at U.S. baby food because no one trusted a ketchup brand with infants.
- **Perspective:** marketing wins and losses compound over time. A short-term win like a price cut often causes long-term brand damage. Discounting boosts sales briefly but trains customers never to pay full price.

chunks.heading: Strategy and execution: singularity, unpredictability, resources
chunks.text:
- **Singularity:** one bold move usually wins, not a dozen scattered attacks. Success comes from strategic precision. His analogy: the Allies didn't win WW2 with 10 small attacks, they won because of Normandy.
- **Unpredictability:** you can't forecast the future, so build agility into plans and assume change is coming. Five-year plans in fast-moving industries are "delusional".
- **Resources:** even brilliant ideas need money to survive. Without dollars behind it, even the best marketing will fail.

chunks.heading: Ego, failure, hype, and trends
chunks.text:
- **Success:** success breeds ego, and ego leads to failure. The moment you believe your brand is invincible, it starts dying. Coca-Cola launched "New Coke" out of arrogance and nearly killed itself.
- **Failure:** failure is part of marketing, and "the only sin is pretending it's not". IBM exited its copier business instead of trying to save it.
- **Hope:** the louder the hype, the less substance there usually is. Real success grows quietly. Ford's Edsel got massive pre-launch buzz and then flopped.
- **Acceleration:** trends build slowly and last, while fads explode and die. Microwaves were a trend, pet rocks a fad.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam describes the traits shared by the successful people he enjoys being around. He prefers kind over cut-throat, people who talk about life and ideas over business, people who grew up poor or middle class, and those who are humble and self-deprecating. It's a personal-taste essay on who to surround yourself with, not a tactical playbook.

chunks.heading: Sam's definition of "successful" and who he enjoys being around
chunks.text:
- Sam's personal definition of success has nothing to do with money or job title: "A poor teacher can be successful to me."
- For the purposes of this essay he narrows it to "rich" business types.
- His observations come from a conference weekend in Austin, Texas, plus a ~30 person friend group there that he "loves like family." Most are entrepreneurs; the rest are very successful at whatever they do.
- Through his job he has met hundreds of people with net worths from $100M to $20B. They "come in all flavors": organized or not, nice or mean, and not even the majority are cut-throat.

chunks.heading: Sam prefers kind people over cut-throat ones
chunks.text:
- Cut-throat people care about numbers, spreadsheets and metrics, and put them above everything else.
- Sam describes one successful acquaintance who brags about how brutal he is to work for ("Perform or die") and says Elon Musk falls into that category.
- He does not enjoy spending time with that type. The successful people he spends time with are "incredibly kind."
- Example: Noah Kagan is very successful, and when Sam talks about business too much, Noah interrupts with "So how's Sam?" Sam teases him for sounding like "a cringy therapist."
- Takeaway for who to surround yourself with: kindness and genuine interest in the person beat intensity about metrics.

chunks.heading: Sam likes successful people who talk about life more than business
chunks.text:
- At the conference he had a 2.5 hour dinner with George Mack (about 30, "incredibly smart") and Paddy Galloway (29, "a YouTube savant"), both wildly successful for their age.
- Sam is a client of Paddy's and was supposed to ask him a bunch of business questions. He forgot, and the conversation was mostly ideas: George's "strange, cool theories" on life, Sam's views on the importance of family, and Paddy's Irish Catholic background (which Sam shares).
- His reaction: "I LOVED it."
- Pattern: the best conversations with high performers are about ideas and life, not tactics.

chunks.heading: Sam gets along best with people who grew up poor or middle class
chunks.text:
- Sam grew up in a working class family in Missouri.
- The successful people he connects with tend to come from poor or middle class backgrounds.
- Contrast: at a recent dinner with venture capitalists, they were "smart, kind, and interesting," but also "vest wearing, fancy education types," which he says is not the type he gets on best with.

chunks.heading: Sam values humility and self-deprecation
chunks.text:
- He says "the best ones are humble and self-deprecating."
- Codie Sanchez and Chris Petkas are his examples: they are "hot shit" but still make fun of themselves (and him).
- Summary of his filter for people: kind, more interested in life and ideas than metrics, modest origins, and able to laugh at themselves.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr's field notes after recording My First Million with ex-Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein. The takeaways are about mindset: thick skin, relatability as a leadership trait, studying history, and the difference between climbing an institution and owning a business.

chunks.heading: Lloyd Blankfein: what Sam observed about power, money habits and upbringing
chunks.text:
Sam recorded My First Million with Lloyd Blankfein, former CEO of Goldman Sachs, on June 3, 2026. Sam has met many billionaires through the podcast, but Blankfein was the first guest who was both powerful because he ran a powerful organization he didn't start, and a big name on a global scale beyond business.

- Blankfein's father worked for the post office and he grew up in the projects. He became "successful" in his 30s, which Sam calls young.
- Sam's takeaway: "growing up poor impacts you for life."
- Blankfein still uses the cheap, ad-supported Netflix subscription.
- He wore a "cheap(ish)" Suit Supply sports jacket.
- Sam assumes he is a multi-billionaire with a fancy life, and finds it funny that small habits from his upbringing remain.

chunks.heading: Blankfein's investing habits: day trading and a mostly individual-stock portfolio
chunks.text:
- Blankfein has been retired for 10+ years. His passion and hobby is day trading.
- He joked that he had to place a bunch of orders right before recording, because he would normally spend that time trading. He said he can't stop checking his phone because he loves it.
- Sam relays rough numbers only: about 25% of his net worth is in an index, and about 75% is individual equities.
- He likes big tech, meaning the big players plus some of the smaller secondary ones.
- His advice for becoming a great investor: the number one thing to study is history. "History goes in cycles," so knowing what happened before helps.
- Sam shares the history-nerd streak. Blankfein is passionate about the founding fathers, the medieval era and Robert Caro's books.

chunks.heading: Climbing a power ladder versus owning a business
chunks.text:
- Sam prefers the term "small business owner" for most entrepreneurs he meets. Even at $10b+, he says most still act like small business owners in some ways.
- Blankfein wasn't that. Goldman was already one of the best firms when he joined as an entry-level employee, and he rose to become CEO and steward of it.
- Sam says he prefers being an entrepreneur because it suits his personality.
- He still found something "intoxicating" in joining a storied, powerful institution and leading it. He doesn't typically think about prestige, but says he gets why it's appealing.

chunks.heading: Why Blankfein was so relatable, and why that explains his rise
chunks.text:
- Blankfein works with and influences presidents, Putin, Warren Buffett and Elon Musk, according to Sam.
- Even so, talking to Sam (who calls himself "a peon"), he was "locked in, kind, charming, and very, very relatable."
- Sam concludes: "I can see why he became CEO."
- His overall read: sharp, charming, very likeable, and it is clear why he is so successful.

chunks.heading: Work ethic and thick skin
chunks.text:
- Blankfein had no work-life balance and it didn't bother him. He was high energy and seemed to enjoy the grind. His career was "go go go."
- During the Occupy Wall Street and mortgage crisis era, Blankfein was "enemy #1" because he represented the big banks. Sam notes the oddity that you can't even get a mortgage from Goldman.
- Protestors gathered outside his apartment building. When Sam asked if that worried him, he joked: "No, that's what doormen help with."
- Sam says he repeatedly came across as quite tough-skinned.
- Sam's lesson: he "internalized" that achieving greatness means having a lot of critics, and that is simply part of it.

chunks.heading: Takeaway: powerful people stay normal in small ways
chunks.text:
- After the recording, Sam asked what Blankfein was doing next. He said he would walk the 2 miles home because he had nothing else going on.
- Sam's framing: powerful people, in his words "ballers," are "just like us" in everyday habits.
- Across the notes, the pattern is frugality from a poor upbringing, a hobby he loves (trading), curiosity about history, charm and relatability, and tolerance for criticism.
- Sam hopes to record with Blankfein again.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains his A, B, Z goal framework: start at A, pick a near-term B 3-6 months out, and set an ambitious 3-5 year Z, working backwards from Z. Goals must be specific, include both process and outcome, and be shared for accountability. He gives finance and fitness examples and a fill-in template.

chunks.heading: Goal setting with A, B, Z: three points, not a full map
chunks.text:
Sam sets goals with a three-point system called A, B, Z (he explained it to Shaan Puri, who coined the name). A is the starting point. B is the next destination, usually 3-6 months out. Z is the big 3-5 year plan. He does not plan C, D, E and the steps in between until he gets there, other than vague ideas he expects may change.

His claim: "Most successful people I've met set goals. And the process of getting specific about goals creates breakthroughs." He says he has interviewed or met thousands of successful people, including billionaires and hundreds of millionaires.

chunks.heading: Why A, B, Z works: distraction, direction, constraint
chunks.text:
Sam gives three reasons:

- **It limits distractions.** People often skip steps A and B because they worry about later stops. In doing A and B you gain new insight, and if you don't, you're still better off.
- **It points the steering wheel.** Ambitious people have high horsepower. For many potential winners, the issue isn't pushing the gas pedal but which direction the wheel points. Z guides you, and you work backwards from it. Z might change, and that's fine, but an end destination beats none.
- **It creates constraints.** Sam relays that "someone once said it's easier to 10x something than 2x" and says he isn't sure that's true. He values the constraint question anyway: if you HAD to 10x this outcome, how would you do it? "If you want to achieve Z, what must B be?"

chunks.heading: Rules for writing goals
chunks.text:
- Goals must be specific. Not "lose weight" but "weigh 198 pounds by May 1st, 2026."
- Goals must contain both process and outcome: "weigh 198 pounds by May 1st, 2026 by eating 2,000 calories a day and lifting weights 3 days a week."
- Z should be ambitious, with about a 50% chance of happening.
- B should have about a 75% chance of happening.
- Everything works backwards from Z.
- Z can change occasionally, but changing it should be a big deal. Sam says it's an art to tell "I'm tired and therefore want to change" (bad) from "this truly isn't what I want anymore."
- Tell a few people (a spouse, business partner, friend) for accountability.
- He splits goals into the 4 F's: family, fitness, finance, fun.

chunks.heading: Worked example: finance and business (made-up numbers)
chunks.text:
Sam's illustrative case is a 25-year-old.

**Goal Z:** By 30, have $10M liquid invested in the S&P 500.
- Sell the media company for $20M while owning at least 70%, netting a little north of $10M after taxes.
- The business needs to do $14M in revenue the year before the sale.

**Goal B (in 6 months):** Currently at an $8M run rate, which is 800k subscribers at $10 of annual revenue each. Target is a $10M run rate, so 1M subscribers at the same $10.
- That's 200k net new subscribers.
- The base churns about 30% a year, so roughly 120k are lost over six months.
- Real target: 320k gross adds.
- At $2.50 blended CAC, that's $800k of spend, about $133k a month.

The result: his main focus becomes spending money to acquire subscribers. He expects life to happen and new variables (CAC may change) to show up, but he knows what he's doing and why, and "most everything else doesn't matter."

chunks.heading: Worked example: fitness
chunks.text:
**Goal Z:** At 36, aiming for age 41, "be an athlete who lasts."
- Run a sub-25 second 200m.
- Hold a 45+ VO2 max.
- Deadlift 2x bodyweight.
- Touch his toes with straight legs.
- Go five years without a soft-tissue injury that cost more than two weeks.
- Pick up his kids "without making a dad noise."

**Goal B:** Complete a full combine on December 1 without injuries.
- Do every workout the coach lists.
- Any pain above 3/10 means an automatic 2 days of rest for that body part.
- Targets at 202 lbs: 40-yard dash 4.7; vertical jump 32"; broad jump 10'1"; deadlift 405 (2x bodyweight); 225 bench for 12 reps; mile in 6:30.

chunks.heading: Goal template
chunks.text:
Sam's fill-in-the-blank format:

- **Z:** By [date, 3-5 yrs], I will [outcome], measured by [number].
- **B:** By [date, 3-6 mo], I will [outcome], by [process].
- **Because:** B gets me to Z because [the link].

His instruction: "Try it. Now."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam reflects on Warren Buffett's time on the Washington Post board, where revenue grew a steady 12% a year and profitability surged but the company became stodgy. He argues that building a Buffett-like company takes tedious, boring work, and entrepreneurs should check whether that fits their own tastes.

chunks.heading: The price of steady, profitable growth is boredom
chunks.text:
- Sam uses Warren Buffett's time on the Washington Post board as a case study of what a steady, profitable company feels like from the inside.
- He quotes Roger Lowenstein's book: the Post was "the antithesis of an entrepreneurial company," and "it is striking how little the Post did do during Buffett's tenure on the board."
- Revenue grew at "a solid but unspectacular rate of 12 percent a year." The only dramatic change was profitability.
- Post president Mark Meagher resigned with a long letter urging the Post go private, since he saw "no point in such a stodgy company holding public capital."
- His successor Richard Simmons dryly remarked after yet another proposal was killed, "The sage of Omaha has spoken again."
- Sam's takeaway: the cost of a company with good, steady revenue growth and profitability is potentially boredom.

chunks.heading: Boring is not the same as bad: the payoff
chunks.text:
- The Washington Post is inherently an exciting place to work by default: daily deadlines, breaking news, impact. Once Buffett's financial discipline took hold and the company became more successful, it became much more boring.
- Sam notes that Buffett's roughly $10m position in the Post turned into north of a billion dollars.
- He says the boredom is "100% fine and can be awesome," and that he "would kill to have his track record."
- He argues that being the best at anything (sports, art, business) likely requires decades of tedious, boring work.

chunks.heading: There are many ways to define a successful company
chunks.text:
- Sam lists several valid paths: get big fast (his example is OpenAI), grow a family dynasty over 100 years, or stay a small mom-and-pop business.
- The point is that "success" depends on how the founder defines it, and none of these is the single right path.
- Buffett's approach is alluring to Sam because the businesses are more predictable, the "aw schucks" attitude makes the results seem attainable, and he explains things simply.

chunks.heading: Match the company you build to your own tastes
chunks.text:
- Sam admits that as an entrepreneur there are times he wants what Buffett has or wants to do what Buffett did.
- His caution: founders don't think enough about the day-to-day work required to achieve that outcome, or about how it fits their own tastes.
- Running or working at a company with Buffett-esque values can feel like boredom, and that is a real cost to weigh, not a footnote.
- Reading the Post story from an employee's perspective is, to him, a useful way to see what it takes to build a Buffett-like company. He says it is "not for everyone, that's for sure."

chunks.heading: Sam's self-awareness as a starter, not a compounder
chunks.text:
- Sam describes his own specialty as starting companies and the more exciting parts of business.
- He treats the Buffett story as a reminder to himself that greatness "might occasionally require accepting tedious and boring."
- Practical read: if you are drawn to the exciting early phase, expect that a steady, high-profit compounding business may demand a different temperament than the one you enjoy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A truncated, subscriber-gated newsletter essay. The visible part covers Sam's Boston Inbound talk "Be Chalant: The Art of Giving a Damn" and one lesson: acting uncool and openly enthusiastic attracted investors, employees and customers. The rest of the essay is locked.

chunks.heading: He opens with a "Missouri 4 to New York 7" glow-up and the point of the whole letter is that visible enthusiasm beats acting cool
chunks.text:
Sam frames the essay as a glow-up story: he used to be "a Missouri 4" and is now "a New York 7 (roughly a Missouri 9)". The setup is that, at 16, he looked and acted like Napoleon Dynamite and couldn't get a girlfriend. He tried to fix it by reading every pick-up-artist book he could find.

- The takeaway he drew from those books was to be "cool" and act like he doesn't care.
- He calls that approach "dumb", and says it got him no girls.
- This is the foundation of the talk he gave at Inbound, "Be Chalant: The Art of Giving a Damn".

chunks.heading: He started openly showing enthusiasm in his 20s, and it worked on every audience that matters in business
chunks.text:
When Sam started his first company in his 20s, he dropped the act of indifference and began showing more enthusiasm openly.

- Result in his words: "People were more attracted to me. Investors. Employees. Customers. Everyone."
- The principle: caring out loud is a growth lever across fundraising, hiring and sales, not just in dating.
- He treats detached "coolness" as a costly default that founders should unlearn.

chunks.heading: The Boston Inbound trip: what a "driver" actually looks like at his stage
chunks.text:
Sam spoke at Inbound (HubSpot's conference) in Boston and uses the trip to puncture the image people have of a wealthy founder's life.

- He hates flying and hates being away from his family.
- His family uses a driver named Shah, who first showed up as an Uber driver. Shah owns a minivan with car seats, so he now drives the family to the airport for $175.
- For Boston, Sam paid Shah $1,300 for a same-day round trip, driving him there and back instead of flying.
- Sam's own description: "People have an image in their head when I say I have a driver. But it's really just my boy Shah in a minivan who wears a track suit with Pumas."
- The practical trade-off he is making: paying roughly $1,300 to avoid flying and to be home the same day, because time with family is worth more to him than the money.

chunks.heading: He tests content with a small subscriber pool and asks for replies as the signal
chunks.text:
The essay is also an example of how Sam is launching a newsletter, framed as an experiment rather than a finished product.

- He says he's "thinking of writing a weekly newsletter" and that this is the second issue.
- Readers who recently signed up for CopyThat were put into his "testing pool".
- The feedback mechanism is direct replies: he asks people to reply if they like it and want to keep getting it, and to tell him what to write about.
- Before the paywall-style gate, the page promises a Monday letter to "32,000+ people" and asks signups to reply to the welcome email, even just "hi", partly to signal to Google that he belongs in the inbox and not in spam.
- The signup flow also asks an optional question (job title, company, company size from "Just me" to "1,000+") so he can "make cool stuff for people like you", which is lightweight audience segmentation at the moment of capture.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam profiles an investor who turned ~$10m into ~$50m making about 2.9 buy/sell decisions a year. He distills four habits of successful stock pickers (few decisions, don't agonize over reversible ones, stay in your circle of competence, write decisions down) and applies them to CEOs. The essay is paywalled, so only the opening is available.

chunks.heading: Sam's "2.9 decisions a year" stock-picking lens: few decisions, written down
chunks.text:
Sam met a Hampton member who sold a company for about $10m in 2016. For the last decade his full-time job has been buying individual public stocks.

- Return: 21.8% a year, versus 13.5% for the S&P 500 over the same period.
- He usually holds only 4-8 stocks.
- His roughly $10m is now worth roughly $50m.
- Sam and the member put his brokerage accounts into Claude and asked how many decisions (buys or sells) he makes a year. The answer was 2.9. In some years it was 0.
- Sam's takeaway: "we often correlate motion with good results," but for the average CEO or person with leverage, that isn't the case.
- Sam's caveat: most people should not trade individual stocks ("Index 4 life"). He studies the rare outperformers' decision making because the habits transfer to business.

chunks.heading: Four habits Sam sees in successful investors that apply to business
chunks.text:
Sam has interviewed many billionaire stock pickers (he names Ray Dalio, David Rubenstein, Lloyd Blankfein and Howard Marks, calling Marks a bond picker, "but close enough"). He says the successful ones share four things:

1. **They make few decisions.** He quotes Buffett: "Lethargy bordering on sloth remains the cornerstone of our investment style."
2. **They don't agonize over small decisions.** They split decisions into ones they can't undo and ones they can easily reverse. Most decisions are two-way doors and don't deserve agonizing.
3. **They know their circle of competence.** They say "no" often, not because something is good or bad, but because it's outside their area of expertise.
4. **They write their big decisions down.** They write pre-mortems and their thought process before deciding, then review afterward to judge whether their reasoning was good or bad.

chunks.heading: Pre-mortems and decision journals
chunks.text:
- Pre-mortem method: imagine it's a year later and the decision blew up, then write why.
- Write the reasoning before the decision, not after.
- Review the notes after the outcome. The goal is judging the reasoning, not just the result.

chunks.heading: Reversible vs irreversible decisions
chunks.text:
- Sort every decision into "can't undo" or "easy to reverse."
- Most fall in the reversible bucket (two-way doors). Decide those fast and move on.
- Save the deliberation for the few one-way doors.

chunks.heading: How the 2.9-decisions-a-year investor actually decides
chunks.text:
Sam texted the investor to ask how he decides. His reply, quoted: "I study a few things I feel I can understand, and I study them very deeply. I keep very detailed notes and then just wait for an opportunity."

- Example from the investor: he studied a company extensively about 6 months before Covid and liked it, but it was expensive. He kept his notes, kept an eye on it, and bought when an opportunity showed up.
- The pattern: go deep on a small set of things, keep detailed notes, then wait for price or timing to come to you.
- Sam's observation: this matches the commonalities above (few decisions, circle of competence, written notes).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr introduces his newsletter and the idea of "natural moneymakers", entrepreneurs who make $100m to $1b through deal making and brokering. He says they are unemotional and logical about money. The essay is paywalled, so only the opening is available.

chunks.heading: Natural moneymakers: who they are and how they differ from other rich founders
chunks.text: Sam uses "natural moneymakers" for entrepreneurs who are "so violently good at making money it looks like cheating." He says he noticed them across the 850 podcast episodes he has done, and that almost no one talks about the pattern. He has interviewed about 10 of them and met a few more inside Hampton, his founder community.

chunks.heading: Where natural moneymakers show up and what they've earned
chunks.text:
- They tend to work in roles built on deal making, brokering and inserting themselves into a situation.
- They rarely build in public.
- They have made between $100m and $1b, in different fields.
- The trait is not tied to one industry. It shows up across fields.

chunks.heading: Being rich is not the same as being a natural moneymaker
chunks.text:
- Sam says you can be successful and rich and still not be a natural moneymaker.
- His example is Ted Turner, who founded CNN and became a multi-billionaire. Sam says he was not a natural moneymaker.
- Turner's strengths, per Sam: he "had vision, took risks, and was charismatic."
- Natural moneymakers are a different type. The edge is not vision, risk appetite or charisma.

chunks.heading: They are unemotional about business
chunks.text:
- Sam's first defining attribute: "They are unemotional about business."
- Natural moneymakers feel anxiety like everyone else. The difference is how they use emotion.
- Sam contrasts this with the usual founder story: being emotional and passionate helps founders succeed.
- Natural moneymakers are "more cold about money. More logical."
- Practical reading: they treat money decisions as logic problems and keep feelings from steering the deal.

chunks.heading: Context for the claim
chunks.text:
- The essay is the opening piece of Sam's newsletter, written to introduce it. He says his job is talking to billionaires, heads of massive companies and the best in their field, and the letter passes on what they tell him.
- Sam defines a rich life as a big career, being fit, and a family who loves him.
- The full list of attributes sits behind a subscriber wall, so only the traits above are covered here.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A short, paywalled teaser from Sam Parr's newsletter test. He reports that content creators he spoke with are earning $1m to $10m+ a year with small teams, cites The Hustle's growth to ~$13m revenue and 1.7m daily readers, and says he believes he can reach $10m+ with 2-4 people in 2-3 years. Most of the essay is behind a subscriber wall.

chunks.heading: Sam's ambition: a ~$10m/year business with 2-4 people
chunks.text:
- Sam's claim to fame: in 2016 he started a newsletter called The Hustle. By about year 5 it was at roughly $13m in revenue and 1.7m daily readers, plus podcasts and events.
- He estimates the sale year would have hit about $18m (they sold early in the year).
- He says: "Knowing what I know now, I think I can grow to +$10m in revenue with 2-4 people." He puts the timeline at 2-3 years.
- He floats that his own newsletter might become that business: "Hell, maybe that's what this newsletter will become."

chunks.heading: Creator economy: small teams are making serious money
chunks.text:
- Sam spoke with 6 content creators in one week.
- 3 were small, with fewer than 100k followers on their platform of choice. Each made over $1m/year.
- 3 were bigger, about the size of My First Million. They did over $10m/year with tiny teams.
- All six had tech audiences.
- His takeaway, in his words: "It's raining money for creators."

chunks.heading: Newsletter test: how Sam is running his own list
chunks.text:
- This was week #3 of a newsletter test. Because of mostly good feedback, he decided to send weekly.
- He is still tinkering with the "schtick." Current positioning: help an already successful person have a better career, business and "rich(er)" life.
- The test pool is about 2,000 people. After 2-3 weeks he plans to send to the other ~50k people who signed up for Copythat or his personal email list, which he hadn't used in years.
- He asks readers to help spread the word when he widens the send.
- Subscribe flow tactics: the rest of the letter is gated ("Join 32,000+ people who get it every Monday"), and clicking any link in a past email unlocks every letter.
- He asks one optional profiling question after signup (job title, company, company size) "so I can make cool stuff for people like you."
- Deliverability tactic: he asks new subscribers to reply to the welcome email, even just "hi." It is "good karma" and "shows the Google gods that I belong in your inbox and not in spam."

*Note: the source is paywalled, so only the opening of the essay is available; the detailed playbook for the 1-person $10m business is not included.*

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Short announcement of Hampton, an executive peer group for CEOs. Sam says the peer group he built while running The Hustle helped him grow and sell the company, which is why he started Hampton. Includes the membership bar of $1m revenue minimum.

chunks.heading: Hampton: an executive peer group for CEOs, built from a peer group Sam ran at The Hustle
chunks.text:
Sam announced a new company called Hampton (joinhampton.com), described as "an executive peer group for CEOs." He expects it "will be amazing."

- Origin: he started it because of a peer group he created while running The Hustle. He says that group "changed my life."
- What the peer group did for him: it helped him sell The Hustle and helped him grow it, "everything."
- The format he chose to scale: CEOs meeting in a peer group, the same mechanism that worked for him personally rather than a new, untested model.

chunks.heading: Hampton membership criteria: $1M minimum revenue, ~$20M average
chunks.text:
Sam states who Hampton is built for.

- Entry bar: members need at least $1M in revenue.
- Typical member: the average member has about $20M in revenue.
- Target "sweet spot": CEOs whose companies fall in that range. His pitch to them is simply "COME."
- The audience is CEOs specifically, not founders at large, so the peer group is composed of people running real businesses with revenue.

chunks.heading: Why Sam builds from his own experience: product-from-personal-use signal
chunks.text:
The essay gives a short, concrete example of how Sam picks what to build.

- He built Hampton because he personally relied on a peer group while running The Hustle and credited it with outcomes that mattered most: growing the company and selling it.
- The reasoning is firsthand: he used the thing, saw it change his results, and then built a company around making it available to others.
- The recommendation he makes to prospects is grounded in outcomes he attributes to the peer group (a sale and growth), not in abstract benefits.

chunks.heading: How Sam launched and promoted Hampton: a direct call-to-action to his audience
chunks.text:
The post shows his announcement approach.

- Channel: a short note on his own blog (originally on his old blog, The Anti-MBA), reposted to samparr.com on March 20, 2023.
- Structure: one line naming the company, a one-sentence definition, a personal origin story, the membership qualifier, and a link. No long pitch.
- Qualification built into the pitch: stating the revenue floor ($1M) and the average ($20M) up front lets the right CEOs self-select and signals the quality of the group.
- Call to action: a direct link to joinhampton.com, with a plain invitation: "if you're a CEO and wanna join…check it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam's annual personal review organized as Family, Fitness, Finance, Fun. Mostly personal, but it shows how he sets goals, how his income accumulated from side projects, and what he learned from real estate and courses.

chunks.heading: How Sam structures an annual review: the four F's
chunks.text:
- Sam sets goals and writes his yearly review in four categories: Family, Fitness, Finance, Fun. Each gets highlights and lowlights.
- He writes these because "they'll be fun to review in a decade" and because writing is therapeutic.
- He doesn't use a template; the framework is just those four headings.
- He also runs quarterly fitness goals, and was goalless for the first time in years after his daughter was born.
- His takeaway for the year: the lowlights (pregnancy complications, his dog dying, injuries, real estate) were as instructive as the wins.

chunks.heading: Sam's 2023 income picture: 13 streams that accumulated by accident
chunks.text:
- Sam says 2023 was a huge year for cash flow and net worth, and that it "wasn't really my intention."
- He has 13 income streams: Hampton, podcasting, courses (CopyThat, Ideation Bootcamp), speaking, real estate, Airbnbs, and a few others.
- His goal was never to build many streams or a big annual cash flow. He expected to make more money starting and selling startups.
- Instead he did side projects over the years and they accumulated into strong cash flow.
- He doesn't count stock gains (S&P 500, HubSpot) as cash flow.
- He is also frugal and bad at spending: he stresses over purchases he shouldn't, and thinks he could "let loose a little more."

chunks.heading: My First Million: growth and monetization in 2023
chunks.text:
- My First Million hit 100 million downloads and views in 2023.
- It has 550 episodes since 2019, 131 of them in 2023.
- Sam says he never expected it to become what it is.
- 2023 was the first year the show focused on YouTube; it reached about 400,000 subscribers.
- Sam says the podcast is "always very profitable."
- It has grown into a community: fans host their own MFM meetups worldwide, and thousands attended.
- Live shows: Sam, Shaan and Andrew Wilkinson sold out a 2,000-person theater in Vancouver. He also did live pods in Austin, and spoke in LA and Boston (HubSpot conference).
- He doesn't love speaking but enjoys seeing people care about what he's doing.

chunks.heading: Hampton: hiring rules, headcount and the Joe Speiser partnership
chunks.text:
- 2023 was the first full calendar year of Hampton, which Sam started with Joe Speiser.
- Their starting rules: don't hire lots of people, and avoid big-city folks because they complain too much.
- They broke both. At 18 months in they had about 16 employees, most in NYC, plus 50+ contractors, nearly 70 jobs created.
- Hampton also hosts member events (rally car driving in Austin, lobster diving in LA and Miami, a team retreat in NYC), which Sam attends as an attendee.
- Sam thinks Hampton will be a legacy-defining company for him and Joe.
- He cold emailed Joe in 2016 and they became close. Joe previously started and sold a few 9-figure companies.
- Sam describes the partnership as aligned on values, with great communication and mutual respect.
- Sam links a Hampton post on the template he and Joe used to make sure they were suited as co-founders.

chunks.heading: Courses: reluctant but they beat expectations
chunks.text:
- Sam launched a second course in 2023, Ideation Bootcamp. The other is CopyThat.
- He doesn't love making courses and calls the process tedious.
- He made them because people kept asking him about copywriting and researching businesses.
- Results "blew past" his expectations, but he doesn't plan to make many more.
- His approach: build the product people are already asking you for.

chunks.heading: Real estate: why Sam is selling it all
chunks.text:
- After selling The Hustle, Sam thought he'd become a real estate guy. He bought a 20-acre ranch, turned it into an Airbnb, and bought more property.
- His verdict: "real estate sucks. I hate it!"
- The properties make decent revenue, but he finds them boring and doesn't want to spend time thinking about them.
- He's selling everything, even at possibly the worst market timing, to get out.
- The lesson he draws is about time and attention: revenue doesn't compensate for assets he finds tedious to manage.

chunks.heading: Fitness and lifestyle notes relevant to how Sam operates
chunks.text:
- Fitness goals he hit in 2023: an NFL-combine-style test scoring average for a wide receiver (4.6 forty, 10'7" broad jump, 32" vertical, 225 bench for 16 reps), lower body fat, and lifts of 420 squat, 325 bench, 460 deadlift at 195 lbs.
- He used MyBodyTutor all year for nutrition and calls it a game changer.
- His biggest fitness limiter is injury (hamstrings, lats, shoulders, Achilles).
- After his daughter was born, his goal became "look good naked with the least amount of time in the gym."
- On fatherhood: he says it has given his life energy and purpose, and that it will change everything, including his career.
- He values loyalty highly and wants more adventure in future years, inspired by Jesse Itzler's point about having only about 30 summers left.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: After 800+ founder conversations and hundreds of books, Sam concludes that for any advice from a successful person, you can still win by doing the opposite. He backs this with paired founder quotes on focus, raising VC, grinding, goals, risk, remote work and ads, then closes on building a life that earns admiration.

chunks.heading: The "opposite advice also works" principle
chunks.text:
- Sam's one takeaway from 10 years and 800+ conversations with successful founders, plus hundreds of books on how to be successful: "We're all idiots."
- For any single piece of advice from a successful person, assume you can still win by doing the opposite.
- He applies this beyond business, to health, relationships and any other area with a guru.
- Famous Silicon Valley advice ("Do things that don't scale," "Build what the customer wants," "Culture eats strategy for breakfast") can raise the odds of success, but you can do the opposite and still be successful.
- His evidence is pairs of conflicting quotes from successful people he interviewed on My First Million.

chunks.heading: Focus vs. doing many things
chunks.text:
Sam's examples of successful people who disagree on focus:

- Ryan Smith (Qualtrics, sold to SAP for $8 billion cash in 2018): "I didn't do anything else... I was literally like Qualtrics for 20 years. Heads down."
- Tom Freston (founded MTV, CEO of Viacom): be a niche network, "do one thing all the time, do it really well."
- Chris Koerner (about $3 million a year from six or seven side businesses): "focus is overrated because compounding doesn't care."
- John Morgan (Morgan & Morgan, says it brings in $2.4 billion a year): people who tell you to focus are also hunting, fishing and golfing.
- Joe Lonsdale (Palantir, 8VC with $13.4 billion): his partners can work on up to six things at once, but an operator should do "one or two at most."

chunks.heading: Funding, hours and goals
chunks.text:
**Raise VC vs. never raise**
- DHH (37signals, profitable every year for 25 years, "tens of millions" in annual profit): "We never raised VC... We always had to earn the money we wanted to spend first."
- Brian Halligan (HubSpot, about $11.7 billion): "you should raise a lot so you can kind of make it through."
- Wade Foster (Zapier, $5 billion): "seed strapped," about a million raised through YC.

**Grind vs. a 40-hour week**
- Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot): you can outthink him, but "you will not out grind me, you will not outwork me." He ties outcome quality to the number of iterations.
- Mark Pincus (Zynga): "I'm not stressed enough. I miss the level of intensity."
- MrBeast: goes "as hard as I can, every ounce of my entire body until I just crash."
- Rob Dyrdek (says $350 million net worth): "I work less now than I've ever worked... about a 40 hour week."
- Jack Smith (Vungle, reportedly sold to Blackstone for $750 million): "balance is important and not having tunnel vision."

**Big goal vs. no goals**
- Sam himself: "I had a goal to make $20 million liquid by the age of 30."
- Graham Weaver (Alpine Investors, says $18.7 billion managed) wrote his goals down daily, multiple times a day, in high school.
- Jason Fried (37signals): "I've never believed in goals."
- Dharmesh Shah: "I tend not to have explicit goals."

chunks.heading: Money, risk and trading
chunks.text:
**Never risk ruin vs. not afraid to lose it all**
- Jason Fried: "I'll take risks, but I don't take risks that put me at risk."
- Syed Balkhi (Awesome Motive, bootstrapped, $100 million+): be very conservative because "I came from nothing. I don't want to go back to that."
- Guy Spier: set things up so that when he misses badly he is still okay.
- Rohan Oza (Vitaminwater marketer, Glacéau sold to Coca-Cola for $4.1 billion): "you have to be willing to lose if you're going to win."
- Craig Fuller (Firecrown, says a $60 million revenue run rate this year): "I'm not afraid of losing it all. And I know that I can get it back."

**Money buys happiness vs. it doesn't**
- Scott Galloway (founded L2, sold to Gartner for $155 million): "all this bullshit that money doesn't buy you happiness... that is a myth."
- Andrew Huberman: "money can't buy happiness, but it absolutely can buffer stress."

**Pick stocks vs. stop trading**
- Barry Ritholtz (Ritholtz Wealth, about $9.4 billion): index funds are best. "Put the phone down. Stop trading."
- Lloyd Blankfein (12 years as Goldman Sachs CEO): holds "10% in ETFs and 90% in single stocks because that's what I like to do."

chunks.heading: Team, speed and growth tactics
chunks.text:
**Remote vs. co-located**
- Wade Foster (Zapier): never had an office, "way before anyone thought that was normal." A 2021 secondary valued Zapier at $5 billion.
- Alex Hormozi (Acquisition.com, says portfolio companies do $250 million+ a year): serious people in "the business Olympics" will be together and co-located.

**Move faster vs. outlast**
- Grant LaFontaine (Whatnot, $11.5 billion valuation in 2025): "If you have time to even think about it, you're moving too slow."
- Laird Hamilton (Laird Superfood, about $62 million raised in its 2020 IPO): "victory through attrition."

**Passion vs. talent**
- Tony Hawk: never considered quitting skating because he never started it for money.
- Scott Galloway: "Don't find your passion, find your talent and then commit to developing mastery."

**Spend on ads vs. never spend $1**
- Alex Lieberman (Morning Brew, sold for hundreds of millions): "my only regret is we couldn't figure out a way... to put more money into Facebook ads."
- Kevin Ryan (Business Insider, sold at a $442 million valuation): at 300 million uniques, "never spent $1 in advertising."

chunks.heading: Admiration and building for your family
chunks.text:
- In his 20s Sam became obsessed with putting in work today that makes his future self proud, and says it drove his success.
- With a family, he now asks what he can do today that makes his future family proud, even something small like skateboarding home with balloons for his kids' birthday.
- He treats admiration as a quality to look for in the people you do life with. He admires his wife (he knew he wanted to marry her on a third date when she handled his kidney stone) and his co-founder Joe, whom he trusts so much that on certain topics he feels bad for whoever Joe is up against.
- His aim: on certain topics, he wants people to think "this guy's a f\*cking animal!"

chunks.heading: Things Sam shares that inform his thinking
chunks.text:
- Hampton (his company) is building Core groups in 18 cities, and its point is access to good advice. Miami and Boston Core groups need an additional member.
- At a Hampton event he met a founder doing $20m a year with an app and 5 employees. He invites readers to send "I met a guy who..." business stories.
- Montana Knife Company: 6 years old, bootstrapped, well over $100 million a year in revenue. Founder Josh Smith: "I registered the name Montana Knife Company when I was 19 years old, and I didn't launch it until I was 39."
- Sam cites a chart on smoking (about 4,300 cigarettes per adult in 1963, less than half that by the early 2000s) and asks what will cause the same drop for cell phones and what year we're in.
- Sam flags S&P 500 annualized returns (3 years +22.9%, 10 years +15.3%, 30 years +10.3%, 50 years +11.9%) as running hot versus the long-run norm of about 10-12%, and notes the last time was the late 1990s before the dotcom crash.
- Robert Greene's point, which Sam shares: advances of $20,000-$50,000 with a year to finish force writers to rush, so the work suffers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2013 essay from Sam Parr's old blog arguing that "overnight success" is mostly a myth. Drawing on Robert Greene's Mastery, he says most monetary success takes decades of apprenticeship, and he built a spreadsheet (the CEO Doc) tracking how long famous founders worked before breaking out.

chunks.heading: The "overnight success" myth and the 5-10 year apprenticeship
chunks.text:
- In 2013, Sam wrote that "overnight success" is "complete nonsense" for most people.
- The internet has produced a few lottery winners who went from $0 to $1B quickly, but he argues most people who reach monetary success needed decades.
- His claim: "Not everyone goes from idea to IPO in months. Behind (nearly) every success is years, and years of hard work."
- Sam presents this as an early-20s view from his old blog, The Anti-MBA, and keeps the post up for nostalgic reasons.

chunks.heading: Mastery and apprenticeships
chunks.text:
- Sam became obsessed with apprenticeships after reading *Mastery* by Robert Greene.
- His summary of the book: successful people and "geniuses" are people who mastered their craft, and mastery requires intense study for 5 to 10 years, which is essentially an apprenticeship.
- Greene illustrates this with the stories of Darwin, Einstein and Ford.
- Takeaway Sam draws: treat the first 5 to 10 years of a career as a deliberate apprenticeship, not as a delay before success.

chunks.heading: The CEO Doc: evidence of how long success takes
chunks.text:
- Sam built a Google spreadsheet he calls "The CEO Doc" that shows how long it took well-known founders and CEOs to become "overnight successes".
- Its purpose is to prove the point with data rather than assertion.
- Observations he draws from it:
  - Andrew Mason and Jeff Bezos "skyrocketed to success" (the fastest cases in the doc).
  - Jack Dorsey has been programming for a long, long time before his success.
  - "The magic age to start something amazing looks to be 27."
- Takeaway Sam draws: even the apparent fast risers had a long runway of prior work, and the typical starting age for the breakout venture sits in the late 20s, not the early 20s.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2014 personal essay where Sam Parr shares what changed after a year of sobriety: fitness, confidence, clarity, and emotional control. Mostly personal reflection, with durable mindset lessons about facing stress head-on, exercise as a mood and work-ethic driver, and conviction building confidence.

chunks.heading: Quitting alcohol: Sam's one-year results (2014 essay, reaffirmed 2017)
chunks.text:
- Sam wrote this in July 2014 on his old blog, The Anti-MBA, after one year sober. In a 2017 update he says everything in it "is still true but 10x" and that he still doesn't drink.
- He frames it as personal, not a campaign: he's fine with others drinking, still goes to bars, and says very little of it is scientific.
- He had stopped for personal reasons and planned a longer post on the effects on his relationships, finances, body and mind.

chunks.heading: Drinking made him gain weight; exercise reversed it
chunks.text:
- He gained about 35 pounds after starting to drink. He attributes it to more than the calories from thousands of calories of beer a week.
- He was a college runner and always fit, but stopped working out once the drinking started because he was too hungover or drunk.
