- Drunk eating compounded it: White Castle, greasy pizza at 3 AM, "late night burritos". A pounding headache plus regret killed motivation.
- After a few months sober he started working out again and the weight came off. He was running again at the time of writing.

chunks.heading: Exercise changed his mood, confidence and work ethic
chunks.text:
- Beyond losing "Drunk Sam weight", the mental effects were the best part: mood up "by a 1000%", happier, more alert, more confident.
- He noticed a better work ethic: working hard physically and mentally started to feel good.
- By his account, if he goes a day without working out he feels like crap.

chunks.heading: Confidence from not drinking made him more attractive to people
chunks.text:
- His biggest fear about sobriety was dating: that women would think he was a freak or a religious nut.
- He relied on booze for "false confidence". After a few months working on his mindset, he was confident enough to tell dates he doesn't drink.
- Women liked him more because he "stuck to my guns and believed in something". That raised his confidence further, a reinforcing loop.
- It wasn't only women: male friends wanted to hang out more, and strangers seemed drawn to him.

chunks.heading: Sober fun is harder but better, with no hangover cost
chunks.text:
- He couldn't remember the last fun night without a hangover. For years he avoided committing to Saturday or Sunday morning plans because he'd be drunk or hungover.
- Having fun sober took work, but done right it felt like "putting on glasses for the first time after years of poor eyesight".
- Going to bed happy and waking up still happy, and not having made drunk decisions, felt great.

chunks.heading: Facing hard moments sober, and controlling emotions
chunks.text:
- He used to drink before big emotional events (mourning, weddings, meeting or breaking up with someone) to avoid facing reality. Facing them sober felt like an adrenaline rush.
- Example: leaving his job to run Hustle Con. He felt every emotion, including the fear and stress, and was excited to get out of bed.
- He now embraces obstacles because he likes feeling the stress, pain and achievement of overcoming them: "Feeling stuff is a total rush."
- His claim: "When you control your emotions you control your reality." Drunk Sam had no control and blurred perception.
- Sober, he says he hadn't been angry once in about 8 months. When something bad happens he steps back, analyzes what's going on and how he feels, then decides, which makes him less impulsive.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam argues negative feedback is more valuable and actionable than positive feedback, provided you separate your performance from your self-worth. He shares a simple three-step method: send an anonymous strengths/weaknesses form to 10 close contacts, then act on the most common weaknesses.

chunks.heading: How Sam treats negative feedback
chunks.text:
- Sam argues that "negative feedback is far more valuable and actionable than positive feedback."
- He backs this with a passage from the book *Smartcuts*, which says negative feedback helps people learn and grow faster than positive feedback.
- Sam wrote this in 2014, in his early 20s, on his old blog The Anti-MBA. He later labeled it an "old post".
- He encourages critical feedback and says he can now laugh off harsh comments that used to upset him.

chunks.heading: Mindset required for negative feedback to work
chunks.text:
Sam quotes *Smartcuts* on when negative feedback helps and when it hurts:
- It only works in the right mindset, otherwise it can be "catastrophic".
- Make it about the thing you did, not about you.
- You have to be "really secure" to feel good about yourself when all you get is critique.
- The fix is to build your self-esteem muscles by showing yourself you are okay when things go wrong. Feedback is about what you do, not who you are.
- "De-couple the performance from the self-esteem."

chunks.heading: Separating useful criticism from noise
chunks.text:
- A popular California blog, The Bold Italic, ran an article on Sam's motorcycle trip, panic attacks and blog.
- Its Facebook comments included insults, such as calling him a douche.
- Sam says that feedback was not helpful: "those guys are just a bunch of jerks." He found the comments funny.
- He notes they were the only negative comments he got. He had 100+ positive comments on reddit.
- The takeaway is that random internet abuse is not the feedback he means. He wants structured, honest critique from people who know him.

chunks.heading: Sam's method for getting actionable negative feedback
chunks.text:
1. Create a Google Form with two questions: what are my 3 biggest strengths, and what are my 3 biggest weaknesses.
   - He added the strengths question as a "red herring". It gets people talking and speaking their minds.
2. Send the form to 10 of your closest co-workers and friends.
   - Tell them you are working on yourself and want feedback because you value their opinion.
   - Tell them the form is anonymous.
3. Take the three most common weaknesses mentioned, print them out, and tape them to your bedroom door.

chunks.heading: Why the process works
chunks.text:
- Anonymity lets people be honest.
- Asking for 3 weaknesses forces specifics instead of vague praise.
- Looking only at the three most common answers filters out one-off opinions and surfaces patterns.
- Taping them to the bedroom door keeps the weaknesses in front of you daily.
- Sam says he got "phenomenal results", and calls it a trick that "sounds crazy" but "works wonders".
- He says that even if people do not call you a douche, the results will still be helpful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how to give customer service feedback so it gets results. Stay polite, say you want to keep using the product, and mention a competitor. His rewritten Uber email got a friend $50 back plus a $20 credit, and a tweet tagging Spotify earned him 3 free months of Premium.

chunks.heading: How Sam writes a complaint that actually gets results
chunks.text: Sam's core claim: most people complain by being "pissy and rude," which is "totally counterproductive." A hostile email gives the company nothing to act on except to let you leave.

chunks.heading: The $80 Uber ride example
chunks.text:
- A friend visiting San Francisco tried Uber for the first time and got hit with 3x surge pricing. A 2 mile ride cost $80. This was before Uber showed many surge notifications.
- The friend's draft email: subject "Pissed customer," saying he would never use Uber again and calling them "Assholes."
- Sam's critique: the company's likely reaction is "looks like this guy will never use us again," so they apologize and move on. The email "wouldn't accomplish a THING": no refund, and Uber loses a customer.
- Sam rewrote it using principles from *How To Win Friends and Influence People*:
  - Subject: "Helpful feedback from an unhappy user" (not "Pissed customer").
  - Open with a positive: he had heard "a ton of amazing things" about Uber.
  - State the specific problem: charged $80 for a 2 mile ride, and while he saw there was 2x surge, he expected $20 or $30.
  - Say he wants to keep using the product, but is unhappy and considering Lyft.
  - Close with a reasonable question: "Doesn't $80 seem a little ridiculous from SOMA to Mission?"
- Result: the friend got $50 back plus a $20 credit on his next ride.

chunks.heading: Make competitors compete for you
chunks.text:
- Sam says to use Twitter when you want to get "real frisky," because you can include the company's competitor in the tweet.
- His reasoning: "most companies care WAYYYYY more about beating their competitors than they care about making you happy. Use this."
- Example: Sam used Slacker Radio daily for 2 years but hated its new design, though he was still considering their premium product. He tweeted about it in a way that involved Spotify.
- Spotify responded by giving him 3 months of Spotify Premium. Sam says he planned to become a full-time paying customer once those months ended.

chunks.heading: Sam's rules for dealing with customer service
chunks.text:
- Don't insult or yell at them.
- Explain that you want to remain a customer if they fix the issue.
- Tell them you will use a competitor's service otherwise.
- Tweet when possible and tag the competitor's Twitter handle.

chunks.heading: Framing
chunks.text:
- Sam's premise: if you use a product, you are probably a fan, and a company would want your feedback. Complaining politely and specifically is feedback; complaining rudely is noise.
- He wrote this in 2014 in his early 20s on his old blog, The Anti-MBA, and labels it an "old post."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains his personal finance process from his early 20s: track spending obsessively, calculate burn and runway, set tiered savings goals up to 36 months, and deliberately feel the pain of underspending. The point is financial independence, not being cheap. Written in 2019 on his old blog.

chunks.heading: Saving 50%+ of income: the core rule and his goal
chunks.text:
- Sam says he has saved "like a mad man" since age 19. He aims to save 50% of post-tax income and often exceeds that.
- Saving equals earning more plus spending less. He treats this essay as the spending-less half.
- Saving is not being cheap. It means having money for things that truly make you happy instead of over-consuming on stuff that "leaves you empty."
- He frames it as partly spiritual: knowing what makes you happy and what doesn't, and knowing you need very little to be happy but can splurge if you want.
- His stated payoff is coming from a "position of fuck you": you don't need much to be happy, and you have the money to do what you want.
- Benchmark he cites: the average American saves a single-digit percentage of post-tax income per year.
- When he earned very little, he still managed to spend only $1,000-$1,500 a month while living in San Francisco. "I lived like a spartan...and I was very happy."

chunks.heading: Why he targets 36 months of savings, not 6
chunks.text:
- His target is 36 months of liquid savings. This is aimed at anyone with less than 36 months saved.
- "Savings" means assets easily liquidated: cash savings, stock, 401k.
- Common expert advice is a 6-month emergency fund. Sam thinks that is "way too short."
- Reason: he is an entrepreneur and very conservative with money. When business booms he is "rolling in it," but when business is bad or he is starting something new, his own income is the first thing to stop.
- 36 months is the number he feels comfortable at.

chunks.heading: Step-by-step system: track, measure burn and runway, set goals
chunks.text:
1. **Aggregate accounts with Personal Capital.** Free, similar to Mint but easier to use in his view, about 10 minutes to set up. Check it monthly for income and expenses. He calls it his favorite tool.
2. **Track spending manually with the My Weekly Budget app ($0.99).** Write down every purchase. Whether or not you have a budget (he says you should), tracking forces you to notice spending and typically leads to improvement.
3. **Build a personal burn and runway spreadsheet.** Take trailing 3 months of spending from Personal Capital and average it; that is your burn. Divide liquid assets by burn to get runway. It doesn't need to be fancy, "just know your numbers."
4. **Set milestone goals:** 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months of runway. If you have under 3 months in cash, reach 3 first, then 6, and so on. Put these in the spreadsheet.

chunks.heading: Setting the budget and feeling the pain
chunks.text:
- Review current expenses in Personal Capital, decide what makes you happy and what doesn't, and cut what doesn't.
- Your monthly burn without those cut items becomes your monthly budget. Convert it to a weekly budget in My Weekly Budget, log every spend, and stick to it.
- "If you're not hurting then you're not saving enough."
- If you are young, in debt, or starting from $0, he says this can take years, maybe decades. "Embrace it. It's worth it. It hurts so good."
- Caveat: if you're happy with your current situation, ignore all of it: "You're winning."

chunks.heading: Debt rules
chunks.text:
- Pay off debt before building savings, and build debt payments into the budget.
- He names two approaches: pay off high-interest debt first, or pay off small loans first to build momentum.
- If you have no debt, do not take on debt again until you've hit your savings goal. "Debt can be crushing."

chunks.heading: Tools he uses to grow the savings
chunks.text:
- **Robinhood:** he buys stock and rarely sells. He says he pretty much only buys Facebook and a general S&P 500 fund.
- **Ally Bank:** savings account at 2% interest at the time of writing. He gives the math: $10,000 earns $200 a year, $100,000 earns $2,000.
- **Robo-advisors:** he likes Wealthfront, and says Betterment and others work too. He keeps "a fair bit of money" in Wealthfront with risk tolerance set as high as it goes.
- Context: the essay is from 2019, written in his early 20s on his old blog, The Anti-MBA, and he keeps it up for nostalgic reasons. The rates and tool choices reflect that time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr recaps Syed Balkhi's path from a WordPress blog to a bootstrapped company with over $100m in revenue, built by buying plugins. He reflects that creativity and gut get you initial traction, but later stages call for a more disciplined capital allocator mindset.

chunks.heading: Syed Balkhi's path from blogger to capital allocator
chunks.text:
- Syed Balkhi started a blog called WP Beginner about WordPress, writing about plugins and how-tos, and it started getting traffic.
- After a few years he began buying WordPress plugins, and "it starts working."
- After roughly 10-13 years he owned something like 30-40 WordPress plugins.
- Sam's account of the outcome: the company does over $100m in revenue and is worth north of $1 billion. It is fully bootstrapped, with no funding or loans, and Syed owns all of it.
- Syed is only 32 and is an immigrant who wasn't wealthy.
- Sam spoke with him on My First Million and called him "one of the most impressive businessmen I've ever chatted with."

chunks.heading: Why discipline and a capital allocator mindset impressed Sam
chunks.text:
- What stood out to Sam was how disciplined Syed was.
- Syed described going from internet founder to capital allocator, and Sam found that "inspiring."
- Sam says Syed's example pushed him to "level up" and focus more on a capital allocator mindset.
- Sam doesn't claim to have made that shift yet. He says he is past the initial scrappy stage: he has "some money, success, and an audience," but admits he hasn't always been great at leveling up.

chunks.heading: Creative versus disciplined: where each fits
chunks.text:
- Sam describes himself as more of a creative in business and "not super disciplined." He thinks of ideas, does them, and "sometimes they work." He follows his gut.
- He argues there is a place for that approach: "I don't think you can Excel sheet your way to initial traction. At least I can't."
- His reasoning is that early traction requires inventing "a better mousetrap," and that takes creativity.
- His implied sequence: creativity and gut find the initial traction, then a later stage calls for discipline and capital allocation.
- Sam treats being past the initial-traction stage as the reason to level up toward the more disciplined mindset.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam argues the real cost of an asset is the maintenance time it demands, not what you paid for it. He went from owning cars and houses to renting and owning little, and says his mind is lighter and life more convenient, even if it earns him criticism.

chunks.heading: Time cost vs. purchase price
chunks.text:
- Sam says the real cost of owning something is "maintenance hours, not purchase price."
- He has owned "cars, houses, other stuff." He now owns little: he rents and has no car.
- He says he is happier with fewer possessions.

chunks.heading: What owning stuff really costs
chunks.text:
- Each owned thing adds a recurring to-do list. Sam names the chores: maintain, fix, register, renew, insure, update, subscribe.
- His test for any purchase is therefore the ongoing hours it demands, not the sticker price.

chunks.heading: Renting instead of buying a home
chunks.text:
- Sam gets criticized often for not owning a home ("You're throwing so much money away!").
- He is unsure the criticism is right. He says he thinks he "makes more money now" by not owning stuff, though he doesn't give figures.
- What he knows for certain is that his mind is lighter and his life more convenient.

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text:
- Count a purchase's ongoing maintenance hours alongside its price.
- Fewer possessions means fewer obligations and less mental load.
- Sam weighs convenience and mental lightness above the "rent is wasted money" argument, and says owning less may also have helped his income.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr shares the repeatable writing process he and John used to launch The Hustle, publishing 3-6 posts a day without formal writing backgrounds. It covers headline-first writing, ugly drafts, ruthless cutting, hooks, and simple language.

chunks.heading: Sam's 14-step writing process for The Hustle
chunks.text:
Sam and John used this process to launch The Hustle. It let them publish high-quality content daily, sometimes 3-6 blog posts a day each, with no formal writing backgrounds. Sam says copying it will help a new writer finish a stalled project.

1. **Headline first.** Writing it first forces focus on the topic.
   - 3-10 words, plain English, as if telling a friend what the article is about.
   - Example: "I went 30 days with no food, living off only Soylent."
2. **Description second.** One or two sentences, the subtitle under the headline and the text shown below it on Facebook. It keeps the core idea in view.
3. **Write a bad draft.** Sam calls this the toughest part, because "most people are deathly afraid of writing and having their thoughts read."
   - "Accept that it will suck."
   - Write anything, even "I don't know how to start, but I'm just starting now."
   - "Motion creates emotion." Dump every thought on paper and ignore quality and word count.
4. **Incubate.** Walk away for 2 minutes or 2 years. Not focusing on a problem helps produce new ideas (fixation forgetting, "showerthoughts"). Sam calls this step "incredibly important."
5. **Edit.** "This is where the magic happens." He quotes David Ogilvy: "I'm a lousy copywriter, but I am a good editor." Editing "turns crap into gold."

chunks.heading: Cutting, openings and the slippery slope
chunks.text:
- **Cut first.** For most people that means deleting the first 25% and the last 25% of the draft.
  - Since grade school, people are trained to write to a word count. Sam says that is wrong.
  - "Every single word must be necessary. Nothing more, nothing less." Don't use 1,500 words for what takes 500, because extra words dilute the message.
- **Make the first sentence "punch the reader in the face."** Attention is hard to get, so the opener must be undeniable.
- **Create a slippery slope.** Each sentence exists only to get the reader into the next one: the first sentence sells the second, the second sells the third, and so on.
  - Tactics: lead with a personal story, hint at what's coming later, or pose a question.
  - His Soylent example: "I spent the last 30 days eating nothing but Soylent... Why would I do something so stupid? I'll explain. But first, if you aren't familiar with Soylent, here's the gist."

chunks.heading: Writing simple
chunks.text:
- Target a 7th to 8th grade reading level. His rule: "a great post has C+ writing and A+ storytelling, insight, or analysis."
- Check the grade level with the Hemingway app.
- Skip flowery or complicated language, whatever a 5th grade English teacher said.
- Keep paragraphs to 2-4 sentences and sentences to about 25 words or fewer, so the page is easier on the eye.
- Warren Buffett's shareholder letters on the complex insurance industry average 13 words per sentence. Sam's point is that even hard topics can be simplified.
- Avoid adverbs (words ending in "ly"), which weaken the verb. "I yelled at the boy" beats "I angrily yelled at the boy." He cites Stephen King: the road to hell is paved with adverbs.

chunks.heading: Headlines: where most of the work goes
chunks.text:
- Sam says 90% of people read the headline and never consume the article, yet people rarely perfect it.
- Return to the headline after editing:
  - Write 25 headline options.
  - Show them to a few friends and ask which one they would click.
  - Pick from those.
- His claim: once the headline is written, "you have spent ninety cents out of your dollar."

chunks.heading: Images and copywork
chunks.text:
- **Image:** don't use the logo. Make it "clicky." Google images may violate copyright, so he recommends Unsplash.
- **Copywork for inspiration:** pick a blogger, author or poet you like and write their work out by hand.
  - It shows how they structure writing and what their texture feels like.
  - Sam spent two hours a day for 6 months copying favorite authors and says it "worked wonderfully."
  - He says you don't need to go that far. Copying a few sentences before starting work helps.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle's revenue streams (ads, conferences, subscriptions) were valued by a strategic buyer, why he took cash and stock with no earn-out, and why he optimizes for time. He also covers a "big hit, then reflect" career model, de-risking via real estate, and cold-emailing 50 people out of his league.

chunks.heading: Why Sam sold The Hustle: the $20M-by-30 goal and the "time billionaire" idea
chunks.text:
- At 21, Sam set a target of $20M liquid by age 30. His logic: at $20M "you're set", it's "kind of hard to screw that up", and family needs (braces, health care, risking a new venture) stop being decisions.
- He worked backwards from that number. He hit it at 29-30 by selling The Hustle to HubSpot after about four years of running it.
- He says what he wants most is to be a "time billionaire" (a phrase he credits to Tim Ferriss). Running a company felt backwards: "everyone's like, 'you're the boss, you could do what you want.' I'm like, it's kind of the opposite. The more people I have, they own me a little bit."
- He took the exit partly because he was burnt out and the economy was uncertain in late 2020. He feared Facebook and Apple tracking changes would hurt ad revenue. He felt "I've only been at this for four years, I'm set after this."
- He still believed he saw a path to $100M a year in revenue if he had kept running it ("if you're willing to run it for 20 years, it's pretty straightforward"). He chose certainty over upside.
- On regret: the HubSpot stock he received went from about $350 at announcement to a peak near $850, and he thinks he could have gotten more by waiting six months because the ad market boomed. He says he has "zero regrets".

chunks.heading: How The Hustle made money and how media companies are valued
chunks.text:
- Revenue streams before the sale:
  - Conferences (Hustle Con): seven figures a year before COVID, with tens of thousands of attendees. These went to zero in the pandemic.
  - The daily email: well over $10M a year, mostly ads.
  - Trends: a paid subscription newsletter and community.
- At sale, the next 12 months were projected at about $20M in revenue. He recalls roughly 1.7M subscribers and rounds to 2M.
- His rule of thumb for media company multiples: roughly 2x to 10x revenue depending on growth, "more likely, it's always in like the 4X range".
- A source of his caution about internet businesses: they can go from a $10M run rate in two or three years to zero in one or two, which is partly why he moved money into real estate.

chunks.heading: Why HubSpot was the right buyer and how they valued the deal
chunks.text:
- Sam had assumed a WeWork or Salesforce would buy The Hustle. HubSpot approached instead, and he thought it was "smart" because HubSpot sells to small businesses, who are exactly what The Hustle's readers were.
- HubSpot was already an advertiser. They knew how much revenue and how many leads they got from advertising with The Hustle, and concluded "we should own this."
- Valuation was strategic and based on customer value, not a revenue multiple. They estimated how many customers HubSpot had acquired through The Hustle, the lifetime value of those customers, and how many more they could expect over the next five years.
- Negotiation took about 90 days, starting around October 2020, and closed at the end of January 2021.
- Takeaway: an existing advertiser who can measure their return from your audience is a natural strategic buyer.

chunks.heading: Deal structure: cash up front, no earn-out, and an exit from the CEO role
chunks.text:
- Sam received "tens of millions in cash upfront" plus a large amount of HubSpot equity, with no earn-out. The stock was given over a short period and he did not have to hit targets to earn it.
- The timing was awkward: he had just hired a replacement CEO (Jordan). His condition was that Jordan would run the company and Sam would only host the podcast (My First Million). HubSpot agreed.
- HubSpot also paid him to host the podcast. Their media group is described as having about 75-80 employees.
- No-earn-out was partly HubSpot's own preference ("we don't like earn-outs"). Sam was also clear with them: "I want to own all of it or I want to own none of it."
- He acknowledges the tradeoff. Keeping a stake is a "second bite of the apple", but it costs your time. He doubts his personality would fit owning 10% of something he no longer runs.
- He says holding a minority only makes sense if the buyer can plausibly grow the business many times over (for example a $1B sale heading to $10B). HubSpot's market cap was around $45B at peak, so The Hustle was not a big needle mover for them.

chunks.heading: Running a business as a war, and the "sell, rest, then go all in" playbook
chunks.text:
- Sam compares starting and scaling a company to going to war. He notes that veteran friends say it was the hardest, scariest, most stressful time and also the happiest, and that they "wish I could do it again."
- His analogy for his own cycle: training for an athletic event. Put in base miles and rest, then "when I'm ready to go race, I'll go all in." He says he is not ready to race yet but will be soon.
- He modeled his life on a few people:
  - Felix Dennis (author of *How to Get Rich*, founder of Dennis Publications and Maxim, died worth roughly $800M-$900M). Dennis wrote that he wished he had gotten as rich as he could by 35 and then retired, instead of staying "punch drunk like an old boxer", which hurt his health and relationships.
  - Travis Kalanick: sold Red Swoosh around age 30, then built Uber.
  - Mark Cuban: sold MicroSolutions at 31-32, took about eight years off, then built Broadcast.com and sold it for a billion.
- His synthesis: take a hit in your 20s or 30s, chill, reflect, find the next thing "very methodically", then go all in, which may let the second company be even bigger.
- He believes he will operate again and says the next time he will start "from a little bit of a different place": because he does it by choice, not need, it will be "more fun."
- Not rushing: he has not yet started the next company.

chunks.heading: Choosing people to learn from
chunks.text:
- Sam says he built his life by following people who play at a higher level, and that hosting Hustle Con (speakers included founders of WeWork, Casper, Away, Headspace and Bonobos) gave him access to many of them.
- His best friend, Jack Smith, started a company at 22 and sold it at 28 for $800M in cash, raising little money. He lives simply in Hawaii and "wants nothing". Sam learned from his curiosity-driven approach and says wanting stuff can make you depressed.
- Another role model, John Arrow (founder of Mutual Mobile, an app development agency started in Austin, roughly 500 employees), works on the company about two days a week and spends the rest tinkering with small experimental projects, such as a vending machine on a Segway bought off Alibaba and a QR code on a stop sign that pays $1 per scan.
- Sam's attitude toward side projects is that they are "just my art", done for expression, not money.

chunks.heading: Investing approach: boring, diversified and relationship-driven
chunks.text:
- Sam says he doesn't love investing but finds it "so much easier to make money that way."
- Allocation as he describes it: most net worth in HubSpot stock and Airbnb stock (his wife works at Airbnb), plus a Vanguard Total Index Fund. Selling the private company diversified him away from a single illiquid asset.
- Angel investing: he runs an AngelList syndicate that has put about $15M into roughly 60-70 startups. He expects strong returns, but credits his network, not skill: he lived in San Francisco for eight years and knows founders who go on to raise from Andreessen Horowitz. "It's a huge unfair advantage."
- Real estate:
  - Bought Austin property that has appreciated, which he says needed little skill.
  - Bought a 20-acre ranch for an Airbnb called Marathon Ranch, a fitness-style stay, turnkey and furnished, with guests booked from April 1. He plans five more cabins.
  - His thesis: a normal short-term rental might return about 15% cash-on-cash, but making it distinctive could push that to 25-30%.
  - Why real estate: the downside is limited (worst case he loses maybe 10-30% in a bad outcome, not zero), and it can be handed to family without it falling apart the way an operating company might.
- On construction delays (a house expected to take 18 months now looking like 24), he blames permits and the city as much as the builders and notes that real estate people don't hustle like internet people.

chunks.heading: Real estate financing and tax lessons he picked up
chunks.text:
- Bigger deals can be easier to finance: "the bigger the deal, the easier it is to get financing." On a primary residence the bank leans on your W-2 income, but on larger buildings (he guesses about $5M or eight-plus units) the building itself is the collateral and banks often underwrite it.
- He found out late that he could borrow tens of millions at around a 1% interest rate by clicking a button, using his balance sheet. He admits this mostly works if you are already rich and says it's why the system favors the wealthy.
- Cost segregation (accelerated depreciation) was something he had just learned about and was excited by. His discussion partner explained that real estate professionals can take depreciation in one year to offset earned income. Sam says he wishes he had been in real estate before the exit.
- Non-recourse agency debt (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac) was raised by the host, not Sam. Sam only says he leverages his balance sheet to invest.

chunks.heading: Why internet businesses beat other options, and his one action step
chunks.text:
- Sam's realization about building online: "I can just write something and people will pay me to read it. Or I can just sell information or pixels... I'm like Picasso. Just give me a can of paint and a canvas and I'm going to create something that creates wealth out of thin air." Learning this felt like finally getting glasses.
- Early path: his parents ran a produce brokerage (buy a million dollars of onions from a farmer, arrange a trucker, sell to Walmart for $1.1M, keep about $100K). He worked for Mike Wolfe of American Pickers, ran a hot dog stand as his first licensed business, and left school to move to San Francisco after cold emailing Airbnb's founder.
- His one action step for anyone seeking financial success: "Make a list of 50 people who you admire who are way out of your league and cold email all of them and keep following up until they tell you to F off."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle grew to roughly 2M daily email readers and sold to HubSpot by starting every piece of content with distribution, riding conversations already happening on Reddit and Hacker News, and writing authentically for one niche. He also admits the biggest mistake was under-spending on growth once the machine worked.

chunks.heading: How Sam launched The Hustle with a stunt post and content-marketing "side door" traffic
chunks.text:
- Sam started The Hustle as a conference business. With no money for ads, he blogged about the speakers to get attendees, and it became profitable.
- He then decided to become a media company and announced it with a post saying he had $500,000 and would build the business "watch us blow all the money." He used a smug photo with his eyes closed on purpose because "it's going to get clicks."
- His second post was about a guy making $60,000 a month selling Kindle books on picking up women. The method: find top sellers, have them rewritten in the Philippines to get past plagiarism checks, pay $5 for a sexy title, pay for reviews, and put "best-selling author" on LinkedIn.
- To launch with a bang, The Hustle copied the method as a joke. It picked romance novels because they have the largest liquidity on Amazon (loads of new titles, readers who eat them up). It made a werewolf-in-the-military title, used Fiverr for a new title and headline, paid people to upload it, and hit the top of its category.
- Romance bloggers got angry and shared it widely. It hit the top of many subreddits, including the self-publishing subreddit.
- Harlequin, a major romance publisher, sent a cease and desist. A call with its lawyer resolved it: add a comment to the post, remove the book from the Amazon page, and apologize to the author.
- Results: with zero backlinks and zero traffic on a freshly bought TheHustle.co, the first week brought about 500,000 visitors and 10,000 email subscribers. The first year brought roughly 150,000 to 200,000 subscribers with no ad spend. He says "that strategy still works."
- Lessons he took away:
  - Look less douchey, because the persona wasn't him and he suffered the consequences.
  - Write like you speak, even if it annoys some people. Big companies can't do this because of committees.
  - Be "a missionary, not a mercenary."
  - This style of content works, so keep doing it.
- The Hustle still publishes these stunt-style posts every Sunday, hundreds of them. Often, not always, they go viral. A strong post gets 5 to 10 million views.

chunks.heading: The distribution-first content cycle
chunks.text:
- Sam starts with distribution, before any article idea. The cycle runs: who do I want to reach, where are they, what medium do they come from, what is the headline, and last, what is the story and what emotion will it make someone feel.
- Most people start at the story. He saves it for last, though he often hears a story first (like the Southern guy in a Ramones shirt who runs a $30 million commodities newsletter with his son) and then works out the headline and where it would get popular.
- Audience locations he names:
  - Tech people: Twitter, which is having a resurgence.
  - Nerdy people: Reddit and Hacker News.
  - Fitness: bodybuilding.com or fitness subreddits.
- He says "most people... just say, we need users, write a blog post. Unfortunately it's not that simple."
- This approach is not search-optimized. It suits someone with no backlinks and no name, who can't rank. He says it can piss some people off, which helps the group who loves you become obsessed.
- His principle: "niches make riches." He appeals to one group of people and goes very hard on them.

chunks.heading: Reddit research method for finding post ideas
chunks.text:
- Sam wants to know what his audience is already talking about and then make his own different version of it.
- The steps:
  1. Go to the relevant subreddit (his example is r/fitness, which has 1 million members).
  2. Sort by top posts over the last month.
  3. Scroll about 10 pages (about 10 minutes) to see what the group cares about.
  4. Pick a post, open the comments, and sort by most upvoted.
  5. Spot a highly voted comment to build on. His example: someone shows a kettlebell made from PVC pipe, which becomes a post on building kettlebells with PVC pipe for $8 from Home Depot.
- For the My First Million podcast he does the same on Hacker News: check what's trending, read the comments for the vibe (like people disagreeing with a headline), then form his own opinion.
- For YouTube, which they were starting the next month, he planned to use search data to see what people look for and cover topics where he has strong opinions or intel.
- Not everything comes from this. The rest of the podcast is whatever he finds interesting.
- Another tactic is newsjacking. When Steve Harvey announced the wrong Miss Universe winner, Sam zoomed in on the card, saw it was badly designed, and posted "don't blame Steve Harvey" the next morning with a redesign. It ranked on Google News and got 500,000 views. He says the goal is to be different, not better.
- Early on he had to tap into conversations already happening. With 2 million subscribers, The Hustle can now call things out and start movements.

chunks.heading: Converting traffic into email subscribers
chunks.text:
- Sam called blog posts a "side door." Visitors arrive from Reddit, Hacker News, Facebook or friends, and the goal is to get them to give an email or go to the homepage. TheHustle.co is just an email capture page.
- He tracked daily visitors versus emails captured in a spreadsheet. Early conversion was about 3%, so a million visitors a month means about 30,000 subscribers.
- Pop-ups followed AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action) with unusual copy:
  - "Oh shit, not another pop-up."
  - "Now that I got your attention," then the post title the visitor came to read.
  - "If you don't like the email after a week, call me" (with his phone number), "and I'll Venmo you a dollar."
- He tailored pop-ups to the source. If analytics showed traffic from a Kindle subreddit, he addressed Reddit Kindle readers.
- On WordPress he used the Ad Inserter plugin to put a native-looking note at the bottom of every post: "you got to the bottom... I worked my ass off to entertain you... if you liked it, enter your email here." It compounded because posts kept getting traffic.
- Referral program:
  - Tiers rewarded 5, 10 and 100 referrals.
  - He knew one email subscriber was worth roughly $10 and set rewards so it stayed profitable.
  - Stickers worked best. They designed tens of them, and "people would do everything for a sticker."
  - A candle called "Elon's Musk" crushed it, but they had to stop selling it for breaking rules.
  - Most people reach the first tier of four referrals. Very few reach 1,000, but those few bring as many people as everyone else, and top referrers brought 30,000 subscribers.

chunks.heading: How The Hustle got a ~45% open rate
chunks.text:
- The Hustle sends to about 2 million people a day. Unique open rate is about 45% and total open rate about 65%, which he believes is the highest he's heard of.
- Counterintuitively, sending more raised opens. It started at 28% sending once a week, then went to twice, three times, and finally six days a week.
- Why it works:
  - It's a daily news product that creates a habit.
  - It includes useful roundup content (for a health niche, "the 10 bullet points of what happened in the health world today").
  - It adds personality, like cute updates ("writing from my couch with my cat Whiskers").
  - It adds reliable extras like weather.
  - It uses cliffhangers ("Tomorrow I'm going to be in New York to meet with one of our biggest customers, I'll let you know how it goes").
- Deliverability tactics:
  - Move to a dedicated IP address once you reach roughly 10,000 to 50,000 subscribers. Mailchimp uses shared IPs.
  - Be consistent and send at the same time, never missing.
  - They paid Return Path about $40,000 a year to vouch for them with email providers.
  - Use Litmus before sending to catch spam triggers, like missing image tags or words like "free porn" when covering a story.
  - "The first, most important thing? Fucking good content."
- He segments subscribers as gold, silver and bronze. They know a gold subscriber stays about three years and study what those people read.
- Email is the last channel you can reasonably own. He compares building on Facebook to renting an office whose landlord raises the rent every three months.

chunks.heading: Business model, the exit, and what he'd do differently
chunks.text:
- The Hustle was a media company with four revenue lines:
  - Native ads in the daily email, which Sam says would have been about $20 million in sales this year, an eight-figure business.
  - Trends.co, a paid subscription community with researchers and analysts, which he calls an eight-figure subscription business.
  - Conferences with tens of thousands of attendees, which would have made millions, but there was none this year.
  - The My First Million podcast.
- HubSpot approached them in October and closed the deal in late January, at about the time Sam turned 31. The price was tens of millions of dollars. Sam owned most of the company and raised no VC.
- HubSpot wanted the users, who might eventually buy HubSpot, not the ad business. It shut down the ad department even though The Hustle went into the year with millions of dollars of ads booked.
- Sam's formula for media value: "the quality of people who you have consuming your stuff, multiplied by the number of people, multiplied by your influence over them." 20,000 doctors who run hospitals can be worth more than 30 million 12-year-olds.
- His main regret was being too frugal because he grew up poor and treated the business money as his own:
  - "If you have a machine that turns $1 into $2, you load up a dump truck... and back it into that machine."
  - He hired a $50,000 employee instead of a $120,000 one who would have been more productive.
  - He wasn't aggressive enough with ads once the machine worked.
  - He didn't launch products fast enough.
  - He bought 35 employees' computers on Facebook Marketplace for $500 each.
- His lesson: he should have "defaulted to optimism." He thinks paranoia is good, but you also need confidence. He believes a path to $100 million or more in revenue existed.
- Because he had no money, he was forced to build something people liked organically, so ad money later was "fuel on the fire," not the fire starter. He says both ad-first and organic-first strategies can work. Ads on a weak product just fill a leaky bucket.
- His distribution reasoning: a good product with bad distribution fails, and a bad product with good distribution can win. His example is Heinz ketchup, which beats a better organic ketchup that's in no stores.

chunks.heading: Building a voice: copy hour and selling
chunks.text:
- Before The Hustle, Sam ran a chain of hot dog stands in Nashville called "Southern Sam's Wieners as Big as a Baby's Arm." Hot dogs all taste the same, so he needed a shtick. The promotion: put your baby's arm in a bun with mustard and get a free hot dog.
- He read Robert Cialdini's *Influence* early and learned copywriting through a course from Noah Madora. He had been blogging since he was 18.
- Copywriting is "figuring out what motivates a human being and conveying or creating a solution that makes it easy for them to want to purchase it."
- His practice, "copy hour": one to two hours every day, hand-copying the best examples word for word. He copied *Catcher in the Rye*, Saturday Night Live scripts, movie scripts, the best sales letters of all time, and great blog posts.
- He compares it to learning guitar by playing other people's songs first. After copying enough, he said he could see the patterns, such as what Stephen King does that makes you feel a certain way, and then wrote his own.
- He wasn't an authority on tech when he started. He was a business nerd who lived and breathed it. He says media is hard unless you're obsessed with the topic, because "internet people have the greatest bullshit detector." He would not start a bone broth blog, even though it's a fine business, because he doesn't care about it. He advises against hiring Upwork writers for keyword filler.

chunks.heading: Managing writers and hiring them
chunks.text:
- Sam says content teams are hard to build and that they hire quickly and fire quickly. They give new hires four weeks to show it works, and say so upfront.
- He hired editor-in-chief Brad Wolverton from NerdWallet (previously the Washington Post) to manage writers.
- On managing writers:
  - "Everyone's a diva. The best ones are divas."
  - They are often late, submit at the last minute, and don't know on Wednesday what they'll publish Friday. He says that's normal and often a sign of good ones.
  - Be patient. Let creative people create as long as they follow most of the rules, hit deadlines and hit goals.
- Example: a writer put "fuck" in every sentence of a piece about the Instagram account "Fuck Jerry," and Goldman Sachs, who sponsored the newsletter, refused to pay for the ad. Sam told the writer he supported it.
- His hiring method: troll Twitter, LinkedIn and publications he loves. He emails or DMs a writer saying he loved a specific article, follows up three weeks later describing the opportunity ("not nearly as prestigious as where you are now, but pretty exciting for this reason"), and says "worst case scenario, you've got a new friend in the industry."

chunks.heading: My First Million podcast: research and growth
chunks.text:
- The podcast gets about a million listens a month. Episodes get from 30,000 to over 100,000 downloads. It's about two years old, and he expects over 100,000 per episode by year three. They had spent nothing on growth and were about to start spending heavily.
- He says it's the hardest thing he has grown. His caveats on why it's hard to copy: The Hustle gave them a built-in audience to tell, and his co-host Sean is "world-class."
- Episodes get more downloads when he does more research. They now have researchers, and Sam spends a full day building a big document before recording.
- The format: he hears a story (like the $30 million subscription business with two people), gets the numbers, deconstructs how it works, and tells Sean. Sean relates it to a similar business and they jump from topic to topic.
- He is always filing away ideas from people he meets, so he can connect them during research.

chunks.heading: Investing criteria and deal flow
chunks.text:
- Sam runs a small fund with a partner who ran the viral site Little Things (200 million monthly uniques). He has invested $10 to $12 million in 40 to 50 startups.
- Since selling to HubSpot he likes subscription revenue and enterprise software ("so boring, but so lucrative"). The business needs to grow about 3x a year for the first two or three years, which correlates with a meaningful exit. He owns a tiny piece, so it has to get big.
- He looks for grit. He asks for every project someone has worked on and passes on anyone who jumps from thing to thing, preferring one or two long stays.
- He always asks how the product will be distributed. Does the team have a sales leader who can build a team, or a content-marketing person? He invested in Hiten Shah's company because Hiten is a content marketing pro who gets small businesses via SEO.
- Returns example: of his first 20 investments, a $15,000 check became $600,000 and a $20,000 check became about $200,000, totaling about $800,000. Until then he had invested only $200,000 to $300,000 of his own money, so two of twenty paid for the whole set.

chunks.heading: Distribution for a new product: the community playbook
chunks.text:
- When asked how a home office accessories business should get attention, Sam said to start with Reddit, with Facebook groups as the second-best option at the moment, and not with Men's Health. Editors there get their ideas from Reddit and Twitter.
- Playbook:
  1. Join the relevant subreddit.
  2. Contribute genuinely, such as photos of your desk setup, a review of a chair, an offer to answer questions.
  3. Make about 10 posts that don't promote anything.
  4. On the 11th, either say you've followed the group for a long time, run one of these companies, and are offering members a discount, or share a problem you noticed everyone is getting wrong.
- Example of the second angle: "your elbows are in a horrible place on your desk," with a post explaining why and how to fix it.
- Paste the whole article into the Reddit post, then say the link is below if people want it. He says it "always gets tons of clicks."
- After you have traction there, email the big publications.
- His rule: avoid bullshitting, provide value a ton, then do your thing.

chunks.heading: Mindset and emotional management
chunks.text:
- Sam says that 90% of the time things suck and 10% are awesome, and the 10% keeps him going.
- Most problems were about people, such as whether to fire someone. When the pandemic hit, he thought for the first three months that the business would go to zero.
- He quit drinking because he had a drinking problem.
- His view: building a business to $100 million in revenue is "very doable in most industries" and intellectually you can write down the steps. You do them consistently eight hours a day for ten years, which also needs some luck. He says the game is 100% emotional.
- His routine: meditation every morning, exercise, vitamins, therapy, self-help reading. All of it exists to keep his mood calm and steady, and he spends most of his non-work energy on it.
- Earlier plan: after reading *How to Get Rich* by Felix Dennis and a Mark Cuban story, he wanted by 30 to have enough money that it was never an issue again. He sold at 31.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Parr explains how The Hustle grew from a conference blog to a 1.5M-subscriber newsletter without ad spend, and when he started paying for growth. He also covers learning copywriting by copying, spotting attention arbitrage, and growing My First Million with ads and fan-made clips.

chunks.heading: Sam's path from event to newsletter to The Hustle
chunks.text:
- Sam sold his previous company and was "looking for something to do." He started Hustle Con (a San Francisco conference) "as a way to kill time" and expected the first one to lose money.
- Event 1 made about $50-60K in six weeks. After a three-month cross-country motorcycle trip, event 2 made roughly $150-200K against about $17K of expenses.
- He did not want to run conferences ("crazy high stress... so much that can go wrong"). He decided to build a content site and use email to make it popular.
- The Hustle began as a blog plus emails announcing new posts. Then he realized the post should live only in the email so people don't have to click off.
- It became a daily email on April 19-20, 2016.
- He chose email because he had seen it work for internet marketers since he was a teen. He recalls the long-form text emails from David DeAngelo's "Double Your Dating" list, which led him to buy a roughly $14 book.
- His insight: he could already sell with his voice (door to door, a hot dog stand). Email was the same selling, "but I only have to write it one time" and can send it to an infinite number of people.
- Many people thought the idea was dumb. An investor friend told him it was "not that good of an idea." Sam trusted his internet-marketer friends who were succeeding on email.
- Hacker News and Reddit drove traffic to the hustle's site. About 3% of visitors entered their email.
- For the first three years, roughly the first $500K in revenue, he spent almost nothing on ads (at most $500-$1,000 total).
- He sent the 3% frequent, interesting emails about the speakers. Blog posts like "How Buffer bootstrapped to $20 million in revenue" grew the list to 10-15K in a couple of months.
- He was 22-24, knew no one, and got attention with a plain site and good copy. Example headline: "The brown Don Draper is coming to Hustle Con," about his friend Neville Medora, then an explanation of what copywriting is and what attendees would learn.

chunks.heading: Copywriting as his most important skill
chunks.text:
- Sam names the ability to control his emotions and copywriting as his most important skills. He says "most everything we did was rooted in copywriting."
- His method is copy work: copying great writing by hand. Musicians learn by copying songs and cooks by copying recipes, so you learn "the texture of what makes a good song."
- Once you see patterns, you know the rules, when to follow them and when to break them, and you develop your own style by stealing from many sources.
- He built a $50 course called "Copy That" with annotated examples of copywriting he likes and why it works. He charges $50 because people are more likely to follow through if they pay.
- Before writing anything, he decides what vibe he wants. He then picks an author or sales page with that vibe and copies a bit by hand to get into the zone.
- When he gets marketing emails, he often replies to ask whether the email is working.
- He says copying without data can mislead, since pages change. Replying to ask about results is his workaround.

chunks.heading: Asking questions and getting information from people
chunks.text:
- Sam has asked questions since childhood. He never took for granted that buildings or companies are "just there"; a person with an idea convinced others. If he can figure out how that was done, he can repeat the pattern.
- He asks uncomfortable questions (revenue, cost) by modeling. He shares his own number first: "I made this much last year. How about you?"
- Intent matters. If your energy is clearly curious and well-meaning, you can "pretty much get away with anything." Humor helps, as in dating: "if I can make a girl laugh, I can get away with... flirting pretty hard."
- He triangulates instead of asking directly. Walking into a $5M house, he asks "do you have to go to a special bank to get like a jumbo loan?" and follows the answer until he knows how much they put down and whether they're stretched.
- He deliberately guesses wrong to get corrected. He says "What is this, like an $8 million house?" or "like a $2 million house?" and the person corrects him with the real number.
- Reading the person: if they want to brag, he flatters them and lets them. If they're nervous, he acts like what they say is no big deal.
- He says billionaires are not nervous-making. At Hustle Con he sat with founders of WeWork, OA Travel and ClassPass plus Casey Neistat, and they complained about the same things he did (firing someone, fear it won't work, stage fright). "You're not a million times different than I am."
- He was nervous only to interview Andrew Huberman and Ariel Helwani, because he admired them and wanted to impress them.
- Wealth alone doesn't impress him. He says that given 25-30 years of dedication, risk-taking and some luck, he is confident he could build a $100M/year revenue business in most industries. He is impressed by bold, courageous visions, with MLK and Jeff Bezos as examples.

chunks.heading: Research habits: biographies, footers and newspaper archives
chunks.text:
- Interview prep is light: he tweets that he's about to interview someone to collect question ideas. He sometimes reads the guest's Wikipedia page and every citation, scans comments on their work, and avoids questions they're asked often.
- He reads one or two biographies a week. For each, he uses newspapers.com (about $10/month, an archive of old newspapers) to see what was said at the time.
- Example: for Dan Gilbert (Rock Financial, now Rocket Mortgage), he found the first mention of Gilbert, then read articles from three or four years before the IPO. The aim is to understand how people perceived him and how confident he was before the outcome was known: "this person wasn't that great early on," which he finds inspiring.
- He follows rabbit holes from small triggers. A huge building on a road trip led him to the website footer (copyright owner: Tyson), then the acquisition price, the founder, the founder's security company, and so on.
- He reads Wikipedia pages and their cited sources, and checks website footers (including advertising links for traffic numbers).

chunks.heading: Podcasting growth and paid acquisition for My First Million
chunks.text:
- Sam says newsletters moved quickly, and starting The Hustle would be harder today because competition and acquisition costs have risen. The Hustle got to 100,000 subscribers organically before they started buying ads.
- He calls podcast tooling "still pretty shitty." Unlike email, he can't tell who a listener is or what they cost. They use Chartable (with deep links), which he finds hard to understand, and Megaphone.
- He is candid that he doesn't know why My First Million works: "I don't know... We worked hard on making good content." They had about 2 million monthly uniques around December/January.
- They had just started buying ads. Plan: Jordan Harbinger showed him how. Harbinger spent $400K in year one, $800K in year two and $1.3M in year three, and earned more than that in podcast ad revenue, so it was profitable.
- Sam's ad-buying playbook:
  - Buy ads on other podcasts, from about $500 to $5,000-$20,000, track which ones work, and repeat the winners.
  - Buy on podcast players too (Castbox, Spotify, Stitcher).
  - Skip agencies when starting. Make a spreadsheet of 30-50 podcasts with a good audience and reach out one by one, including swaps ("we'll mention you, you mention us").
  - Track results per source.
- Video: Twitter videos looked good but "didn't drive much views" and gave no ROI. About 95% of views come from podcast players and 5% from YouTube, and he is struggling to grow YouTube.
- What worked was a fan contest: $5,000 to one to three people (judged on views and creativity) who made TikTok clips from their YouTube clips. It produced about 20 million views in about 10 days, and friends started saying "you're all over my feed."
- Result: dozens of fan accounts, and the main account reached about 37,000 followers and 600,000 likes. Mistake: he gave two different hashtags (MFM clip and MFM clips).
- He would repeat the contest, expects diminishing returns, and would consider putting a few contest winners on retainer.

chunks.heading: Avoid building a prison: content creation and delegation
chunks.text:
- His warning to creators is "make sure you don't build a prison."
- A daily email is a huge amount of work. At first The Hustle was built around him, which makes traction easier because people feel they know you. He couldn't sustain it, so he hired people and "can make money in my sleep." He thinks the product got a little worse as a result.
- Creators must decide whether to delegate or be the only person. Being the only person is fine, but know it is "grind mode" for years. Casey Neistat stopped daily vlogs, and the Paul brothers struggled with it.
- To make it big in content you need to ship every day, or at minimum every week. For most people listening, "you're pretty much gonna have to make shit every day."
- Ways around it: hire people, don't cover current events, and don't tie yourself to a daily schedule for too long.

chunks.heading: When and how to spend on paid acquisition
chunks.text:
- Sam's mentor Kevin Ryan (Business Insider) gave him an analogy. If a machine turned $1 into $1.20, you would "get a dump truck, fill it with money and back it up into that machine." Paid acquisition is that machine.
- Start spending once you understand LTV, your cash flow cycle and how long payback takes. It took about 10 months to a year to figure that out, then he "started spending hard."
- Mistake: he was too frugal and should have spent more, because Facebook ads cost far more now. TikTok ads are cheap now. "Those windows close."
- Channel concentration follows an 8020 rule: about 80% of users come from one or two channels. For The Hustle, 100% of the first 100,000 users came from blogging, then Facebook ads (he could spend $1.50 to make $10).
- He compares to NerdWallet, which gets 80-90% of revenue from Google searches like "best credit card."
- Product Hunt-style channels (a bunch of small publishers) can be cheaper but need people to manage each relationship. One person can manage hundreds of millions of dollars on Facebook.
- Calculating LTV for a creator: measure revenue per post. Example: post to a million people at $300 product price with click and conversion rates, and earn $100K, so $100K per million. Test it several times, then work out what you can spend to acquire a follower.
- For ad-based creators: a million followers at $30 CPM is $30,000 per post. Divide to get revenue per user per post, and spend below that. Be willing to go a year without profit on an acquired user, and keep checking weekly that conversion matches your assumptions. Put ad spend on a good rewards credit card.
- Even a small craft business shouldn't guess. Know what you make per person so you know what you can spend.

chunks.heading: Platform picks and attention arbitrage (2022)
chunks.text:
- Sam looks for arbitrage between the supply and demand of attention. LinkedIn once had more viewers than creators, so posts were shown widely and he got "millions of impressions" until the gap dried up.
- In 2022, his top pick was TikTok. It has a lot of supply but still a gap, because it's good at matching content to viewers.
- He also likes long-form YouTube (20-minute videos). A creator's ad value is roughly audience quality, times audience size, times influence over them.
- Illustration: 1,000 billionaires shopping for a 747 jet are more valuable than 10,000,012-year-olds in Missouri.
- Influence correlates with time spent consuming you. He just watched a 40-minute review of a Ford Raptor and now feels he knows the reviewer, so he'd buy whatever he recommends.
- He prefers the longer-form treadmill for creative fulfilment and because long-form is more evergreen than a TikTok that disappears.

What’s the difference between a $10m, $100m, and $1b lifestyle?

Asked this question in Hampton's Slack community since we have people worth $10m - $2b.

A few takeaways from the 50+ replies:

$50k – $100k liquid
 
• The first “I feel rich” for many in 20s. 
• Bills stop hurting. You breathe.
• $1M net worth rarely changes anything. In high-cost cities, it’s just “comfortable professional.” Still very income-dependent.

$10M liquid - This is the first real unlock.

• Safety net feels permanent
• You stop looking at the right side of the menu
• Business-class by default, 5 hotels when you want
• You can cover friends’ flights to make trips happen
• Life doesn’t run you anymore.

$20M–$25M liquid: 

• “I can spend $50k/mo forever and still compound.”
• Nicer primary home (or rent ultra-nice; fewer ownership headaches)
• Staff for convenience (nanny, cleaners)
• Family support start to be normal, not “splurge”

$50M liquid 

• Cash flow is thick and hard to fully redeploy.
• 2nd homes, extended travel
• Serious privacy planning begins
• You’re learning trusts, tax vehicles, and who to not trust

$100M: 

• Life becomes frictionless.
• Fly private often (some buy; many rent because ownership is work)
• Full household team + exec assistants + specialists
• Family office(s), capital allocation becomes a job
• You choose projects; problems get solved without you

Past $100M
• personal lifestyle doesn’t change much—scale and privacy do.
• Land for privacy buffers
• Private gyms/courts/spas at home
• You’ll never fly commercial unless you want to

$1 billion 
• Money becomes institutional.
• You never see a bill
• Global properties, fully private travel
• Governments, universities, and CEOs court you
• It’s legacy season: foundations, endowments, monuments

A few real anecdotes from the thread:

• A billionaire bought a pro sports team mid-flight on his jet. His right-hand guy became COO.
• A friend group dropped $200k–$300k on a yacht week just to get everyone together.
• Multiple members set up dual family offices (JPM + independent) to manage life + investments.

The biggest trap everyone warned about:

• “Coming into money without accomplishing anything is a curse.”
• Lottery-winner energy breaks people. Purpose > purchases.

Cash flow > net worth (psychologically).
• Even people with $50M–$100M feel “poor” during low-cashflow years. Meaning, even if you have a high net worth -- if your business income goes away even if you don't need it, it feels horrible. Mentally brutal.  

What actually brings joy at scale:

• Buying back time (coaches, chefs, pilots, concierge)
• Funding memories (fly the whole crew, pick up every tab)
• Being present (one member took a year as a stay-at-home dad - “wouldn’t trade it for anything”)

What gets old fast:
• More “stuff” to manage
• Identity tied to net worth
• Chasing bigger dopamine (toys) instead of deeper meaning (health, family, service, community)

--

What I do is to get good men [as employees], and I never give them orders. My directions seldom go beyond suggestions. Here in the morning I get reports from them. Within an hour I have disposed of everything, sent out all of my suggestions, the day's work is done.

Something I’ve been thinking about a lot lately:
Most decisions are small. 

What’s for lunch. Which app to cancel. Whether to take the meeting at 3pm or 4pm.

Tiny stuff that moves the needle maybe 1%. 

But every few years, you get a choice that acts like a lever. 

One decision that tilts everything that comes after.

For example, in 2012 I moved to San Francisco after googling "where rea internet companies started?".

in July of 2014 I quit drinking. Everything change. 

In 2016 I started a newsletter that I eventually sold and changed my life.

However, what’s hard is big decisions don’t always look important when you’re making them.

They can just show up disguised as regular Tuesday choices.

- Join the gym or stay on the couch

- Start the side project or keep watching Netflix.

- Cold email that person you admire or scroll twitter instead (i’ve made so many huge connections over cold email, including with my co-founder Joe!).

Small decisions compound daily. 

Big decisions compound for decades. 

Here’s how to spot the big ones: The choice makes you slightly uncomfortable. 

If it feels too easy, it’s probably not the lever you’re looking for. 

It involves other people who are ahead of where you want to be. 

Growth happens fastest when you’re the least experienced person in the room. 

This makes you feel nervous almost. And there’s no immediate payoff. 

The best decisions pay dividends for years, not quarters. It costs something real - time, money, comfort, or pride. 

Free rarely changes everything. 

Most people miss these moments because they’re optimizing for the wrong thing. They want guarantees. 

They want to see the ROI spreadsheet. They want proof it’ll work before they try. But leverage doesn’t work that way.

I think about this a lot because I see it with Hampton. 

Many join thinking they need help with some specific business problem. 

Should I ask my co-founder to leave? How do I price this new product? Is this investor term sheet fair?

Fair enough. Those are real problems.

But the actual value isn’t solving one problem. 

It’s having 7 other people like you in your corner for the next thousand problems. 

One choice - surrounding yourself with people who’ve been where you want to go - influences every choice that comes after.

Anyway, that’s my take. Most choices are small. 

A few change everything. 

Obviously the hard part is recognizing which is which.

I sold my company for over $40 million when I was 31.

Here’s every idea I tried before my big win:

1. In high school I made $2,500 one summer flipping seniors’ used sports gear on eBay.

2. At 20, I launched a hot dog stand called Southern Sam’s: Wieners as Big as a Baby’s Arm. Made up to $1,000 a day. Learned how to sell - and how to blow all my money on beer.

3. That same year, I started an online liquor store selling rare whiskey. It lasted three months before a lawyer told me I wasn't doing things correctly. Still made $10K in profit.

4. In San Francisco, I started a weekly business book club called The Anti-MBA. Couldn't figure out how to monetize it, but met lifelong friends.

5. Tried selling an accountability program to The Anti-MBA. $20/month and you were paired with another member to encourage you to read a book. No one wanted it.

6. In 2014, I hosted Bootstrap Live, a mini event interviewing three founders. 150 people showed up. Made $1,090.

7. Then came Bunk - parties for people finding roommates. We funded it with $15k, it didn't succeed and got acqui-hired 9 months later. 

8. We turned Bunk into a Tinder-style roommate app. Tens of thousands of users, zero revenue. Should’ve just made it a dating app - that’s what people used it for anyway.

9. Next, The Miracle Craigslist Template. A simple email script for finding apartments on Craiglist. Made $500–$1,000 a month for two years.

10. Itch Juice - a poison ivy treatment. I bulk-bought generic ointment and rebranded it as I knew I could buy Google ads for cheap. Shut it down after two months. Dumb idea, smart lesson: schemes are dumb.

11. Hosted a weekend copywriting class with @nevmed. We each made $10k.

12. Then came Hustle Con - a conference for startup founders. Made $40k in profit. Ran it three more times, revenue doubled each time.

13. I saved $300k and pivoted Hustle Con into a media company called The Hustle. Spent six months writing hundreds of articles. Traction was good, but consistently getting traffic was hard.

14. The big one: we pivoted again - from a blog to a newsletter. Biz model was so much better. It didn’t feel huge at first, but it was a rocket ship. $12m in revenue by year four, sold the company when I was 31. Changed my life.

15. Inside The Hustle we launched Trends - a $300-a-year community for entrepreneurs. Great revenue, tough margins. Lesson: low price, high volume = hard business.

16. The Hustle expanded our events. $1.5M in revenue, almost no profit. Then Covid killed it overnight.

17. The Hustle published My First Million - a podcast that now has 700+ episodes and millions of downloads.

18. Bought a ranch in Texas to turn into an Airbnb. Broke even. Bought other real estate...lost money on all them!

And now…Hampton. Easily the most impactful. 

We create peer groups and chapters for founders doing at least $3m in revenue. We have a team of 20, mostly in NYC where I live, and change our member's lives.

Lessons from all this:

1. Stay focused. Many times I had something good but didn't stay focused!

2. Everything's hard, even when its working!

3. Have smart friends, peers around you who you can rely on to hold you accountable, keep you humble, and hear you out.

How to write better than 99% of people:

- Object then action: “the boy hit the ball” is better than “the ball was hit by the boy.” Both sentences mean the same, but it’s easier to imagine the object (the boy) before the action (the hitting). All brains work that way. (Notice I didn’t say, “That is the way all brains work”?)

- Get rid of needless words. How do you know what’s important? If you remove a word, but the sentence still makes sense, then it’s useless. Notice I didn’t say “If you can remove the word then it’s useless.” “Can” was useless.

- Don't use adverbs. Stephen King once said, “adverbs pave the way to hell.” Adverbs are anything that describes an verb. He ran fast is the same thing as he ran very fast. The word "very" is an adverb, and it’s useless.

- Write simply. 4-7th grade reading level. Use the Hemingway app to help (its free).

- Hit the reader. You then make the first sentence punch the reader in the face. Read the first sentence of this post. Its simple but sharp.

Do that and you're better than most.

Something I've noticed:

You get done doing something creative at work. 

Writing copy, designing something, whatever.

Then you show it to coworkers for feedback. 

80% of the feedback is nitpicky, unimportant stuff that just takes too much time to fix or kills the creative, unique stuff that make the thing cool. 

I try my hardest to do a few things:

1. If I'm the creator, I purposely leave in a mistake or obvious part of the work. This way they have an easy thing to critique and I can do it and they feel heard.

2. Often I ignore most the feedback tbh. I listen to some people, but only if they have a history of being right, are highly skilled, or smarter than me on the topic. I used to listen to everyone then the output was this group think bullshit. 

3. When I'm the giving feedback: if something major needs to be changed, I say it. If its minor, I say "i would do this, but up to you" or I don't even say anything. I want people to have room to explore. 

4. I make it clear who the decision maker is and let the creator know who's in charge. If them, I try to say "my opinion is X, but you're the boss". 

5. If I'm giving feedback and its major, I try to be blunt on the work, but kind to the person.

We’ve now done 25 episodes of Moneywise where wealthy people share EVERYTHING about their finances.

Their actual numbers, regrets, fears, family drama. Stuff they'd normally never say publicly.

-@profgalloway: "I often joke that my success in my 20s and 30s cost me my hair and my first marriage and that it was worth it. I have a lot of balance now because I didn't have much when I was young. So, you can have it all, you just can't have it all at once.”

-“Jennifer” (who was anonymous) walked away from millions in her divorce despite her lawyer begging her not to. Why? "There's more money where that came from. Cut your losses and bet on yourself and just move on and build your business.”

@mikebeckhamsm: “giving is, in many ways, the antidote to the cancer that we have inside of ourselves. It is a thing that naturally helps keep in check.” (he’s worth $200m and tries to donate 50% of his income every year).

-@GoodInside (Dr. Becky): “Frustration, tolerance, is actually one of the most important skills for life. Not only to avoid entitlement, it's actually the skill that helps you learn.”

Some of the patterns I noticed:

-Most people who retired early got depressed
-“Enough” doesn’t exist for most people. Many people worth 9 figures are still working. But for those who stopped, focusing on family, their health, and giving back was key.
-If a parent, most are terrified of ruining their kids with their wealth
-Most regrets weren't about money lost, but time lost with family
-The happiest ones often lived simply

My biggest takeaway: Past a certain point (and there’s most certainly a number for that), one should focus on serving others more than earning.

I’ve been building communities (online and offline) for +13 years. 

A few things I’ve been thinking about lately. 

Sponsors. Don’t do it (in most cases). Charge customers membership fees and don’t let sponsors muddy the waters. Communities are sacred. Sponsors aren’t. We don’t do it. Sponsoring a podcast, fine. But community is for members. If you’re an online platform, ads maybe are ok. 

 Integrity. Speaking of, if you have a bar for who gets in and what values the community stands for, don’t bend the rules for anyone.this is hard! We have thousands who apply and let in a tiny fraction (4-5% maybe). It sucks turning down money. But If you say admissions are X but the sales person is willing to bend the rules, likely bad sign. If someone breaks the rules, regardless who they are, punish them. 

Be suspicious of fast growth early on. A community can last 100 years and make you a billionaire. Great business. But early on, growth should likely be slower than you want. Community is so easy to sell, particularly if you’re new. But so hard to maintain. You need to indoctrinate early members carefully. Help them feel special. Then slowly add. It will take years. Or decades. But will be worth it. 

Decentralization. Just about every big, powerful, successful community I know of is decentralized. Meaning there are local nodes that sorta call the shots, create the culture, then a centralized hq that creates the infrastructure. This feels unnatural because you won’t to control everything. Don’t listen to that urge. 

I’ve made all these mistakes. And will make many more (these examples included). But these are the things I’m thinking about lately.

I knew nothing when I started a media company (The Hustle). Nothing! Had never worked in the industry, didn’t know what CPM meant, didn’t know a single person who worked in the field.

So I reached out to a bunch of successful media founders, hoping they’d guide me.

But how on earth do you find someone super successful to give you, a piss ant with next to nothing to give in exchange, some good life changing advice?

I ended up finding this guy, Kevin Ryan, who, I think, is a billionaire. He started Gilt, MongoDB, and Business Insider.

I found his email and sent him a note asking to talk. Zero reply. So I kept following up with updates on the business and my life. Revenue growth, issues in the business, how I was feeling about it all. Almost like an investor update, but written in an entertaining way. 

After doing this for months, I finally got a reply saying he was available in NYC for a very quick meeting

“What a coincidence,” I told him, "I happen to be in NYC, let’s do it!”

I was in SF at the time. And obviously didn’t have a trip planned to NYC but I booked the next flight anyway.

And it worked! Kevin met with me and in our short meeting gave me very needle moving advice that had a huge impact on my business and life.

This habit of googling cool people and then cold emailing them, it likely was the #1 most impactful thing on my career. I’d cold email them, get no reply, then follow up with business/life updates until I got a reply. I made the emails fun to read and people would get invested and think “ok, this guy might be legit, I’ll give him a chance.”

That’s how I met my Hampton cofounder Joe - I googled something generic like “fast growing media startups” and then I asked to hang out. We ended up becoming close buddies, after 6 years of being friends, cofounders.

In fact, this is how I met Shaan!

Nowadays, Twitter makes this much easier. Use the same profile picture across gmail, social, etc…post a ton, reply a ton, and people get to know you.

Moral of the story - nobody is out of reach. Make the ask…and follow up, follow up, follow up!

You might know about QSBS (but surprisingly a lot of founders don’t). You don’t pay taxes on the first $10m when you sell your company OR 10x your basis, whichever is bigger.

The key is the second part of that.

Here’s a real scenario about a founder:

-Started as an LLC (was losing money early on, helped offset other income)
-Company started making money
-Converted to C-Corp when company was worth ~$40m
-Key part: stayed under the $50m QSBS asset cap during conversion

Because they converted at $40m valuation, they can now use the 10x basis exemption.

That means they could exclude up to $400m from capital gains taxes on their exit (10x their $40m basis).

They were an LLC for 2+ years before learning about this rule. Pure accident that's gonna save them hundreds of millions in taxes if they exit.

A few things if you're thinking about this:

-Most impactful for bigger exits
-5 year holding clock starts at C-Corp conversion
-Gotta be under $50m valuation before the conversion
-Should have good lawyers/accountants

I've got a buddy who sold his company for ~$70m.

So, it was a massive financial success. 

However, he HATED the life he made for himself while running it.

His company felt like a prison:

- 16-hour days. Skipped his honeymoon. 
- Micromanaged everything. 
- Built his entire identity around the selling.

After selling, like all of us idiots, he started his second company.

My buddy, btw, is @jnpayne.

But for his next company, he made a bunch of rules. Rules so that he'd be happier during the build process.

- The hours were 8 to 5. 
- No weekends. 
- Fully remote. 
- No meetings where he wasn't essential.
- And a month-long family trip to Europe every summer with his wife and three kids.

Recently, he did something super cool: moved his entire family of five to Spain.

Other things Josh did that I like:

- he removed himself from operational meetings
- scaled every 1:1 to monthly
- muted Slack channels where he wasn't essential
- assigned owners to projects and stopped poking around. 

His words: "I frankly just dropped the ball on a lot of things."

But...it seems to be working. 

His new company, its called Onward, and they're very profitable with 20 people.

I LOVE hearing stories like this.

Because the entire point of this business thing, at least for me, is to put your dent into the world but doing it your way.

On twitter, podcasts, etc...there are so many rules that we take for granted. So we often just fit into a box of business building. 

But I've done so many interviews with baller founders + see it in Hampton...there are 10,000's ways to kill it.
